practice.stem: A language-learning app for children in Malaysia counts vowels in words.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write pseudocode for the function CountVowels(Word : STRING) RETURNS INTEGER. The function returns the number of vowels (a, e, i, o, u) in Word. Vowels may be upper or lower case.
parts.answer:
FUNCTION CountVowels(Word : STRING) RETURNS INTEGER
   DECLARE Count, Index : INTEGER
   DECLARE Ch : CHAR
   Count ← 0
   FOR Index ← 1 TO LENGTH(Word)
      Ch ← LCASE(MID(Word, Index, 1))
      IF Ch = 'a' OR Ch = 'e' OR Ch = 'i' OR Ch = 'o' OR Ch = 'u' THEN
         Count ← Count + 1
      ENDIF
   NEXT Index
   RETURN Count
ENDFUNCTION
parts.working: 1 mark each: function header and ENDFUNCTION with Count initialised to 0; loop from 1 to LENGTH(Word); extract each character with MID; correct test for all five vowels in both cases (e.g. using LCASE); increment count and RETURN Count (not OUTPUT).

practice.stem: A cinema in Lahore sells tickets through a kiosk.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write pseudocode that asks the user for the number of tickets, repeats the input until it is a whole number from 1 to 8 inclusive, then outputs the total cost. Each ticket costs Rs 750. Assume the input is always an integer.
parts.answer:
DECLARE Tickets : INTEGER
REPEAT
   OUTPUT "Enter number of tickets (1 to 8)"
   INPUT Tickets
UNTIL Tickets >= 1 AND Tickets <= 8
OUTPUT "Total cost: Rs ", Tickets * 750
parts.working: 1 mark prompt and INPUT inside a loop; 1 mark loop repeats while invalid (REPEAT…UNTIL or WHILE with pre-input); 1 mark correct range condition 1 to 8 inclusive; 1 mark output of Tickets × 750 after the loop.

parts.answer: Total cost: Rs 2250 (0 and 9 are rejected).

practice.stem: A weather station in Murree stores the rainfall, in mm, for each day of a 30-day month in the global array Rainfall[1:30] OF REAL.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write pseudocode for a procedure WettestDay() that finds the largest value in Rainfall and outputs the day number and the rainfall on that day. If two days have the same largest value, output the first one.
parts.answer:
PROCEDURE WettestDay()
   DECLARE Day, MaxDay : INTEGER
   MaxDay ← 1
   FOR Day ← 2 TO 30
      IF Rainfall[Day] > Rainfall[MaxDay] THEN
         MaxDay ← Day
      ENDIF
   NEXT Day
   OUTPUT "Day ", MaxDay, " had ", Rainfall[MaxDay], " mm"
ENDPROCEDURE
parts.working: 1 mark procedure header/end; 1 mark initialise max (to first element, or index 1); 1 mark loop through all 30 elements; 1 mark compare with strict > so that the first is kept, updating index; 1 mark output day number and rainfall after the loop.

practice.stem: A science club in Kampala records temperatures from a classroom thermometer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write pseudocode that inputs temperatures until the value −999 is entered. −999 is not a temperature. The program then outputs the average temperature, or the message "No data" if no temperatures were entered.
parts.answer:
DECLARE Temp, Total : REAL
DECLARE Count : INTEGER
Total ← 0
Count ← 0
INPUT Temp
WHILE Temp <> -999
   Total ← Total + Temp
   Count ← Count + 1
   INPUT Temp
ENDWHILE
IF Count = 0 THEN
   OUTPUT "No data"
ELSE
   OUTPUT Total / Count
ENDIF

practice.stem: A courier company in Lahore gives each parcel a tracking code.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write pseudocode for the function IsValidCode(Code : STRING) RETURNS BOOLEAN. A valid code has exactly 8 characters: three upper-case letters, a hyphen, then four digits, for example "LHR-2041". The function returns TRUE if Code is valid and FALSE otherwise.
parts.answer:
FUNCTION IsValidCode(Code : STRING) RETURNS BOOLEAN
   DECLARE Index : INTEGER
   DECLARE Ch : CHAR
   IF LENGTH(Code) <> 8 THEN
      RETURN FALSE
   ENDIF
   FOR Index ← 1 TO 3
      Ch ← MID(Code, Index, 1)
      IF Ch < 'A' OR Ch > 'Z' THEN
         RETURN FALSE
      ENDIF
   NEXT Index
   IF MID(Code, 4, 1) <> '-' THEN
      RETURN FALSE
   ENDIF
   FOR Index ← 5 TO 8
      Ch ← MID(Code, Index, 1)
      IF Ch < '0' OR Ch > '9' THEN
         RETURN FALSE
      ENDIF
   NEXT Index
   RETURN TRUE
ENDFUNCTION
parts.working: 1 mark each: header/ENDFUNCTION returning BOOLEAN; length check of 8; loop over characters 1 to 3; test each is 'A'–'Z' (or UCASE/ASC range); check character 4 is '-'; loop over characters 5 to 8 testing '0'–'9' (or IS_NUM); RETURN TRUE only after all tests pass and FALSE otherwise. Accept a flag variable instead of early returns.

practice.stem: A water-quality sensor at a treatment plant in Johannesburg logs pH readings to a text file.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write pseudocode for the function CopyHigh(Limit : REAL) RETURNS INTEGER. The function reads every line of the text file "Readings.txt". Each line holds one reading as a string. Every reading greater than Limit is written to a new text file "High.txt". The function returns the number of readings written.
parts.answer:
FUNCTION CopyHigh(Limit : REAL) RETURNS INTEGER
   DECLARE Line : STRING
   DECLARE Count : INTEGER
   Count ← 0
   OPENFILE "Readings.txt" FOR READ
   OPENFILE "High.txt" FOR WRITE
   WHILE NOT EOF("Readings.txt")
      READFILE "Readings.txt", Line
      IF STR_TO_NUM(Line) > Limit THEN
         WRITEFILE "High.txt", Line
         Count ← Count + 1
      ENDIF
   ENDWHILE
   CLOSEFILE "Readings.txt"
   CLOSEFILE "High.txt"
   RETURN Count
ENDFUNCTION
parts.working: 1 mark each: open Readings.txt FOR READ; open High.txt FOR WRITE; loop WHILE NOT EOF("Readings.txt"); READFILE each line into a variable; convert with STR_TO_NUM and compare with the parameter Limit; WRITEFILE and increment counter (initialised to 0); close both files and RETURN Count. Do not credit INPUT of Limit.

practice.stem: An electricity company charges for each month: the first 100 units at Rs 10 per unit, the next 200 units (units 101 to 300) at Rs 15 per unit, and every unit above 300 at Rs 22 per unit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write pseudocode for the function BillAmount(Units : INTEGER) RETURNS INTEGER that returns the bill in rupees.
parts.answer:
FUNCTION BillAmount(Units : INTEGER) RETURNS INTEGER
   DECLARE Cost : INTEGER
   IF Units <= 100 THEN
      Cost ← Units * 10
   ELSE
      IF Units <= 300 THEN
         Cost ← 1000 + (Units - 100) * 15
      ELSE
         Cost ← 1000 + 3000 + (Units - 300) * 22
      ENDIF
   ENDIF
   RETURN Cost
ENDFUNCTION
parts.working: 1 mark header/end with RETURN; 1 mark first band Units × 10; 1 mark correct boundary tests (≤ 100, ≤ 300); 1 mark second band 1000 + (Units − 100) × 15; 1 mark third band 4000 + (Units − 300) × 22; 1 mark nested IF / CASE structure correct.

parts.label: b

parts.answer: 80 units: Rs 800; 350 units: Rs 5100.

practice.stem: An auditorium in Kuala Lumpur has 10 rows of 20 seats. The global 2D array Booked[1:10, 1:20] OF BOOLEAN stores TRUE if a seat is booked and FALSE if it is free.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write pseudocode for a procedure BestRow() that outputs the number of the row with the most free seats and how many free seats it has. If several rows have the same number, output the lowest row number.
parts.answer:
PROCEDURE BestRow()
   DECLARE Row, Seat, Free, BestRowNo, BestFree : INTEGER
   BestFree ← -1
   BestRowNo ← 0
   FOR Row ← 1 TO 10
      Free ← 0
      FOR Seat ← 1 TO 20
         IF Booked[Row, Seat] = FALSE THEN
            Free ← Free + 1
         ENDIF
      NEXT Seat
      IF Free > BestFree THEN
         BestFree ← Free
         BestRowNo ← Row
      ENDIF
   NEXT Row
   OUTPUT "Row ", BestRowNo, " has ", BestFree, " free seats"
ENDPROCEDURE
parts.working: 1 mark each: outer loop 1 to 10 for rows; reset count of free seats for each row; inner loop 1 to 20 for seats; test Booked[Row, Seat] = FALSE and increment; compare with best so far using > (lowest row kept); store best row and count; output after both loops.

practice.stem: A text-analysis tool for a newspaper in Dhaka counts words typed by reporters.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write pseudocode for the function CountWords(Sentence : STRING) RETURNS INTEGER. Words are separated by one or more spaces, and the sentence may begin or end with spaces. For example "  the  cat sat " contains 3 words.
parts.answer:
FUNCTION CountWords(Sentence : STRING) RETURNS INTEGER
   DECLARE Index, Count : INTEGER
   DECLARE InWord : BOOLEAN
   DECLARE Ch : CHAR
   Count ← 0
   InWord ← FALSE
   FOR Index ← 1 TO LENGTH(Sentence)
      Ch ← MID(Sentence, Index, 1)
      IF Ch = ' ' THEN
         InWord ← FALSE
      ELSE
         IF InWord = FALSE THEN
            Count ← Count + 1
            InWord ← TRUE
         ENDIF
      ENDIF
   NEXT Index
   RETURN Count
ENDFUNCTION

practice.stem: A teacher in Karachi wants a small tool that shows how denary numbers are stored in binary.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a program function DenaryToBinary(Number) that takes a non-negative integer and returns its binary representation as a string, using repeated division by 2. Do not use a built-in conversion function. Then write a main program that calls the function with 45, 0, 255 and 130 and outputs each result. Give the outputs of your test run. (Python shown; Java or VB.NET solutions are equally acceptable.)
parts.answer:
def DenaryToBinary(Number):
    # Number is a non-negative integer
    if Number == 0:
        return "0"
    Result = ""
    while Number > 0:
        Remainder = Number % 2
        Result = str(Remainder) + Result
        Number = Number // 2
    return Result

for Value in [45, 0, 255, 130]:
    print(Value, DenaryToBinary(Value))

Test output:
45 101101
0 0
255 11111111
130 10000010
parts.working: 1 mark each: function header with one parameter; special case 0 returns "0"; loop while Number > 0; remainder with MOD (%) prepended to the result string; integer division by 2; returns the string (not printed inside the function); main program calls with all four values and evidence of output 101101, 0, 11111111, 10000010.

practice.stem: A security club at a school in Rawalpindi is learning about simple ciphers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write pseudocode for the function Encrypt(Message : STRING, Shift : INTEGER) RETURNS STRING. Each upper-case letter is replaced by the letter Shift places later in the alphabet, wrapping from Z back to A. Shift is from 1 to 25. All other characters are copied unchanged.
parts.answer:
FUNCTION Encrypt(Message : STRING, Shift : INTEGER) RETURNS STRING
   DECLARE Result : STRING
   DECLARE Index, Code : INTEGER
   DECLARE Ch : CHAR
   Result ← ""
   FOR Index ← 1 TO LENGTH(Message)
      Ch ← MID(Message, Index, 1)
      IF Ch >= 'A' AND Ch <= 'Z' THEN
         Code ← ASC(Ch) - ASC('A')
         Code ← MOD(Code + Shift, 26)
         Ch ← CHR(Code + ASC('A'))
      ENDIF
      Result ← Result & Ch
   NEXT Index
   RETURN Result
ENDFUNCTION
parts.working: 1 mark each: initialise result to empty string; loop through each character with MID; test for upper-case letter; convert to 0–25 using ASC; add Shift and wrap with MOD 26 (or IF > 'Z' subtract 26); convert back with CHR; concatenate every character (changed or not) and RETURN the result.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the value returned by Encrypt("ZEBRA 9", 3).
parts.answer: "CHEUD 9"

practice.stem: A warehouse in Gwadar keeps sorted lists of product codes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write pseudocode for the function RemoveDuplicates(Size : INTEGER) RETURNS INTEGER. The first Size elements of the global array Codes[1:500] OF INTEGER are in ascending order and may contain repeated values. The function moves the elements so that each value appears once, at the start of the array, keeping ascending order, and returns the number of distinct values. For example, if Size is 7 and the elements are 3, 3, 5, 8, 8, 8, 9, then afterwards the first four elements are 3, 5, 8, 9 and 4 is returned.
parts.answer:
FUNCTION RemoveDuplicates(Size : INTEGER) RETURNS INTEGER
   DECLARE ReadPos, WritePos : INTEGER
   IF Size = 0 THEN
      RETURN 0
   ENDIF
   WritePos ← 1
   FOR ReadPos ← 2 TO Size
      IF Codes[ReadPos] <> Codes[WritePos] THEN
         WritePos ← WritePos + 1
         Codes[WritePos] ← Codes[ReadPos]
      ENDIF
   NEXT ReadPos
   RETURN WritePos
ENDFUNCTION
parts.working: 1 mark each: header/ENDFUNCTION; handle Size = 0 (or Size < 2); write position starts at 1; loop from 2 to Size; compare current element with the last kept element; increment write position and copy the element; RETURN the number of distinct values.

practice.stem: A teacher in Mombasa keeps test scores in a text file.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write pseudocode for the procedure AboveAverage(). The text file "Scores.txt" has one line per student in the form StudentID,Score, for example "S0412,67". Score is an integer from 0 to 100 and StudentID is always 5 characters. The procedure must calculate the average score, then write the StudentID of every student whose score is above the average to the file "Above.txt", and finally output the average. Assume the file contains at least one line.
parts.answer:
PROCEDURE AboveAverage()
   DECLARE Line : STRING
   DECLARE Total, Count, Score : INTEGER
   DECLARE Average : REAL
   Total ← 0
   Count ← 0
   OPENFILE "Scores.txt" FOR READ
   WHILE NOT EOF("Scores.txt")
      READFILE "Scores.txt", Line
      Score ← STR_TO_NUM(MID(Line, 7, LENGTH(Line) - 6))
      Total ← Total + Score
      Count ← Count + 1
   ENDWHILE
   CLOSEFILE "Scores.txt"
   Average ← Total / Count
   OPENFILE "Scores.txt" FOR READ
   OPENFILE "Above.txt" FOR WRITE
   WHILE NOT EOF("Scores.txt")
      READFILE "Scores.txt", Line
      Score ← STR_TO_NUM(MID(Line, 7, LENGTH(Line) - 6))
      IF Score > Average THEN
         WRITEFILE "Above.txt", LEFT(Line, 5)
      ENDIF
   ENDWHILE
   CLOSEFILE "Scores.txt"
   CLOSEFILE "Above.txt"
   OUTPUT "Average score: ", Average
ENDPROCEDURE
parts.working: Level-style marking, 1 mark each to max 8: open Scores.txt for READ; loop until EOF; READFILE each line; extract the score after the comma (MID/RIGHT and STR_TO_NUM); total and count, then average calculated after the first pass; close and reopen the file (second pass) or store the data in arrays; open Above.txt for WRITE and write LEFT(Line, 5) when Score > Average; close all files and output the average.

practice.stem: A word-game app in Egypt checks phrases entered by players.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write pseudocode for the function IsPalindrome(Phrase : STRING) RETURNS BOOLEAN. It returns TRUE if the phrase reads the same forwards and backwards when spaces are ignored and upper and lower case are treated as the same. For example "Never odd or even" is a palindrome.
parts.answer:
FUNCTION IsPalindrome(Phrase : STRING) RETURNS BOOLEAN
   DECLARE Clean : STRING
   DECLARE Index, LeftPos, RightPos : INTEGER
   DECLARE Ch : CHAR
   Clean ← ""
   FOR Index ← 1 TO LENGTH(Phrase)
      Ch ← MID(Phrase, Index, 1)
      IF Ch <> ' ' THEN
         Clean ← Clean & LCASE(Ch)
      ENDIF
   NEXT Index
   LeftPos ← 1
   RightPos ← LENGTH(Clean)
   WHILE LeftPos < RightPos
      IF MID(Clean, LeftPos, 1) <> MID(Clean, RightPos, 1) THEN
         RETURN FALSE
      ENDIF
      LeftPos ← LeftPos + 1
      RightPos ← RightPos - 1
   ENDWHILE
   RETURN TRUE
ENDFUNCTION
parts.working: 1 mark each: build a string without spaces; convert to one case; set pointers to both ends (or build reversed string); compare matching characters; move pointers inwards / loop to the middle; RETURN FALSE on a mismatch and TRUE otherwise.

FUNCTION FindName(SearchName : STRING) RETURNS INTEGER

      IF Names[Index] = SearchName THEN
         RETURN Index
      ENDIF

   RETURN -1

practice.stem: A quiz website in Turkey ranks the scores of 100 players.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write pseudocode for the procedure SortScores() which uses an efficient bubble sort to put the global array Scores[1:100] OF INTEGER into descending order (highest first). The sort must stop as soon as a complete pass makes no swaps.
parts.answer:
PROCEDURE SortScores()
   DECLARE Index, Temp, Last : INTEGER
   DECLARE Swapped : BOOLEAN
   Last ← 99
   REPEAT
      Swapped ← FALSE
      FOR Index ← 1 TO Last
         IF Scores[Index] < Scores[Index + 1] THEN
            Temp ← Scores[Index]
            Scores[Index] ← Scores[Index + 1]
            Scores[Index + 1] ← Temp
            Swapped ← TRUE
         ENDIF
      NEXT Index
      Last ← Last - 1
   UNTIL Swapped = FALSE OR Last = 0
ENDPROCEDURE
parts.working: 1 mark each: outer conditional loop; flag reset to FALSE at the start of each pass; inner loop 1 to 99 (or reducing upper bound); compare adjacent elements with < for descending order; swap using a temporary variable; set flag TRUE when a swap happens; outer loop ends when no swaps (reducing the bound is credit-worthy but not required).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why reducing the upper bound of the inner loop after each pass makes the algorithm more efficient.
parts.answer: After each pass the smallest remaining value has moved to its final position at the end, so it does not need to be compared again; fewer comparisons are made.
parts.working: 1 mark last element is in its correct place after each pass; 1 mark so fewer comparisons/iterations are needed.

FUNCTION Mystery(N : INTEGER) RETURNS INTEGER
   DECLARE Steps : INTEGER
   Steps ← 0
   WHILE N <> 1
      IF MOD(N, 2) = 0 THEN
         N ← DIV(N, 2)
      ELSE
         N ← 3 * N + 1
      ENDIF
      Steps ← Steps + 1
   ENDWHILE

practice.stem: A weather station in Jacobabad stores daily maximum temperatures in the text file temps.txt, one real number per line.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Write program code for a function summarise(filename) that:
• opens the text file and reads every reading (ignoring blank lines)
• calculates the number of readings, the average (rounded to 1 decimal place) and the highest reading
• writes these three results to a new file summary.txt on three lines
• returns the three values
• outputs "File not found" and returns nothing if the file does not exist.
Write a main program that calls the function with temps.txt and outputs the result.
parts.answer:
def summarise(filename):
    try:
        f = open(filename, "r")
    except FileNotFoundError:
        print("File not found")
        return None
    count = 0
    total = 0.0
    highest = None
    for line in f:
        line = line.strip()
        if line != "":
            value = float(line)
            count += 1
            total += value
            if highest is None or value > highest:
                highest = value
    f.close()
    if count == 0:
        print("No readings")
        return None
    average = round(total / count, 1)
    out = open("summary.txt", "w")
    out.write("Readings: " + str(count) + "\n")
    out.write("Average: " + str(average) + "\n")
    out.write("Highest: " + str(highest) + "\n")
    out.close()
    return count, average, highest

# main program
result = summarise("temps.txt")
print(result)
(Java or VB.NET solutions with the same logic are equally acceptable.)

Readings: 5
Average: 32.9
Highest: 36.8
With temps.txt missing it outputs: File not found

• average calculated and rounded to 1 d.p.

practice.stem: A text editor stores codes for the user's recent actions so they can be undone. It uses a stack held in the global array UndoStack[1:50] OF INTEGER with the global pointer TopOfStack, initialised to 0 (empty).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write pseudocode for the function Push(Action : INTEGER) RETURNS BOOLEAN, which adds Action to the stack. It returns FALSE if the stack is full, otherwise TRUE.
parts.answer:
FUNCTION Push(Action : INTEGER) RETURNS BOOLEAN
   IF TopOfStack = 50 THEN
      RETURN FALSE
   ELSE
      TopOfStack ← TopOfStack + 1
      UndoStack[TopOfStack] ← Action
      RETURN TRUE
   ENDIF
ENDFUNCTION
parts.working: 1 mark check for full (TopOfStack = 50); 1 mark increment TopOfStack; 1 mark store at new top (in that order); 1 mark correct BOOLEAN returns.

parts.text: Write pseudocode for the function Pop() RETURNS INTEGER, which removes and returns the top item. It returns −1 if the stack is empty.
parts.answer:
FUNCTION Pop() RETURNS INTEGER
   DECLARE Item : INTEGER
   IF TopOfStack = 0 THEN
      Item ← -1
   ELSE
      Item ← UndoStack[TopOfStack]
      TopOfStack ← TopOfStack - 1
   ENDIF
   RETURN Item
ENDFUNCTION
parts.working: 1 mark check for empty; 1 mark read item at top; 1 mark decrement after reading; 1 mark return item / −1.

practice.stem: A print server in a Karachi office holds print-job names in a circular queue using the global array Queue[0:9] OF STRING and the global integers HeadPointer, TailPointer and NumberInQueue.

parts.label: a

parts.answer:
FUNCTION Dequeue() RETURNS STRING
   DECLARE Item : STRING
   IF NumberInQueue = 0 THEN
      Item ← "EMPTY"
   ELSE
      Item ← Queue[HeadPointer]

      IF HeadPointer > 9 THEN
         HeadPointer ← 0
      ENDIF
      NumberInQueue ← NumberInQueue - 1
   ENDIF
   RETURN Item
ENDFUNCTION

5 | 6 | 3 | 0
6 | 0 | 15 | 18
7 | 9 | 4 | 7

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Write program code to:
• store the data in a 2D array (list of lists) with 7 rows (days) and 3 columns (cities)
• define a function city_totals(data) that returns a list of the total rainfall for each city
• define a function wettest_day(data) that returns the day number (1–7) with the greatest total rainfall across the three cities, and that total
• output each city's name with its total, and the wettest day.
parts.answer:
rainfall = [[12, 0, 5],
            [30, 8, 0],
            [0, 0, 2],
            [45, 22, 10],
            [6, 3, 0],
            [0, 15, 18],
            [9, 4, 7]]
cities = ["Lahore", "Islamabad", "Karachi"]

def city_totals(data):
    totals = [0, 0, 0]
    for day in range(7):
        for city in range(3):
            totals[city] += data[day][city]
    return totals

def wettest_day(data):
    best_day = 0
    best_total = sum(data[0])
    for day in range(1, 7):
        day_total = 0
        for city in range(3):
            day_total += data[day][city]
        if day_total > best_total:
            best_total = day_total
            best_day = day
    return best_day + 1, best_total     # day number 1-7

totals = city_totals(rainfall)
for i in range(3):
    print(cities[i], totals[i], "mm")
print("Wettest day:", wettest_day(rainfall))

Islamabad 52 mm
Karachi 42 mm

practice.stem: A quiz app stores players' scores in ascending order in the global array Scores[1:100] OF INTEGER. The global integer NumScores holds how many elements are in use (they are Scores[1] to Scores[NumScores]).

parts.label: a

Write pseudocode for the procedure InsertScore(NewScore : INTEGER).
If the array is full the procedure outputs "Array full". Otherwise it inserts NewScore in the correct position, keeping the array in ascending order, and updates NumScores. You must not sort the whole array again.
parts.answer:
PROCEDURE InsertScore(NewScore : INTEGER)
   DECLARE Index : INTEGER
   DECLARE Placed : BOOLEAN
   IF NumScores = 100 THEN
      OUTPUT "Array full"
   ELSE
      Index ← NumScores
      Placed ← FALSE
      WHILE Index >= 1 AND Placed = FALSE
         IF Scores[Index] > NewScore THEN
            Scores[Index + 1] ← Scores[Index]
            Index ← Index - 1
         ELSE
            Placed ← TRUE
         ENDIF
      ENDWHILE
      Scores[Index + 1] ← NewScore
      NumScores ← NumScores + 1
   ENDIF
ENDPROCEDURE
parts.working:
1 mark each:
• check for full array and output message
• start at the last used element (NumScores)
• loop that moves backwards while elements are larger
• larger elements shifted one place right
• loop stops at the start of the array without accessing Scores[0] (flag or equivalent)
• NewScore stored at Index + 1
• NumScores incremented
Example: Scores 12, 18, 25, 31 with NewScore 20 becomes 12, 18, 20, 25, 31.

FUNCTION LongestRun(RowNum : INTEGER) RETURNS INTEGER

   Current ← 0

         Current ← Current + 1

      ELSE
         Current ← 0
      ENDIF
   NEXT Seat
   RETURN Longest
ENDFUNCTION

Write pseudocode for the function BinToDenary(BinString : STRING) RETURNS INTEGER. BinString contains only the characters '0' and '1' (up to 16 of them). The function returns the denary value. For example, BinToDenary("101101") returns 45.
You may use the pseudocode functions LEFT, RIGHT, MID, LENGTH, TO_UPPER, TO_LOWER, NUM_TO_STR, STR_TO_NUM, IS_NUM, ASC, CHR, INT, MOD and DIV.
parts.answer:
FUNCTION BinToDenary(BinString : STRING) RETURNS INTEGER
   DECLARE Value, Index : INTEGER
   Value ← 0
   FOR Index ← 1 TO LENGTH(BinString)
      Value ← Value * 2
      IF MID(BinString, Index, 1) = '1' THEN
         Value ← Value + 1
      ENDIF
   NEXT Index
   RETURN Value
ENDFUNCTION
parts.working: 1 mark each: Value initialised to 0; loop over every character; extract character with MID; correct place-value method (double then add, or add place value that doubles from the right); RETURN Value. Max 5.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the value returned by BinToDenary("11111111").

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Write pseudocode for the function FormatDate(ThisDate : DATE) RETURNS STRING, which returns the date as a string in the form DD/MM/YYYY, with a leading zero for days and months below 10. For example, the date 5 March 2026 is returned as "05/03/2026".
You may also use the functions DAY(ThisDate), MONTH(ThisDate) and YEAR(ThisDate), which return integers.
You may use the pseudocode functions LEFT, RIGHT, MID, LENGTH, TO_UPPER, TO_LOWER, NUM_TO_STR, STR_TO_NUM, IS_NUM, ASC, CHR, INT, MOD and DIV.
parts.answer:
FUNCTION FormatDate(ThisDate : DATE) RETURNS STRING
   DECLARE DayStr, MonthStr : STRING
   DayStr ← NUM_TO_STR(DAY(ThisDate))
   IF DAY(ThisDate) < 10 THEN
      DayStr ← "0" & DayStr
   ENDIF
   MonthStr ← NUM_TO_STR(MONTH(ThisDate))
   IF MONTH(ThisDate) < 10 THEN
      MonthStr ← "0" & MonthStr
   ENDIF
   RETURN DayStr & "/" & MonthStr & "/" & NUM_TO_STR(YEAR(ThisDate))
ENDFUNCTION
parts.working: 1 mark each: uses DAY, MONTH and YEAR; converts each to a string with NUM_TO_STR; adds leading zero to day when < 10; adds leading zero to month when < 10; concatenates with '/' separators in the correct order and RETURNs the string.

practice.stem:
A bank in Lahore checks new online-banking passwords. A password scores one point for each rule it meets:
• it has at least 8 characters
• it contains at least one upper-case letter
• it contains at least one lower-case letter
• it contains at least one digit.
A score of 4 is "Strong", 2 or 3 is "Medium", and 0 or 1 is "Weak".

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Write a program that:
• defines a function password_strength(password) that returns "Strong", "Medium" or "Weak" using the scoring rules above, examining the string one character at a time (do not use built-in methods such as isupper())
• tests the function with each of these passwords and prints the password and its result:
Karachi2026, karachi, PESHAWAR, abc, Abc12, 12345678
Save your program, run it, and show the output as evidence.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 8: function header with parameter; loop over every character; detects upper case; detects lower case; detects digit; length test ≥ 8; score calculated correctly (one point per rule, not per character); returns correct category for 4, 2–3 and 0–1 points; returns (not prints) the result inside the function; test calls for all six passwords with output; screenshot/evidence of the output matching the expected results.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Write pseudocode for the function IsPalindrome(Text : STRING) RETURNS BOOLEAN.
The function returns TRUE if Text reads the same forwards and backwards when spaces are ignored and upper and lower case are treated as the same. For example, IsPalindrome("Never odd or even") returns TRUE and IsPalindrome("Lahore") returns FALSE.
Do not use a separate reverse function.
You may use the pseudocode functions LEFT, RIGHT, MID, LENGTH, TO_UPPER, TO_LOWER, NUM_TO_STR, STR_TO_NUM, IS_NUM, ASC, CHR, INT, MOD and DIV.
parts.answer:
FUNCTION IsPalindrome(Text : STRING) RETURNS BOOLEAN
   DECLARE Clean : STRING
   DECLARE Index, Last : INTEGER
   DECLARE Match : BOOLEAN
   Clean ← ""
   FOR Index ← 1 TO LENGTH(Text)
      IF MID(Text, Index, 1) <> " " THEN
         Clean ← Clean & TO_UPPER(MID(Text, Index, 1))
      ENDIF
   NEXT Index
   Match ← TRUE
   Index ← 1
   Last ← LENGTH(Clean)
   WHILE Index < Last AND Match = TRUE
      IF MID(Clean, Index, 1) <> MID(Clean, Last, 1) THEN
         Match ← FALSE
      ENDIF
      Index ← Index + 1
      Last ← Last - 1
   ENDWHILE
   RETURN Match
ENDFUNCTION
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 7: correct header with BOOLEAN return; loop through Text; removes/skips spaces; converts case consistently; builds cleaned string; compares characters from both ends (first with last, moving inwards) or builds a reversed copy in-line; loop stops at the middle / when a mismatch found; sets result FALSE on mismatch; RETURN of a Boolean value in all cases.

practice.stem:
A car park in Islamabad records vehicle registrations in this format:
• three upper-case letters, then
• a hyphen '-', then
• three or four digits.
For example, "LEA-1234" and "ICT-567" are valid; "LE-12345" is not.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Write pseudocode for the function ValidReg(Reg : STRING) RETURNS BOOLEAN that returns TRUE only if Reg is in the correct format.
You may use the pseudocode functions LEFT, RIGHT, MID, LENGTH, TO_UPPER, TO_LOWER, NUM_TO_STR, STR_TO_NUM, IS_NUM, ASC, CHR, INT, MOD and DIV.
parts.answer:
FUNCTION ValidReg(Reg : STRING) RETURNS BOOLEAN
   DECLARE Index : INTEGER
   DECLARE ThisChar : CHAR
   DECLARE Valid : BOOLEAN
   Valid ← TRUE
   IF LENGTH(Reg) <> 7 AND LENGTH(Reg) <> 8 THEN
      Valid ← FALSE
   ELSE
      FOR Index ← 1 TO 3
         ThisChar ← MID(Reg, Index, 1)
         IF ThisChar < 'A' OR ThisChar > 'Z' THEN
            Valid ← FALSE
         ENDIF
      NEXT Index
      IF MID(Reg, 4, 1) <> '-' THEN
         Valid ← FALSE
      ENDIF
      FOR Index ← 5 TO LENGTH(Reg)
         ThisChar ← MID(Reg, Index, 1)
         IF ThisChar < '0' OR ThisChar > '9' THEN
            Valid ← FALSE
         ENDIF
      NEXT Index
   ENDIF
   RETURN Valid
ENDFUNCTION
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 7: check length is 7 or 8; length check done before characters are accessed; loop over the first three characters; test each is in range 'A' to 'Z'; test fourth character is '-'; loop from 5 to LENGTH(Reg); test each is a digit '0'–'9' (or IS_NUM on the substring, provided it rejects signs/decimal points); return TRUE only if all tests pass, FALSE otherwise.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Give the value returned by ValidReg for each string.
(i) "lea-1234" (ii) "ICT-567" (iii) "LEA 1234"
parts.answer: (i) FALSE (ii) TRUE (iii) FALSE
parts.working: 1 mark each. (i) lower-case letters; (iii) space instead of hyphen.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Write pseudocode for the function Encrypt(Message : STRING, Shift : INTEGER) RETURNS STRING.
Each upper-case letter in Message is replaced by the letter Shift places later in the alphabet, wrapping round from 'Z' back to 'A'. All other characters are unchanged. Shift is between 1 and 25. ASC('A') returns 65.
You may use the pseudocode functions LEFT, RIGHT, MID, LENGTH, TO_UPPER, TO_LOWER, NUM_TO_STR, STR_TO_NUM, IS_NUM, ASC, CHR, INT, MOD and DIV.
parts.answer:
FUNCTION Encrypt(Message : STRING, Shift : INTEGER) RETURNS STRING
   DECLARE Result : STRING
   DECLARE ThisChar : CHAR
   DECLARE Index, Code : INTEGER
   Result ← ""
   FOR Index ← 1 TO LENGTH(Message)
      ThisChar ← MID(Message, Index, 1)
      IF ThisChar >= 'A' AND ThisChar <= 'Z' THEN
         Code ← MOD(ASC(ThisChar) - 65 + Shift, 26) + 65
         Result ← Result & CHR(Code)
      ELSE
         Result ← Result & ThisChar
      ENDIF
   NEXT Index
   RETURN Result
ENDFUNCTION
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 7: header with two parameters and STRING return; result initialised; loop through each character; extract with MID; test for upper-case letter; use ASC to get code and add Shift; wrap round correctly (MOD 26, or IF Code > 90 THEN Code ← Code − 26); convert back with CHR and concatenate; non-letters copied unchanged; RETURN result.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the value returned by Encrypt("ZOO 7", 3).
parts.answer: "CRR 7"
parts.working: B1: Z→C (wraps), O→R, O→R, space and 7 unchanged.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Write pseudocode for the function ValidEmail(Address : STRING) RETURNS BOOLEAN. The function returns TRUE only if all of these rules are met:
• Address contains exactly one '@' character, which is not the first character
• at least one '.' appears after the '@'
• no '.' appears immediately after the '@'
• the last character is not '.'
You may use the pseudocode functions LEFT, RIGHT, MID, LENGTH, TO_UPPER, TO_LOWER, NUM_TO_STR, STR_TO_NUM, IS_NUM, ASC, CHR, INT, MOD and DIV.
parts.answer:
FUNCTION ValidEmail(Address : STRING) RETURNS BOOLEAN
   DECLARE Index, AtCount, AtPos : INTEGER
   DECLARE DotAfter : BOOLEAN
   DECLARE ThisChar : CHAR
   AtCount ← 0
   AtPos ← 0
   DotAfter ← FALSE
   FOR Index ← 1 TO LENGTH(Address)
      ThisChar ← MID(Address, Index, 1)
      IF ThisChar = '@' THEN
         AtCount ← AtCount + 1
         AtPos ← Index
      ENDIF
      IF ThisChar = '.' AND AtPos > 0 AND Index > AtPos + 1 THEN
         DotAfter ← TRUE
      ENDIF
   NEXT Index
   IF AtCount <> 1 OR AtPos = 1 OR DotAfter = FALSE THEN
      RETURN FALSE
   ENDIF
   IF MID(Address, AtPos + 1, 1) = '.' OR RIGHT(Address, 1) = '.' THEN
      RETURN FALSE
   ENDIF
   RETURN TRUE
ENDFUNCTION
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 7: loop through each character with MID; count '@' characters; record position of '@'; reject if count not exactly 1; reject '@' at position 1; detect a '.' after the '@'; reject '.' directly after '@'; reject final '.'; returns BOOLEAN in every path. (Note: AtPos + 1 cannot exceed the length when a dot after '@' exists, as that dot is at least two places after '@'.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one example of a string that passes this check but is still not a working email address, and state why validation cannot prevent this.
parts.answer: e.g. "zainab@notreal.xyz" – it has the correct format, but validation only checks format/reasonableness, not whether the address actually exists.
parts.working: B1 suitable example; B1 validation checks rules/format, not correctness/existence.

practice.stem:
The function FindSpace(Text : STRING) RETURNS INTEGER should return the position of the first space in Text, or −1 if there is no space. It contains four errors.
01 FUNCTION FindSpace(Text : STRING) RETURNS INTEGER
02    DECLARE Index, Position : INTEGER
03    Position ← 0
04    Index ← 1
05    WHILE Index < LENGTH(Text) AND Position = -1
06       IF MID(Text, 1, Index) = " " THEN
07          Position ← Index
08       ENDIF
09       Index ← Index + 1
10    ENDWHILE
11    RETURN Index
12 ENDFUNCTION

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the line number of each of the four errors in the function and write the corrected line.
parts.answer:
Line 03: Position ← -1
Line 05: WHILE Index <= LENGTH(Text) AND Position = -1
Line 06: IF MID(Text, Index, 1) = " " THEN
Line 11: RETURN Position
parts.working: For each error: B1 line number, B1 correct replacement. Line 03 – Position must start at −1, otherwise the loop never runs and 0 would be wrong for 'not found'. Line 05 – '<' misses the last character. Line 06 – MID parameters wrong: must take 1 character at position Index. Line 11 – must return Position, not Index.

practice.stem: A sports academy in Sialkot registers children for coaching.

parts.label: a
parts.text:

• input an age, repeating the input until it is a whole number between 5 and 18 inclusive, with an error message after each invalid entry
• then output "Junior" for ages 5 to 11 and "Senior" for ages 12 to 18.
You may assume the user always types a number, but it may not be a whole number. You may use the function INT.
parts.answer:
DECLARE Age : REAL
INPUT Age
WHILE Age < 5 OR Age > 18 OR Age <> INT(Age)
   OUTPUT "Age must be a whole number from 5 to 18"
   INPUT Age
ENDWHILE
IF Age <= 11 THEN
   OUTPUT "Junior"
ELSE
   OUTPUT "Senior"
ENDIF
parts.working: 1 mark each: input inside a conditional loop; range test with correct inclusive boundaries; whole-number test (Age = INT(Age)); error message only for invalid entries; correct selection for Junior/Senior after the loop. A REPEAT…UNTIL version with the error message inside an IF is equally acceptable.

parts.text: Explain why a count-controlled (FOR) loop is not suitable for the validation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between a procedure and a function.
parts.answer: A function returns a single value to the point where it was called and is used in an expression; a procedure does not return a value through its name and is called as a statement using CALL.
parts.working: 1 mark each: function returns a value (used in an expression / assignment); procedure called with CALL as a statement / does not return a value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the difference between passing a parameter by value and by reference.
parts.answer: By value, a copy of the value is passed, so changes inside the subroutine do not affect the original variable. By reference, the address of the variable is passed, so changes inside the subroutine change the original variable.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

PROCEDURE Adjust(BYVAL X : INTEGER, BYREF Y : INTEGER)

   Y ← Y + X
   OUTPUT X, " ", Y
ENDPROCEDURE

B ← 3

OUTPUT A, " ", B

OUTPUT A, " ", B

practice.stem: A global array Scores : ARRAY[1:50] OF INTEGER holds the scores of 50 players in a cricket league in Lahore. Every element contains a value.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write pseudocode for the procedure FindRange(BYREF Lowest : INTEGER, BYREF Highest : INTEGER), which finds the lowest and highest values in the global array Scores and passes them back through its parameters.
parts.answer:
PROCEDURE FindRange(BYREF Lowest : INTEGER, BYREF Highest : INTEGER)
   DECLARE Index : INTEGER
   Lowest ← Scores[1]
   Highest ← Scores[1]
   FOR Index ← 2 TO 50
      IF Scores[Index] < Lowest THEN
         Lowest ← Scores[Index]
      ENDIF
      IF Scores[Index] > Highest THEN
         Highest ← Scores[Index]
      ENDIF
   NEXT Index
ENDPROCEDURE
parts.working: 1 mark each: header and ENDPROCEDURE; initialise both to Scores[1] (not 0 or a fixed guess); loop through remaining elements; correct comparison and update for Lowest; correct comparison and update for Highest; no RETURN / OUTPUT used to pass values back. Max 5.

OUTPUT High - Low

parts.answer: A function can return only one value, but two values (lowest and highest) must be passed back.

practice.stem:
An electricity company in a fictional city uses this monthly tariff:
• the first 100 units cost Rs 10 per unit
• the next 100 units (101 to 200) cost Rs 15 per unit
• every unit above 200 costs Rs 22 per unit
• a fixed charge of Rs 75 is added to every bill.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Write a program that:
• defines a function calc_bill(units) that returns the total bill in rupees using the tariff above
• defines a function get_units() that asks the user for the units used, repeating until a whole number of 0 or more is entered, and returns it as an integer
• tests calc_bill with 0, 100, 101, 150, 200 and 250 units, printing each result
• then calls get_units() and prints the bill for the value entered.
Run the program, entering abc, then -5, then 320, and show the output as evidence.
parts.answer:
Python model answer (Java or VB.NET also accepted):
FIXED_CHARGE = 75

def calc_bill(units):
    if units <= 100:
        energy = units * 10
    elif units <= 200:
        energy = 100 * 10 + (units - 100) * 15
    else:
        energy = 100 * 10 + 100 * 15 + (units - 200) * 22
    return energy + FIXED_CHARGE

def get_units():
    valid = False
    while not valid:
        entry = input("Enter units used: ")
        if entry.isdigit():
            units = int(entry)
            valid = True
        else:
            print("Units must be a whole number of 0 or more")
    return units

for u in [0, 100, 101, 150, 200, 250]:
    print(u, calc_bill(u))
units = get_units()
print("Bill: Rs", calc_bill(units))

Output:
0 75
100 1075
101 1090
150 1825
200 2575
250 3675
Enter units used: abc
Units must be a whole number of 0 or more
Enter units used: -5
Units must be a whole number of 0 or more
Enter units used: 320
Bill: Rs 5215
parts.working: calc_bill (max 4): parameter used (not input inside the function); correct first band; correct second band with 100 × 10 plus the excess; correct third band; fixed charge added and value returned. get_units (max 3): loop until valid; rejects non-numeric and negative entries with a message; returns an integer. Testing (max 2): six test values with correct outputs (75, 1075, 1090, 1825, 2575, 3675); run with abc, −5, 320 giving Rs 5215.

parts.label: a

parts.answer: A non-composite data type is defined without reference to any other data type (it holds a single value, e.g. an enumerated or pointer type). A composite data type is made up of / refers to one or more other data types (e.g. a record, set, array or class).

parts.answer: The built-in types may not match the data in the problem; user-defined types make the program easier to read and maintain and let the translator check that only suitable values are used.

practice.stem:
TYPE TSeason = (Spring, Summer, Autumn, Winter)
A farmer in Punjab uses a program that plans crops by season.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write pseudocode for a function NextSeason(S : TSeason) RETURNS TSeason that returns the season after S. The season after Winter is Spring.
parts.answer:
FUNCTION NextSeason(S : TSeason) RETURNS TSeason
   DECLARE Result : TSeason
   CASE OF S
      Spring : Result ← Summer
      Summer : Result ← Autumn
      Autumn : Result ← Winter
      Winter : Result ← Spring
   ENDCASE
   RETURN Result
ENDFUNCTION
parts.working: B1 function header and ENDFUNCTION. B1 CASE (or IF) structure on S. B1 Spring→Summer, Summer→Autumn, Autumn→Winter. B1 Winter→Spring and value returned. Accept IF S = Winter THEN RETURN Spring ELSE RETURN S + 1 if the language allows arithmetic on ordinal values.

parts.answer: The code is easier to read and understand (Summer rather than 2), and the variable can only take one of the four valid values, so invalid values such as 7 are rejected.
parts.working: B1 readability / self-documenting. B1 restricts to valid values / fewer errors.

      IF Squad[Index].Innings = 0 THEN
         OUTPUT Squad[Index].Name, " no innings"

         OUTPUT Squad[Index].Name, " ", Squad[Index].Runs / Squad[Index].Innings

practice.stem:
A linked list is held in dynamic memory.
TYPE TNodePtr = ^TNode
TYPE TNode
   DECLARE Data : INTEGER
   DECLARE Next : TNodePtr
ENDTYPE

address 3040: Data 12, Next 3016

address 3088: Data 7, Next NULL

parts.answer:
FUNCTION ListTotal() RETURNS INTEGER
   DECLARE Current : TNodePtr
   DECLARE Total : INTEGER
   Total ← 0
   Current ← StartPtr
   WHILE Current <> NULL
      Total ← Total + Current^.Data
      Current ← Current^.Next

   RETURN Total

import math   # at the top of the program

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Describe each method of file organisation.
(i) serial
(ii) sequential
(iii) random
parts.answer: (i) Records are stored one after another in the order in which they were added (chronological), not sorted. (ii) Records are stored in order of a key field. (iii) The address of each record is calculated from its key using a hashing algorithm, so records can be stored anywhere in the file.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the difference between sequential access and direct access.
parts.answer: Sequential access reads records one after another from the start of the file until the required one is found. Direct access goes straight to the required record's location (e.g. by hashing the key or using an index) without reading the others.
parts.working: B1 sequential. B1 direct.

parts.label: a
parts.text:

(i) a log of every card transaction made at a supermarket checkout during the day
(ii) a monthly payroll file of 3000 employees, processed in employee number order
(iii) a flight booking system where any passenger's booking must be found instantly
parts.answer: (i) serial – records only need adding to the end as they happen; no order needed. (ii) sequential – every record is processed in key order in one batch run. (iii) random – the record can be accessed directly using a hash of the booking reference, giving fast access to individual records.
parts.working: B1 organisation and B1 reason for each.

practice.stem: A warehouse in Karachi stores product records in a random file with 97 record locations, numbered 0 to 96. The hashing algorithm is: location = ProductCode MOD 97.

parts.label: a
parts.text:

(iii) 30172
(iv) 15601

parts.answer: Two different keys (20451 and 15601) hash to the same location (a collision). 1: Open hashing / linear probing – store the record in the next free location after 81 (82, 83 …); a search starts at 81 and checks onwards. 2: Overflow area – store the record in a separate overflow area that is searched serially when the home location holds a different key (or chain the records with pointers).

parts.answer: Because records are in key order, the search can stop as soon as it reads a record with a larger ID than the one wanted.

practice.stem:
Student ID numbers are stored in a hash table so they can be found quickly. Write your answers in Python. (Java or VB.NET are also accepted.)
The global list HashTable has 11 elements, numbered 0 to 10. An element with the value −1 is empty. The hash value of a key is Key MOD 11. Collisions are dealt with by linear probing (wrapping round from 10 to 0).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a function Insert(Key) that stores Key in HashTable and returns True, or returns False if the table is full.
parts.answer:
TableSize = 11
HashTable = [-1] * TableSize

def Hash(Key):
    return Key % TableSize

def Insert(Key):
    Index = Hash(Key)
    Count = 0
    while HashTable[Index] != -1 and Count < TableSize:
        Index = (Index + 1) % TableSize
        Count = Count + 1
    if Count == TableSize:
        return False
    HashTable[Index] = Key
    return True
parts.working: 1 mark each: hash calculated with MOD 11; loop while location not empty; index incremented with wrap-around (MOD 11); full table detected and False returned; key stored and True returned.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write a function Search(Key) that returns the index where Key is stored, or −1 if it is not in the table. The search must stop at an empty element.
parts.working: 1 mark each: starts at hash position; loops until key found; returns −1 at an empty element or after checking every element; returns index when found.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The keys 4521, 3307, 1189, 8806, 2214, 6630, 7015, 9874 are inserted in this order. Give the final contents of HashTable and the values returned by Search(9874) and Search(5000).
parts.working: B1 first six keys at their hash positions (0, 7, 1, 6, 3, 8). B1 7015 at 9 (collision at 8). B1 9874 at 10 (7, 8, 9 full). B1 Search(9874) = 10 and Search(5000) = −1 (checks 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 0, 1 then empty 2). Tested in Python 3.

practice.stem:
A clinic in Faisalabad stores patient data in the table PATIENT. Some of the data is shown.
PATIENT
PatientID | FirstName | LastName | City | BloodGroup | Age
P101 | Ayesha | Khan | Lahore | O+ | 34
P102 | Bilal | Ahmed | Faisalabad | A+ | 51
P103 | Sana | Raza | Lahore | B+ | 27
P104 | Hamza | Qureshi | Faisalabad | O+ | 45
P105 | Mehwish | Iqbal | Multan | O+ | 62
P106 | Usman | Tariq | Lahore | O+ | 19
P107 | Zara | Malik | Faisalabad | AB- | 38

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an SQL query to return the first name and last name of every patient with blood group O+ who is older than 30. List the patients with the oldest first.
parts.answer:
SELECT FirstName, LastName
FROM PATIENT
WHERE BloodGroup = 'O+' AND Age > 30
ORDER BY Age DESC;
parts.working: 1 mark each: SELECT FirstName, LastName; FROM PATIENT; WHERE BloodGroup = 'O+' AND Age > 30 (both conditions); ORDER BY Age DESC.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write down the output of the query from part (a) when it is run on the data shown.
parts.answer: Mehwish Iqbal; Hamza Qureshi; Ayesha Khan (in this order).
parts.working: 1 mark for the correct three patients only, 1 mark for the correct order.

parts.label: c
parts.text:
State the output of this query:
SELECT COUNT(PatientID) FROM PATIENT WHERE City = 'Lahore';

practice.stem:
A school library in Nairobi uses the table:
BOOK(BookID, Title, Author, YearPublished, OnLoan)
BookID is a string such as 'B0123'. YearPublished is an integer. OnLoan is a Boolean.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A new book has arrived: BookID B0457, title 'Ocean Engineers', author 'L. Marsh', 2023, available. Write an SQL statement to add this book to the table.
parts.answer:
INSERT INTO BOOK (BookID, Title, Author, YearPublished, OnLoan)
VALUES ('B0457', 'Ocean Engineers', 'L. Marsh', 2023, FALSE);
parts.working: 1 mark INSERT INTO BOOK (with or without field list); 1 mark VALUES with all five values in the correct order; 1 mark strings in quotes and Boolean/number not in quotes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Book B0219 has just been borrowed. Write an SQL statement to record this.
parts.working: 1 mark UPDATE BOOK SET OnLoan = TRUE; 1 mark WHERE BookID = 'B0219'.

parts.label: c
parts.text: All books published before 1990 are being given to another library. Write an SQL statement to remove them from the table.
parts.answer:
DELETE FROM BOOK
WHERE YearPublished < 1990;
parts.working: 1 mark DELETE FROM BOOK; 1 mark WHERE YearPublished < 1990.

practice.stem:
A school in Quetta has these two tables:
STUDENT(StudentID, StudentName, ClassID)
CLASS(ClassID, TeacherName, Room)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an SQL query to output the name of each student together with the room of that student's class, for all students in classes taught by 'Mr Siddiqui'.
parts.answer:
SELECT STUDENT.StudentName, CLASS.Room
FROM STUDENT
INNER JOIN CLASS ON STUDENT.ClassID = CLASS.ClassID
WHERE CLASS.TeacherName = 'Mr Siddiqui';
parts.working: 1 mark SELECT StudentName, Room; 1 mark FROM STUDENT INNER JOIN CLASS; 1 mark ON STUDENT.ClassID = CLASS.ClassID; 1 mark WHERE TeacherName = 'Mr Siddiqui'. Accept FROM STUDENT, CLASS WHERE STUDENT.ClassID = CLASS.ClassID AND …

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the attribute ClassID is needed in both tables.
parts.answer: ClassID is the primary key of CLASS and a foreign key in STUDENT; it links each student to one class so the tables can be joined.
parts.working: 1 mark: primary key in CLASS / foreign key in STUDENT; 1 mark: creates the relationship/link so data from both tables can be combined (joined) without storing teacher and room for every student.

practice.stem:
A bakery in Karachi records sales in the table SALE.
SALE
SaleID | Item | Quantity
S01 | Naan | 40
S02 | Rusk | 15
S03 | Naan | 25
S04 | Cake | 6
S05 | Rusk | 20
S06 | Naan | 35
S07 | Cake | 4

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Write the output of this query.
SELECT Item, SUM(Quantity)
FROM SALE
GROUP BY Item
ORDER BY Item;
parts.answer:
Cake 10
Naan 100
Rusk 35
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct row (Cake 10, Naan 100, Rusk 35) in alphabetical order; deduct 1 if order wrong.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write an SQL query to output the number of sales (rows) recorded for the item 'Naan'.
parts.working: 1 mark SELECT COUNT(…) FROM SALE; 1 mark WHERE Item = 'Naan'. (Output would be 3.)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write an SQL query to output the average quantity per sale of 'Rusk'.
parts.working: 1 mark SELECT AVG(Quantity) FROM SALE; 1 mark WHERE Item = 'Rusk'. (Output would be 17.5.)

practice.stem:
A weather service stores monthly rainfall readings for one month each year.
READING
ReadingID | Station | YearTaken | RainfallMM
M1 | Lahore | 2023 | 18.4
M2 | Murree | 2023 | 41.2
M3 | Lahore | 2024 | 22.6
M4 | Karachi | 2024 | 5.8
M5 | Murree | 2024 | 36.0
M6 | Karachi | 2023 | 7.4

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an SQL query to output the station and the rainfall for every reading taken in 2024 with more than 20 mm of rain.
parts.working: 1 mark SELECT Station, RainfallMM; 1 mark FROM READING; 1 mark WHERE YearTaken = 2024 AND RainfallMM > 20.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The query SELECT AVG(RainfallMM) FROM READING WHERE YearTaken = 2024; is run. Calculate the value output, correct to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write an SQL query to output each station once, with the total rainfall recorded at that station.
parts.working: 1 mark SELECT Station, SUM(RainfallMM); 1 mark FROM READING; 1 mark GROUP BY Station.

practice.stem:
A sports club in Singapore uses three tables:
MEMBER(MemberID, MemberName, JoinDate)
COURT(CourtID, Surface, Indoor)
BOOKING(BookingID, MemberID, CourtID, BookingDate, StartTime)
Indoor is a Boolean field.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an SQL query to output the name of each member and the number of bookings that member has made, for bookings of courts that are indoor. Output the members with the most bookings first.
parts.answer:
SELECT MEMBER.MemberName, COUNT(BOOKING.BookingID)
FROM MEMBER
INNER JOIN BOOKING ON MEMBER.MemberID = BOOKING.MemberID
INNER JOIN COURT ON BOOKING.CourtID = COURT.CourtID
WHERE COURT.Indoor = TRUE
GROUP BY MEMBER.MemberName
ORDER BY COUNT(BOOKING.BookingID) DESC;
parts.working: 1 mark each: SELECT MemberName, COUNT(BookingID); join MEMBER to BOOKING on MemberID; join BOOKING to COURT on CourtID; WHERE Indoor = TRUE; GROUP BY MemberName (or MemberID); ORDER BY COUNT(…) DESC. Accept joins written as conditions in WHERE.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why GROUP BY is needed in your query.
parts.answer: Without GROUP BY, COUNT would give one total for all rows; GROUP BY makes a separate count for each member.
parts.working: 1 mark: aggregate function COUNT combines rows; 1 mark: GROUP BY makes one result row (count) per member instead of a single overall count.

practice.stem:
An airline at Islamabad airport wants a list of flight numbers, destinations and departure times for flights to Dubai that still have seats, earliest first. A trainee wrote:
SELECT FlightNo Destination, DepartTime
FROM FLIGHT
ORDER BY DepartTime ASCENDING
WHERE Destination = Dubai AND Seats > 0;
The table is FLIGHT(FlightNo, Destination, DepartTime, Seats).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The script contains four errors. Identify three of the errors and write the fully corrected script.
parts.answer:
Any three of the four errors: (1) SELECT list items must be separated by commas (FlightNo, Destination); (2) the condition is written 'Destination = Dubai' without quotes – a string must be in quotes 'Dubai'; (3) ORDER BY is written before WHERE – WHERE must come before ORDER BY. (4) ASCENDING is not valid – use ASC or omit it.
Corrected:
SELECT FlightNo, Destination, DepartTime
FROM FLIGHT
WHERE Destination = 'Dubai' AND Seats > 0
ORDER BY DepartTime;
parts.working: 1 mark for each error identified (max 3): comma missing between FlightNo and Destination; 'Dubai' not in quotes; clause order (WHERE must come before ORDER BY); 'ASCENDING' should be ASC or omitted. 3 marks for the corrected script: 1 mark SELECT list with commas; 1 mark WHERE Destination = 'Dubai' AND Seats > 0 placed before ORDER BY; 1 mark ORDER BY DepartTime (or DepartTime ASC).

practice.stem:
A software company stores staff data.
STAFF
StaffID | Name | Department | Salary | Office
E1 | Rahim | Sales | 52000 | Dhaka
E2 | Leila | IT | 61000 | Karachi
E3 | Tom | IT | 48000 | Dhaka
E4 | Nadia | Sales | 45000 | Karachi
E5 | Imran | HR | 39000 | Karachi
E6 | Mei | IT | 70000 | Dhaka

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State the output of this query.
SELECT Name FROM STAFF
WHERE Department = 'IT' OR Salary > 50000
ORDER BY Salary DESC;
parts.answer: Mei, Leila, Rahim, Tom
parts.working: 1 mark correct four names only (Rahim is included because Salary > 50000; Tom because Department = 'IT'); 1 mark correct order by salary descending.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
State the output of this query.
SELECT Name FROM STAFF
WHERE Department = 'IT' AND Office = 'Dhaka' OR Salary < 40000
ORDER BY Name;
parts.answer: Imran, Mei, Tom
parts.working: AND is applied before OR. 1 mark correct three names (Tom and Mei: IT in Dhaka; Imran: salary < 40000); 1 mark alphabetical order.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write an SQL statement to give every member of the Sales department a pay rise of 2000.
parts.working: 1 mark UPDATE STAFF; 1 mark SET Salary = Salary + 2000; 1 mark WHERE Department = 'Sales'.

practice.stem: A secondary school in Hyderabad stores its data in separate files.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The school's fee office and exam office each keep their own file containing students' names and addresses. Describe two problems this file-based approach can cause.
parts.answer: Data redundancy: the same student data is stored twice, wasting storage. Data inconsistency: if a family moves and only one office updates the address, the two files disagree.
parts.working: Max 2 problems, 2 marks each (identify + describe in context): data redundancy – same data stored in several files; data inconsistency – copies updated in one file but not another; data dependence – programs tied to file structure so changing a file means rewriting programs; difficult to share / search across files.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how a relational database would reduce one of these problems.
parts.answer: Student details are stored once in one table and linked to other tables using keys, so there is only one copy to update.
parts.working: B1: data stored once / in one table, linked by primary–foreign keys.

practice.stem: A hospital in Peshawar uses a relational DBMS.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a data dictionary.
parts.answer: A file/table, managed by the DBMS, that stores metadata – data about the data in the database.
parts.working: B1: stores metadata / data about the data (descriptions of the database structure).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give three items that would be stored in the data dictionary for this database.
parts.answer: Any three of: table names; field (attribute) names; data types of fields; field lengths; primary keys; foreign keys / relationships; validation rules; indexes; access rights of users.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three valid items.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what is meant by the logical schema of a database.
parts.answer: A model of the whole database showing its tables, attributes, keys and relationships, independent of how the data is physically stored.
parts.working: 1 mark: overall view/model of the structure (tables, fields, relationships); 1 mark: independent of the physical storage / DBMS software.

practice.stem: A private medical centre in Islamabad stores patient records, appointments and diagnoses in a database.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe three ways the DBMS can be used to keep the patient data secure.
parts.answer: Access rights: each user group (e.g. receptionists) is given permission to read/edit only some tables, so receptionists cannot see diagnoses. Usernames and passwords: only authorised staff can log in to the database. Backups: regular copies of the database are made (e.g. nightly) so data can be restored after loss.
parts.working: 2 marks per method (identify + describe in context), max 3 methods: access rights/user privileges; usernames and passwords; encryption of stored data; regular backups; audit trail/logging of access; views limiting what a user sees.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why receptionists should be given different access rights from doctors.
parts.answer: Receptionists only need contact and appointment details; restricting them protects confidential medical data and reduces the chance of accidental or malicious changes.
parts.working: 1 mark: they only need some of the data (appointments/contact details); 1 mark: medical records are confidential / prevents unauthorised viewing or changing.

practice.stem: A developer is building a stock database for an electronics shop in Dubai.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the purpose of the developer interface of a DBMS.
parts.answer: It lets a developer create and manipulate the database structure and objects (tables, queries, forms, reports) without writing all the code, e.g. using design views and drag-and-drop tools.
parts.working: 1 mark: allows developers to create/design tables, queries, forms, reports; 1 mark: by a visual interface / without writing low-level code / with wizards.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the purpose of the query processor of a DBMS.
parts.answer: It takes a query (e.g. in SQL), checks and optimises it and then executes it on the database, returning the results.
parts.working: 1 mark: receives/interprets queries (SQL); 1 mark: optimises and executes them, searching the data and returning results.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one reason why the developer would use SQL directly instead of the developer interface.
parts.answer: Any one: SQL can be embedded in a program/website; complex queries are easier to write precisely; SQL scripts can be saved and re-run; works on any relational DBMS.
parts.working: B1 any valid reason.

practice.stem: A car-rental firm in Lahore has the tables CUSTOMER(CustomerID, Name, Phone) and RENTAL(RentalID, CustomerID, CarReg, StartDate).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by referential integrity.
parts.answer: Every foreign key value must match an existing primary key value in the linked table (or be null), so no record refers to a record that does not exist.
parts.working: 1 mark: foreign key value must exist as a primary key in the related table; 1 mark: prevents records referring to non-existent records / orphan records.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The DBMS enforces referential integrity. Describe two actions that would be refused.
parts.answer: Adding a RENTAL record with a CustomerID that is not in CUSTOMER would be refused. Deleting a CUSTOMER record while RENTAL records still contain that CustomerID would be refused.
parts.working: 2 marks each: inserting a child (RENTAL) record whose foreign key does not exist in the parent table; deleting/changing a parent (CUSTOMER) primary key that is still used by child records.

practice.stem: A regional cricket league in Sialkot keeps player details, team lists, match scores and player medical notes in several spreadsheets, one per team. Many players appear in more than one spreadsheet. Results are also shown on a public website.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how using a relational database managed by a DBMS will improve data integrity, data privacy and data independence for the league, compared with the spreadsheets. Refer to the scenario.
parts.answer: Integrity: each player is stored once in a PLAYER table and linked by PlayerID, so there are no conflicting copies; validation rules and referential integrity stop scores being recorded for non-existent players. Privacy: access rights mean coaches can view only their own team's medical data, and the public website account can only read results. Independence: the data dictionary/schema separates the data from the programs, so a new field (e.g. strike rate) can be added without rewriting the scoring and website programs.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for each of the three areas (1 for the DBMS feature, 1 for linking it to the cricket scenario): integrity – single copy, validation, referential integrity; privacy – access rights, passwords, views, encryption; independence – structure held separately in schema/data dictionary so applications unaffected by changes.

practice.stem: A vehicle-licensing office stores data about vehicles and their owners in two tables, VEHICLE and OWNER(OwnerID, Name, Address).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define each of these terms: entity, tuple, attribute.
parts.answer: Entity: a thing about which data is stored (e.g. a vehicle). Tuple: one row/record in a table. Attribute: one field/column in a table holding one item of data.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the primary key of the table VEHICLE(RegNo, Make, Model, Colour, OwnerID) and justify your choice.
parts.answer: RegNo – every vehicle has a unique registration number.
parts.working: 1 mark RegNo; 1 mark it is unique for each vehicle/record.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify the foreign key in VEHICLE and state the table it links to.
parts.answer: OwnerID; it links to the OWNER table (where OwnerID is the primary key).
parts.working: 1 mark OwnerID; 1 mark links to OWNER / primary key in owner table.

practice.stem:
A bank in Kenya uses three tables:
BRANCH(BranchCode, Town, ManagerName)
ACCOUNT(AccountNo, HolderName, BranchCode, Balance)
TRANSACTION(TransID, AccountNo, TransDate, Amount)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the primary key of each table.
parts.answer: BRANCH: BranchCode; ACCOUNT: AccountNo; TRANSACTION: TransID.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the foreign keys, and for each one name the table where it is the primary key.
parts.answer: ACCOUNT.BranchCode → BRANCH; TRANSACTION.AccountNo → ACCOUNT.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A university in Lahore stores staff data in the table STAFF(StaffID, CNIC, Email, FirstName, LastName, Department). Each member of staff has a unique StaffID, a unique CNIC number and a unique email address.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a candidate key. Use this table to illustrate your answer.
parts.answer: An attribute (or smallest set of attributes) that could uniquely identify every record and so could be chosen as the primary key; here StaffID, CNIC and Email are all candidate keys.
parts.working: 1 mark: attribute(s) that could be a primary key / uniquely identify each tuple; 1 mark: example StaffID or CNIC (or Email).

parts.label: b
parts.text: StaffID has been chosen as the primary key. State the term for a candidate key that is not chosen as primary key, and give one example from the table.
parts.answer: Alternate key; CNIC (or Email).
parts.working: 1 mark alternate key; 1 mark CNIC/Email.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the database designer might create a secondary key (index) on LastName.
parts.answer: Staff are often searched by last name; an index on LastName lets the DBMS find matching records quickly without scanning the whole table.
parts.working: 1 mark: LastName is frequently used to search/sort; 1 mark: index makes searching faster. Note LastName is not unique, so it cannot be a primary key.

practice.stem:
An exam centre stores:
STUDENT(StudentID, Name, DateOfBirth)
EXAM(ExamID, Subject, ExamDate)
RESULT(StudentID, ExamID, Mark)
Each student takes each exam at most once.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why ExamID alone is not a suitable primary key for RESULT.
parts.answer: The same exam is taken by many students, so ExamID repeats in many rows and cannot uniquely identify a record.
parts.working: 1 mark ExamID values repeat; 1 mark so not unique for each row.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify a composite primary key for RESULT and explain why it is suitable.
parts.answer: (StudentID, ExamID): each student takes each exam once, so the pair is unique.
parts.working: 1 mark StudentID + ExamID; 1 mark the combination is unique.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the relationship between STUDENT and RESULT, and between EXAM and RESULT.
parts.answer: STUDENT to RESULT is one-to-many; EXAM to RESULT is one-to-many.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem:
An online shop in Doha has:
PRODUCT(ProductID, Description, Price) containing products K10, K11 and K12
ORDERS(OrderID, CustomerID, OrderDate) containing orders O77 and O78
ORDERLINE(OrderID, ProductID, Quantity), which is empty before the statements below are run in order.

parts.label: a
parts.answer: (i) Accepted – K12 exists in PRODUCT (and O77 exists in ORDERS). (ii) Refused – there is no product K30 in PRODUCT. (iii) Refused – order line O77/K12 still refers to product K12.
parts.working: 1 mark each with reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one change to the data that would allow statement (iii) to be accepted.
parts.answer: Delete (or change) all ORDERLINE records that refer to product K12 first.

practice.stem:
A gym membership table is shown.
MEMBER
MemberNo | FirstName | LastName | Email | Phone
A01 | Hira | Farooq | hira.f@mail.pk | 0300-111
A02 | Ali | Shah | ali.s@mail.pk | 0300-222
A03 | Hira | Shah | hshah@mail.pk | 0300-333
A04 | Kamran | Farooq | kf@mail.pk | 0300-222

parts.label: a
parts.text: From the data shown, identify which single attributes could be candidate keys. Give a reason for each attribute you reject.
parts.answer: Candidate keys: MemberNo and Email (all values are unique and every member has their own). Rejected: FirstName – 'Hira' appears twice; LastName – 'Farooq' and 'Shah' repeat; Phone – '0300-222' is shared by two members (a family phone).
parts.working: 1 mark MemberNo and Email identified; 1 mark FirstName rejected (repeat); 1 mark LastName rejected (repeat); 1 mark Phone rejected (two members share a number).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a database designer cannot decide that an attribute is a candidate key just by looking at the current data.
parts.answer: The current data may happen to be unique, but future records could repeat the value; the designer must know the rule in the real world (e.g. emails must be unique) that guarantees uniqueness.
parts.working: 1 mark: current values unique by chance / more data will be added; 1 mark: must be guaranteed unique by the business rule / real-world meaning.

practice.stem: A hospital in Karachi is designing a database.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each pair of entities, state the type of relationship (one-to-one, one-to-many or many-to-many).
(i) DEPARTMENT and DOCTOR: each doctor works in one department; a department has many doctors.
(ii) DOCTOR and PATIENT: a doctor treats many patients; a patient can be treated by many doctors.
(iii) WARD and BED: a bed belongs to one ward; a ward has many beds.
parts.answer: (i) one-to-many (DEPARTMENT to DOCTOR). (ii) many-to-many. (iii) one-to-many (WARD to BED).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the one-to-many relationship between WARD and BED is shown in an E-R diagram.
parts.answer: A line joins the WARD and BED boxes; the end at BED has a crow's foot (many) and the end at WARD a single line (one).
parts.working: 1 mark line connecting the two entity boxes; 1 mark crow's foot at the BED (many) end only.

practice.stem: An online learning platform used across South Asia has STUDENT(StudentID, Name, Country) and COURSE(CourseCode, Title, Hours). A student enrols on many courses and a course has many students.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the many-to-many relationship between STUDENT and COURSE cannot be implemented directly in a relational database.
parts.answer: A field can only hold one value, so a student record cannot hold a list of courses (or a course a list of students) without repeating groups / redundancy.
parts.working: 1 mark: attributes are atomic – cannot store several foreign keys in one field; 1 mark: would cause repeating groups/redundant rows.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the design should be changed. Give the attributes and primary key of any new table and describe the new relationships.
parts.answer: Add a link entity ENROLMENT(StudentID, CourseCode, StartDate) with composite primary key (StudentID, CourseCode), each part being a foreign key. STUDENT to ENROLMENT is one-to-many; COURSE to ENROLMENT is one-to-many.
parts.working: 1 mark new link table; 1 mark contains StudentID and CourseCode as foreign keys; 1 mark composite primary key (StudentID, CourseCode); 1 mark two one-to-many relationships replace the many-to-many.

practice.stem: A ride-hailing company in Islamabad: each driver registers exactly one car and each car belongs to exactly one driver. A driver makes many rides. Each ride has one passenger, and a passenger can make many rides.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the relationships that should appear in the E-R diagram for DRIVER, CAR, RIDE and PASSENGER, stating the degree of each.
parts.answer: DRIVER–CAR: one-to-one (each driver registers one car, each car has one driver). DRIVER–RIDE: one-to-many. PASSENGER–RIDE: one-to-many. CAR–RIDE: one-to-many (optional; implied through driver).
parts.working: 1 mark each for DRIVER–CAR 1:1, DRIVER–RIDE 1:M, PASSENGER–RIDE 1:M; 1 mark for showing RIDE as the 'many' side holding the foreign keys DriverID and PassengerID.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the foreign keys that the RIDE table must contain.
parts.answer: DriverID and PassengerID.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A wildlife park near Lahore wants a database. Each animal has an ID, a name and a date of birth, belongs to one species and lives in one enclosure. Each species has a common name and a conservation status. Each enclosure has an ID, a zone and an area in m². Each keeper has an ID, a name and a phone number. A keeper looks after many animals and each animal is looked after by several keepers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Design a set of tables in third normal form for this scenario. Give each table in the form TABLE(Attribute1, Attribute2, …), show the primary key by writing it in capitals, and describe every relationship in the E-R diagram in words.
parts.answer:
SPECIES(SPECIESID, CommonName, ConservationStatus)
ENCLOSURE(ENCLOSUREID, Zone, AreaM2)
ANIMAL(ANIMALID, Name, DateOfBirth, SpeciesID, EnclosureID)
KEEPER(KEEPERID, KeeperName, Phone)
CARES(KEEPERID, ANIMALID) – link table
Relationships: SPECIES 1–M ANIMAL; ENCLOSURE 1–M ANIMAL; KEEPER 1–M CARES; ANIMAL 1–M CARES (resolving KEEPER M–M ANIMAL).
parts.working: 1 mark each to max 8: SPECIES table with key; ENCLOSURE table with key; ANIMAL table with key; SpeciesID and EnclosureID as foreign keys in ANIMAL; KEEPER table with key; link table for keepers and animals; composite key of link table; correct description of all relationships (1:M each, M:M resolved). Accept CommonName as the primary key of SPECIES (with CommonName as the foreign key in ANIMAL) if justified as unique.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the condition for a table to be in first normal form (1NF).
parts.answer: It has no repeating groups of attributes (each field holds a single atomic value).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the extra condition for a table in 1NF to be in second normal form (2NF).
parts.answer: It has no partial dependencies: every non-key attribute depends on the whole of the primary key, not on just part of a composite key.
parts.working: 1 mark depends on the whole key; 1 mark no partial key dependency (relevant to composite keys).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the extra condition for a table in 2NF to be in third normal form (3NF).
parts.answer: It has no non-key (transitive) dependencies: no non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute.
parts.working: 1 mark no non-key dependencies; 1 mark every non-key attribute depends only on the key.

practice.stem:
A community centre in Abu Dhabi stores members and the courses they attend:
MEMBERCOURSES(MemberID, MemberName, Phone, Courses)
Example row: M17, Faisal Haider, 050-1234567, 'C3 Arabic; C5 First Aid; C9 Chess'
Each course has a code and a title.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the table is not in 1NF.
parts.answer: It has a repeating group – the Courses attribute holds several course codes in one field.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show the data in 1NF and 2NF. Write each table in the form TABLE(Attribute1, …), with the primary key in capitals.
parts.answer:
1NF: ENROL(MEMBERID, COURSECODE, MemberName, Phone, CourseTitle)
2NF: MEMBER(MEMBERID, MemberName, Phone); COURSE(COURSECODE, CourseTitle); MEMBERCOURSE(MEMBERID, COURSECODE)
parts.working: 1 mark 1NF table with composite key MemberID + CourseCode; 1 mark MEMBER table; 1 mark COURSE table; 1 mark link table with composite key.

practice.stem:
A spare-parts dealer in Gujranwala stores invoices as:
SALES(InvoiceNo, InvoiceDate, CustomerID, CustomerName, CustomerCity, PartNo, PartName, UnitPrice, Quantity)
One invoice can contain many parts; the quantity is for that part on that invoice.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The table is in 1NF with primary key (InvoiceNo, PartNo). Identify the partial dependencies and the transitive (non-key) dependency.
parts.answer: Partial: InvoiceDate, CustomerID, CustomerName and CustomerCity depend on InvoiceNo only; PartName and UnitPrice depend on PartNo only. Transitive: CustomerName and CustomerCity depend on CustomerID (a non-key attribute).
parts.working: 1 mark invoice attributes depend on InvoiceNo only; 1 mark part attributes depend on PartNo only; 1 mark CustomerName/CustomerCity depend on CustomerID.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Normalise the data to 3NF. Write each table in the form TABLE(Attribute1, …), with the primary key in capitals, and identify the foreign keys.
parts.answer:
INVOICE(INVOICENO, InvoiceDate, CustomerID) – CustomerID foreign key
CUSTOMER(CUSTOMERID, CustomerName, CustomerCity)
PART(PARTNO, PartName, UnitPrice)
INVOICELINE(INVOICENO, PARTNO, Quantity) – both parts are foreign keys
parts.working: 1 mark each table with correct key (4); 1 mark foreign keys correctly identified. Quantity must stay with the composite key.

practice.stem: A tourism board is building a database of heritage sites such as Lahore Fort and Mohenjo-daro.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the SQL to create the database HERITAGE.
parts.answer: CREATE DATABASE HERITAGE;

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the SQL to create the table SITE with these fields: SiteID (exactly 5 characters, primary key), SiteName (up to 40 characters), City (up to 25 characters), YearBuilt (whole number), EntryFee (a decimal number), UNESCO (true/false).
parts.answer:
CREATE TABLE SITE(
 SiteID CHARACTER(5),
 SiteName VARCHAR(40),
 City VARCHAR(25),
 YearBuilt INTEGER,
 EntryFee REAL,
 UNESCO BOOLEAN,
 PRIMARY KEY (SiteID)
);
parts.working: 1 mark CREATE TABLE SITE( … ); 1 mark SiteID CHARACTER(5); 1 mark VARCHAR for SiteName and City with lengths; 1 mark INTEGER, REAL and BOOLEAN types correct; 1 mark PRIMARY KEY (SiteID).

practice.stem: A railway booking system has the tables TRAIN(TrainNo, TrainName, Coaches) and JOURNEY(JourneyID, TrainNo, TravelDate, DepartureTime).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the SQL to add a new field Platform, a whole number, to the table TRAIN.
parts.answer: ALTER TABLE TRAIN ADD Platform INTEGER;
parts.working: 1 mark ALTER TABLE TRAIN; 1 mark ADD Platform INTEGER.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The table JOURNEY was created without keys. Write SQL to make JourneyID its primary key and TrainNo a foreign key that refers to TRAIN.
parts.answer:
ALTER TABLE JOURNEY ADD PRIMARY KEY (JourneyID);
ALTER TABLE JOURNEY ADD FOREIGN KEY (TrainNo) REFERENCES TRAIN(TrainNo);
parts.working: 1 mark ALTER TABLE JOURNEY ADD PRIMARY KEY; 1 mark (JourneyID); 1 mark ADD FOREIGN KEY (TrainNo); 1 mark REFERENCES TRAIN(TrainNo).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one data type suitable for DepartureTime and one suitable for TravelDate.
parts.answer: DepartureTime: TIME; TravelDate: DATE.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A city air-quality project in Lahore records PM2.5 readings. Each sensor has a 4-character ID, a location (up to 30 characters) and the date it was installed.
