parts.working: 2 marks all correct; 1 mark two or three correct.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why RISC processors are well suited to pipelining.
parts.answer: RISC instructions are of fixed length and most take one clock cycle, so each stage takes the same time and the stages stay in step / the pipeline flows smoothly.
parts.working: 1 mark fixed length / one cycle; 1 mark stages balanced.

practice.stem: A RISC processor uses a 5-stage pipeline.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the problem caused when an interrupt occurs in a pipelined processor, and describe one way it can be handled.
parts.answer:
Problem: several instructions are partly processed in different stages when the interrupt arrives, so the processor state cannot be saved simply by storing one program counter value.
Handling (any one, 2 marks): the instructions in the early stages are flushed/erased, the instruction(s) already in the execute stage are completed, and the address of the next instruction to restart is saved before the interrupt service routine runs; OR each stage has its own program-counter register so the contents of the pipeline can be saved and restored after the interrupt.
parts.working: 1 mark problem; 2 marks a described method.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a conditional branch (jump) instruction reduces the performance of the pipeline.
parts.answer: The next instructions are fetched in sequence before the branch is executed; if the branch is taken, these instructions are wrong and must be discarded (pipeline flushed), so cycles are wasted until the pipeline refills.
parts.working: 1 mark wrong instructions already fetched; 1 mark flush / wasted cycles.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one technique used to reduce this loss.
parts.answer: Branch prediction / speculative execution / delayed branch (filling the slot after a branch with a useful instruction).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term pixel.
parts.answer: The smallest addressable element (dot) of a bitmap image, which has a single colour.
parts.working: B1: smallest element / dot of a bitmap image that can be given a colour.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define the term image resolution.
parts.answer: The number of pixels in the image, given as width × height in pixels.
parts.working: B1: number of pixels (wide × high) in the image. Do not accept screen resolution or 'pixels per inch of a screen'.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Define the term colour depth.
parts.answer: The number of bits used to store the colour of each pixel.
parts.working: B1: number of bits per pixel (used to represent its colour).

parts.label: d
parts.text: A bitmap file has a file header. State two items of data that are stored in the file header.
parts.answer: Any two of: image width in pixels, image height in pixels, colour depth (bits per pixel), file type / format, file size, compression type used.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: width; height (or resolution); colour depth; file type; file size; compression method; colour palette information.

practice.stem: A digital camera used by a wildlife survey team in the Margalla Hills takes bitmap photographs with a resolution of 1600 × 1200 pixels and a colour depth of 24 bits. Ignore any file header data.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the file size of the image in bytes. Show your working.
parts.answer: 5 760 000 bytes

parts.label: b
parts.text: Convert your answer to part (a) into mebibytes (MiB). Give your answer correct to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: 5.49 MiB

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each use below, state whether a bitmap or a vector graphic is more suitable and give a reason.
(i) A photograph of the Badshahi Mosque at sunset
(ii) A floor plan of a new school building made from lines and rectangles
(iii) A road-sign icon that will appear in an app at many different sizes
parts.answer: (i) Bitmap – a photograph has continuous colour/shading and fine detail that cannot be made from simple shapes. (ii) Vector – it is made of simple geometric shapes, so file size is small and it can be scaled/edited precisely. (iii) Vector – it can be resized to any size without losing quality.
parts.working: Each item: B1 correct choice, B1 matching reason. Reason must fit the use, e.g. (i) photo detail / varying colours; (ii) geometric shapes, precise editing of objects; (iii) scaling without pixelation.

practice.stem: A photo booth at a wedding hall in Lahore saves each photograph as a bitmap image of 800 × 600 pixels that can show 256 different colours.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the colour depth that is needed for 256 colours.
parts.answer: 8 bits

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the file size of one photograph in kibibytes (KiB). Ignore the file header.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The booth stores the photographs on a 2 GiB memory card. Calculate the maximum number of complete photographs that can be stored on the card.
parts.answer: 4473 photographs
parts.working: M1: 2 × 2³⁰ ÷ 480 000 (= 4473.9…); A1: 4473 (must round down to whole photographs).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the effect on the image and on the file size of increasing the colour depth from 8 bits to 16 bits, without changing the resolution.
parts.answer: More colours can be shown (65 536 instead of 256) so colours are more accurate/realistic; the file size doubles because each pixel needs twice as many bits.
parts.working: 1 mark each: more colours available / smoother, more accurate colour; file size increases (doubles) as more bits per pixel.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student reduces the resolution of a bitmap image from 1200 × 900 pixels to 400 × 300 pixels and then displays it at the original size. Explain why the displayed image looks blocky (pixelated).
parts.answer: There are fewer pixels (one ninth as many), so each pixel must be enlarged to fill the same area; detail is lost and individual pixels become visible as blocks.
parts.working: 1 mark each: fewer pixels store less detail; each pixel is stretched over a larger area so the pixels become visible / edges become jagged.

practice.stem: A cricket club in Sialkot is designing a logo made from simple shapes. The logo will be printed on small membership cards and on a large banner above the stadium entrance. The designer stores it as a vector graphic.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a drawing list in a vector graphic.
parts.answer: A list of the commands/objects that make up the image; each object is stored with its properties (for example coordinates, size, colours) so the image can be redrawn from the list.
parts.working: 1 mark each: a set of instructions/commands to draw the shapes (objects); each object has its properties stored, e.g. position, dimensions, line colour, fill colour.

parts.label: b
parts.text: One object in the logo is a circle. Its centre is at (120, 80) and its radius is 40. State three other properties that would be stored for the circle in the drawing list.
parts.answer: Any three of: line (outline) colour, line thickness, fill colour, line style (solid/dashed), layer/drawing order, transparency.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three relevant properties other than centre and radius: line colour; line width/thickness; fill colour; line style; layer/z-order; opacity.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a vector graphic is more suitable than a bitmap for this logo.
parts.answer: The logo is printed at very different sizes; a vector graphic can be scaled to any size without losing quality because it is redrawn from the drawing list, and its file size is small because it only has simple shapes.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 2: scales without pixelation / loss of quality (needed for both card and banner); file size small for simple geometric shapes / independent of output size; shapes can be edited individually.

practice.stem: A tourism office in Gilgit has a simple map of hiking routes made of coloured lines and labelled triangles. It has one version stored as a bitmap and one as a vector graphic.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what happens to the quality of each image when it is enlarged to four times its width and height.
parts.answer: Bitmap: each pixel is enlarged so the image becomes pixelated/blocky with jagged edges; no new detail is added. Vector: the shapes are recalculated from their properties and redrawn, so lines stay sharp and quality is unchanged.
parts.working: Bitmap (2): pixels stretched/made larger; image becomes blocky / blurred / jagged. Vector (2): objects redrawn using coordinates/properties; no loss of quality / edges remain smooth.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one reason why the vector version of the map has a much smaller file size than the bitmap version.
parts.answer: Only the properties of a few shapes (lines, polygons) are stored, rather than the colour of every pixel.
parts.working: B1: stores shape definitions/properties instead of data for every pixel.

practice.stem: A weather satellite takes bitmap images of 2048 × 1024 pixels. Each image must be no larger than 3 MiB of pixel data so that it can be sent to the ground station in Karachi during one pass.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the maximum colour depth that can be used. Show your working.
parts.answer: 12 bits
parts.working: M1: 3 × 2²⁰ × 8 (= 25 165 824 bits available); M1: ÷ (2048 × 1024) (= 2 097 152 pixels); A1: 12 bits per pixel.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the maximum number of different colours that each image can then contain.
parts.answer: 4096 colours
parts.working: B1: 2¹² = 4096 (follow through from (a)).

parts.label: c
parts.text: The stored files turn out to be slightly larger than 3 MiB. Give one reason why.
parts.answer: The file also contains a file header (metadata such as width, height and colour depth).
parts.working: B1: file header / metadata is stored in addition to the pixel data.

practice.stem: A quality-control camera in a textile factory in Faisalabad captures images of cloth with a resolution of 1920 × 1080 pixels and a colour depth of 24 bits.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the file size of one uncompressed frame in MiB. Give your answer correct to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: 5.93 MiB

parts.label: b
parts.text: The camera records 30 frames every second. Calculate the storage needed for 10 seconds of uncompressed frames in GiB. Give your answer correct to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: 1.74 GiB

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the factory stores the images as bitmaps and not as vector graphics.
parts.answer: The images are photographs of real objects with continuous variation of colour and fine detail; these cannot be described efficiently as geometric shapes, and the camera captures pixels directly.
parts.working: 1 mark each: real-world image / photograph with complex detail; would need a huge number of objects (or cannot be represented) as a vector; camera sensor produces pixel data.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Convert the denary number 181 into 8-bit binary.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Convert the denary number 181 into hexadecimal.
parts.answer: B5

parts.label: c
parts.text: Convert the hexadecimal number 3E7 into denary. Show your working.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Represent the denary number 739 in Binary Coded Decimal (BCD).
parts.working: B1: 0111 0011 1001 (one 4-bit nibble per denary digit).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one example of where BCD is used and explain why it is suitable.
parts.answer: A digital clock or calculator display: each digit is shown separately, so storing each denary digit as its own 4-bit code makes it easy to send to each display segment.
parts.working: B1 use: digital clock / calculator / electronic display / financial values. B1 reason: each denary digit coded separately so it maps directly to a display digit (or avoids rounding errors in money).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the 4-bit pattern 1100 can never appear in valid BCD.
parts.answer: 1100 is 12 in denary; BCD only uses the patterns for 0 to 9 (0000 to 1001).
parts.working: B1: it represents 12, which is not a single denary digit (0–9).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A register holds the 16-bit pattern 0100 1001 0010 0101. State the denary value it represents when it is interpreted as:
(i) Binary Coded Decimal
(ii) an unsigned binary integer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the same 16-bit pattern in hexadecimal.
parts.working: B1: 4925 (hex). Note it looks the same as the BCD reading because every nibble is 9 or less.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the number of bytes in 3 MiB.
parts.answer: 3 145 728 bytes

parts.label: b
parts.text: A shopkeeper in Hyderabad buys a USB flash drive labelled 2 GB. His computer reports the capacity in GiB. Calculate the difference, in bytes, between 2 GiB and 2 GB.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the computer shows a number smaller than 2 for the capacity of the drive.
parts.answer: The drive has 2 × 10⁹ bytes, but a GiB is 2³⁰ bytes (larger than 10⁹), so 2 × 10⁹ bytes is only about 1.86 GiB.
parts.working: B1: manufacturer uses decimal prefix (10⁹) but computer uses binary prefix (2³⁰), which is bigger, so fewer GiB.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of memory locations from hexadecimal address 3A00 to 3AFF inclusive.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A file is 1F400 bytes long (hexadecimal). Convert this size to kibibytes.
parts.answer: 125 KiB

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one reason why programmers often write memory addresses in hexadecimal rather than binary.
parts.answer: Hexadecimal is shorter and easier to read and remember, so there are fewer mistakes; each hex digit is exactly 4 bits so conversion is easy.
parts.working: B1: shorter / easier to read/remember / fewer errors / converts easily (1 hex digit = 4 bits).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Convert the binary number 1010111100 into hexadecimal.
parts.answer: 2BC
parts.working: B1: group from the right: 10 1011 1100 → 2BC.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A sensor sends a temperature to a control unit as two BCD digits in one byte. The byte received is 1001 0110. State the temperature it represents.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The same byte 1001 0110 is read by mistake as an unsigned binary integer. State the value that would be read and the error made.
parts.answer: 150; the reading is 54 too high.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the difference between lossy and lossless compression.
parts.answer: Lossless compression reduces file size without losing any data, so the original file can be reconstructed exactly. Lossy compression permanently removes some data (usually detail people will not notice), so the original cannot be restored exactly.
parts.working: 1 mark each: lossless – no data lost / original can be restored exactly; lossy – data permanently removed / original cannot be restored.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
For each file below, state whether lossy or lossless compression should be used and give a reason.
(i) A spreadsheet of student fees for a school in Multan
(ii) A video clip to be shared on social media
parts.answer: (i) Lossless – every number must be kept exactly; losing data would change the fees. (ii) Lossy – a smaller file is needed for fast upload/streaming, and the small loss of quality is not noticed.
parts.working: Each: B1 choice + B1 reason. (i) exact data required / text and numbers must not change. (ii) much smaller file / faster to send; loss of quality acceptable or not noticeable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show how the string AAAAABBBCDDDDDDDD could be compressed using run-length encoding.
parts.answer: 5A 3B 1C 8D
parts.working: M1: counts with characters; A1: 5A 3B 1C 8D.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Each count and each character is stored in one byte. Calculate the number of bytes saved.
parts.answer: 9 bytes

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why using RLE on the string 'PAKISTAN' would increase its size.
parts.answer: There are no repeated adjacent characters, so every character becomes a run of 1 and needs a count byte as well; 8 bytes become 16 bytes.
parts.working: 1 mark each: no consecutive repeats / every run has length 1; each character now needs 2 bytes, doubling the size (8 → 16).

practice.stem:
One row of a bitmap image uses these colour codes, from left to right (W = white, B = blue, R = red):
W W W W W W B B B W W W W W W W W R R B B B B B

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show the result of compressing this row using run-length encoding (RLE). Write each run as a count followed by the colour code.
parts.answer: 6 W 3 B 8 W 2 R 5 B
parts.working: M1: runs identified correctly (at least three); A1: 6W 3B 8W 2R 5B in order.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Each colour code and each count is stored in one byte. Before compression, each pixel uses one byte. Calculate the number of bytes saved by compressing this row.
parts.answer: 14 bytes
parts.working: M1: original 24 bytes, compressed 5 × 2 = 10 bytes; A1: 14 bytes saved.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why RLE is not effective for a photograph of a busy bazaar.
parts.answer: In a photograph neighbouring pixels are rarely exactly the same colour, so runs are very short (often length 1); each pixel would need a count as well as its colour, so the file may get bigger.
parts.working: 1 mark each: few / short runs of identical pixels; each run still needs two bytes so file size may increase.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The 8-bit greyscale image data below has been compressed with run-length encoding. Each pair of numbers is (count, grey value):
12, 0, 4, 255, 7, 0, 9, 128
State how many pixels are in the decompressed data.
parts.answer: 32 pixels

parts.label: b
parts.text: Each number in the compressed data is stored in one byte. Calculate the ratio of uncompressed size to compressed size, in its simplest form.
parts.working: M1: uncompressed 32 bytes, compressed 8 bytes; A1: 4 : 1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe the decompressed data by stating the first 14 grey values in order.

practice.stem: A music streaming service based in Karachi compresses its songs before sending them to listeners' phones.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how lossy compression reduces the size of a music file.
parts.answer: Perceptual coding removes sounds that the human ear cannot hear or will not notice: frequencies outside the range of human hearing are removed, quiet sounds masked by louder sounds at the same time are removed, and the sampling resolution / bit rate is reduced.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 3: uses perceptual music shaping / psychoacoustics; removes frequencies humans cannot hear; removes quieter sounds masked by louder ones; reduces bit rate / sampling resolution; data removed is lost permanently.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A hospital in Quetta stores X-ray images that doctors use for diagnosis. Justify why the hospital should use lossless compression for these images.
parts.answer: Lossy compression could remove fine detail or create artefacts; a doctor might miss a small fracture or misdiagnose, so every pixel must be kept exactly as captured.
parts.working: 1 mark each: all original detail must be kept / no artefacts; missing detail could lead to wrong diagnosis (medical/legal consequences).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Convert −45 into an 8-bit two's complement binary integer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Convert the 8-bit two's complement integer 10110110 into denary.
parts.working: M1: −128 + 32 + 16 + 4 + 2; A1: −74 (the minus sign is needed).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Add these two 8-bit binary integers. Show your working.
01101100 + 01011010
parts.working: M1: correct carries shown; A1: 11000110.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The two numbers in part (a) are stored as 8-bit two's complement integers. Explain why the result of the addition is not correct.
parts.answer: 108 + 90 = 198, which is greater than 127 (the largest 8-bit two's complement value); the answer 11000110 has a 1 in the sign bit so it is read as −58. This is overflow.
parts.working: 1 mark each: 108 + 90 = 198 is out of range (max +127) / overflow; result's MSB is 1 so it is read as a negative number (−58).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write 87 and −113 as 8-bit two's complement integers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use two's complement addition to calculate 87 − 113. Show your working and give the result in binary and in denary.

practice.stem: A depth sensor on a research ship records readings as 12-bit two's complement integers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the range of values that can be stored in 12-bit two's complement.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write −300 as a 12-bit two's complement integer.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The 12-bit value from part (b) is copied into a 16-bit register. State the 16-bit pattern that keeps the same value, and explain how it was formed.
parts.answer: 1111 1110 1101 0100; the sign bit (1) is copied into the four new most significant bits (sign extension).
parts.working: B1: 1111 1110 1101 0100. B1: extended by repeating the sign bit / MSB.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term sampling rate.
parts.answer: The number of samples of the sound (amplitude) taken per second.
parts.working: B1: number of samples taken per second (measured in Hz).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define the term sampling resolution.
parts.answer: The number of bits used to store each sample.
parts.working: B1: number of bits per sample (bit depth).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how an analogue sound wave is converted to digital data.
parts.answer: The amplitude of the sound wave is measured at regular time intervals (sampling); each measured amplitude is approximated to the nearest available level (quantised); each value is stored as a binary number using a fixed number of bits.
parts.working: 1 mark each: amplitude measured/sampled; at regular (set) intervals; each sample rounded to nearest value that can be represented and stored in binary (using the sampling resolution); uses an ADC. Max 3.

practice.stem: A qawwali group records a 3-minute song in stereo (2 channels) with a sampling rate of 44.1 kHz and a sampling resolution of 16 bits. Ignore any file header.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the file size of the recording in bytes. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Convert your answer to MiB, correct to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the effect of increasing the sampling rate on the recording and on the file size.
parts.answer: More samples are taken per second, so the digital sound is closer to the original analogue wave (higher frequencies captured); the file size increases because more samples are stored.
parts.working: 1 mark each: more accurate / closer to original / higher quality; larger file.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the effect of increasing the sampling resolution from 8 bits to 16 bits.
parts.answer: Each sample can take one of 65 536 levels instead of 256, so amplitudes are stored more precisely (less quantisation error, better dynamic range); each sample needs twice the bits, so the file size doubles.
parts.working: 1 mark each: more levels / more accurate amplitude / less rounding error; file size doubles (more bits per sample).

practice.stem: A journalist in Peshawar uses a voice recorder that stores mono sound with a sampling resolution of 8 bits on a 512 MiB memory card. Ignore any file header.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the maximum whole-number sampling rate, in Hz, that would allow 6 hours of recording to fit on the card. Show your working.
parts.working: M1: card size in bits 512 × 2²⁰ × 8; M1: ÷ (8 × 6 × 3600); A1: 24 855 Hz (rounded down).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The journalist decides to use 8 kHz instead. Give one advantage and one disadvantage of this choice.
parts.answer: Advantage: far more recording time / smaller files, and speech is still understandable. Disadvantage: lower quality – higher frequencies are lost, so voices sound less clear.
parts.working: B1 advantage: smaller files / more recording time / quicker to upload. B1 disadvantage: lower quality / higher frequencies not captured.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In ASCII the character 'D' has the denary code 68. State the 8-bit binary code for the character 'K'.
parts.working: M1: K is 7 letters after D so 68 + 7 = 75; A1: 01001011.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a text-messaging app used in Pakistan stores its text in Unicode rather than ASCII.
parts.answer: ASCII only has 128 (or 256 extended) codes, which cover English letters but not Urdu script; Unicode uses more bits per character, so it can represent characters from almost all languages, including Urdu and emojis.
parts.working: 1 mark each: ASCII has limited characters (7/8 bits) / no Urdu characters; Unicode uses more bits (16/32) giving many more characters, covering other languages/scripts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The ASCII code for 'g' is 103. State the ASCII code for 'G' and explain the relationship between them.
parts.answer: 71; uppercase codes are 32 less than the matching lowercase codes.
parts.working: B1: 71. B1: difference of 32 (bit 5 is 0 for uppercase / 1 for lowercase).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A message has 350 characters. Calculate how many more bytes it needs when it is stored using a 16-bit Unicode encoding than when it is stored using 8-bit ASCII.
parts.answer: 350 bytes more

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the ASCII codes for the digit characters '0' to '9' are not the same as the numbers 0 to 9.
parts.answer: They are character codes (48 to 57) used to display/store text; the character '7' is a symbol, not the numeric value 7.
parts.working: B1: digits are stored as characters with their own codes (48–57), not as their numeric value.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Define each of these object-oriented terms.
(i) class (ii) object (iii) attribute (iv) method
parts.answer: (i) A template/blueprint that defines the attributes and methods shared by objects of one type. (ii) An instance of a class, with its own values for the attributes. (iii) A data item (property) belonging to a class/object. (iv) A procedure or function defined in a class that acts on an object's data.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by encapsulation.
parts.answer: Combining the data (attributes) and the methods that act on it in one class, and hiding the data (PRIVATE) so it can only be accessed or changed through the class's own public methods.
parts.working: 1 mark: data and methods bundled together in a class/object. 1 mark: attributes hidden – accessed only via methods (getters/setters).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A transport app has a class Vehicle with attributes RegNumber and MaxPassengers and a method Describe(). The classes Rickshaw and Bus are derived from Vehicle. Explain what is meant by inheritance, using these classes.
parts.answer: Inheritance means a subclass (derived class) automatically gets the attributes and methods of its parent (base) class. Rickshaw and Bus inherit RegNumber, MaxPassengers and Describe() from Vehicle and can add their own, e.g. Bus could add RouteNumber.
parts.working: 1 mark: subclass receives attributes and methods of the superclass. 1 mark: applied to Vehicle/Rickshaw/Bus.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by polymorphism, using the method Describe().
parts.answer: Polymorphism allows a method inherited from the base class to be redefined (overridden) in a subclass so that it behaves differently: calling Describe() on a Rickshaw object gives a different output from calling it on a Bus object, even though both use the same method name.
parts.working: 1 mark: same method name, different behaviour in different classes (overriding). 1 mark: example with Describe() for Rickshaw/Bus.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a class Student, the attribute DateOfBirth is declared PRIVATE and is accessed with the methods GetDateOfBirth() and SetDateOfBirth(). Explain why the attribute is private and accessed through these methods.
parts.answer: Making it PRIVATE means code outside the class cannot read or change it directly (encapsulation/data hiding). Access is only through the getter and setter, so the class controls how the data is used. The setter can validate the new value (e.g. reject a future date) before storing it, keeping the object's data valid.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: cannot be accessed directly from outside the class; encapsulation/information hiding; getter returns the value; setter changes it in a controlled way; setter can validate data; internal representation can change without affecting other code.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the purpose of a constructor.
parts.answer: A method that is called automatically when an object is created (instantiated), to set the initial values of its attributes.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A bookshop in Lahore uses a class Book with these private attributes: ISBN (STRING), Title (STRING), Price (REAL). It has a constructor that takes values for all three attributes, a getter for Price and a method ApplyDiscount(Percent : INTEGER) that reduces Price by that percentage.
Write pseudocode for the class Book.
parts.answer:
CLASS Book
   PRIVATE ISBN : STRING
   PRIVATE Title : STRING
   PRIVATE Price : REAL
   PUBLIC PROCEDURE NEW(GivenISBN : STRING, GivenTitle : STRING, GivenPrice : REAL)
      ISBN ← GivenISBN
      Title ← GivenTitle
      Price ← GivenPrice
   ENDPROCEDURE
   PUBLIC FUNCTION GetPrice() RETURNS REAL
      RETURN Price
   ENDFUNCTION
   PUBLIC PROCEDURE ApplyDiscount(Percent : INTEGER)
      Price ← Price * (100 - Percent) / 100
   ENDPROCEDURE
ENDCLASS
parts.working: 1 mark each for: CLASS Book … ENDCLASS; three PRIVATE attribute declarations with types; constructor PUBLIC PROCEDURE NEW with three parameters; assignments to the attributes in the constructor; GetPrice function returning Price; ApplyDiscount procedure with correct calculation.

parts.label: b

parts.label: a

parts.answer: Overloading: several methods in the same class have the same name but different parameter lists (number or types), and the one called depends on the arguments given. Overriding: a subclass redefines a method inherited from its superclass with the same name and parameters.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A class Shape has a method Area(). Classes Circle and Rectangle inherit from Shape. A program stores a mixture of Circle and Rectangle objects in one array of type Shape and calls Area() on each element in a loop. Explain how polymorphism makes this possible, and why it is useful.
parts.answer: Each subclass overrides Area() with its own formula. At run time, the version of Area() that runs depends on the actual class of each object, so the same call Area() gives the correct result for every shape. This means the loop does not need IF statements to test the type, and new shapes (e.g. Triangle) can be added without changing the loop.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A bank uses this class.
CLASS Account
   PRIVATE AccountNo : STRING
   PRIVATE Balance : REAL
   PUBLIC PROCEDURE NEW(GivenNo : STRING)
      AccountNo ← GivenNo
      Balance ← 0
   ENDPROCEDURE
   PUBLIC FUNCTION GetBalance() RETURNS REAL
      RETURN Balance
   ENDFUNCTION
   PUBLIC PROCEDURE Deposit(Amount : REAL)
      Balance ← Balance + Amount
   ENDPROCEDURE
   PUBLIC FUNCTION Withdraw(Amount : REAL) RETURNS BOOLEAN
      IF Amount <= Balance THEN
         Balance ← Balance - Amount
         RETURN TRUE
      ENDIF
      RETURN FALSE
   ENDFUNCTION
ENDCLASS
A class SavingsAccount inherits from Account. It has an extra private attribute WithdrawalsLeft (INTEGER), set to 3 by its constructor. Its Withdraw method overrides the parent's: it allows a withdrawal only if WithdrawalsLeft is greater than 0 and the parent's Withdraw succeeds, and it then reduces WithdrawalsLeft by 1.
Write pseudocode for the class SavingsAccount.
parts.answer:
CLASS SavingsAccount INHERITS Account
   PRIVATE WithdrawalsLeft : INTEGER
   PUBLIC PROCEDURE NEW(GivenNo : STRING)
      SUPER.NEW(GivenNo)
      WithdrawalsLeft ← 3
   ENDPROCEDURE
   PUBLIC FUNCTION Withdraw(Amount : REAL) RETURNS BOOLEAN
      IF WithdrawalsLeft > 0 THEN
         IF SUPER.Withdraw(Amount) = TRUE THEN
            WithdrawalsLeft ← WithdrawalsLeft - 1
            RETURN TRUE
         ENDIF
      ENDIF
      RETURN FALSE
   ENDFUNCTION
ENDCLASS
parts.working: 1 mark each for: CLASS SavingsAccount INHERITS Account … ENDCLASS; PRIVATE WithdrawalsLeft : INTEGER; constructor NEW with GivenNo parameter; SUPER.NEW(GivenNo) called; WithdrawalsLeft ← 3; Withdraw header matching the parent (overriding) and check WithdrawalsLeft > 0; calls SUPER.Withdraw(Amount), decrements WithdrawalsLeft only on success and returns the correct Boolean.

parts.label: b

parts.answer: Balance is PRIVATE to Account, so it cannot be accessed directly from the subclass; it can only be changed through Account's public methods.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Describe each of these methods of file organisation.
(i) serial (ii) sequential (iii) random
parts.answer: (i) Records are stored one after another in the order in which they were added (chronological), not sorted. (ii) Records are stored one after another in order of a key field. (iii) Records are stored at an address calculated from the key field by a hashing algorithm, so they can be accessed directly.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the difference between sequential access and direct access.
parts.answer: Sequential access reads records one after another from the start of the file until the required record is reached; direct access goes straight to the required record (using its address/index/hash) without reading the earlier records.
parts.working: 1 mark for each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by an exception and by exception handling.
parts.answer: An exception is an unexpected event/error that occurs while a program is running and would normally cause it to crash (a run-time error). Exception handling is code that detects (catches) the exception and deals with it, so that the program can continue or end tidily.
parts.working: 1 mark: exception = run-time error/unexpected event. 1 mark: handling = catching it and responding without the program crashing.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give three situations that could cause an exception in a program that reads data from a file.
parts.answer: Any three of: the file does not exist/wrong name; the file is already in use/no permission; reading past the end of the file; data in the file is the wrong type (e.g. text where a number is expected); disk/drive error or removable drive disconnected; division by zero when processing the data.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each application, state the most suitable file organisation (serial, sequential or random) and give a reason.
(i) A log of every card swipe at an office door, added in the order they happen.
(ii) A monthly payroll file where every employee record is processed in employee-number order.
(iii) A bank's ATM system that must find one customer's record very quickly.
parts.answer: (i) Serial – records are simply appended in time order and there is no need to sort them. (ii) Sequential – all records are processed in key order in a batch, so storing them in key order is efficient. (iii) Random – direct access using a hash of the account number finds a single record without reading others.
parts.working: For each: 1 mark for organisation, 1 mark for a reason.

parts.label: a

parts.label: b
parts.text: A new customer with ID 1611 is added. Explain the problem that occurs and describe one way of dealing with it.
parts.answer: 1611 MOD 97 = 59, the same address as customer 4521 – a collision. One method: linear probing (open addressing / closed hashing) – look at the next position(s) (60, 61 …) until an empty one is found and store the record there (when searching, start at the hashed address and keep checking the following positions). Alternatively use an overflow area where colliding records are stored and searched serially.
parts.working: 1 mark: address 59 / same as 4521 – collision. 1 mark: method named (linear probing / overflow area / chaining). 1 mark: method described, including how the record is found later.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A shop stores products in the random file "Stock.dat". Each record has the type:
TYPE TProduct
   DECLARE ProductCode : INTEGER
   DECLARE Description : STRING
   DECLARE Quantity : INTEGER
ENDTYPE
The record for a product is stored at the address given by the function Hash(ProductCode) (assume there are no collisions).
Write a pseudocode procedure UpdateStock(Code : INTEGER, Sold : INTEGER) that finds the record for the product, reduces its Quantity by Sold, and writes the record back to the file.
parts.answer:
PROCEDURE UpdateStock(Code : INTEGER, Sold : INTEGER)
   DECLARE ThisProduct : TProduct
   DECLARE Address : INTEGER
   Address ← Hash(Code)
   OPENFILE "Stock.dat" FOR RANDOM
   SEEK "Stock.dat", Address
   GETRECORD "Stock.dat", ThisProduct
   ThisProduct.Quantity ← ThisProduct.Quantity - Sold
   SEEK "Stock.dat", Address
   PUTRECORD "Stock.dat", ThisProduct
   CLOSEFILE "Stock.dat"
ENDPROCEDURE
parts.working: 1 mark each for: declare a variable of type TProduct; Address calculated with Hash(Code); OPENFILE … FOR RANDOM; SEEK to the address then GETRECORD into the variable; update the Quantity field using dot notation; SEEK again, PUTRECORD and CLOSEFILE.

parts.label: a

parts.working: 1 mark: 6. 1 mark: explanation (each unordered pair once, since ages are all different).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write a rule teenager(X) that is true if X is aged from 13 to 19 inclusive.
parts.answer: teenager(X) :- age(X, A), A >= 13, A =< 19.
parts.working: 1 mark: age(X, A) in body. 1 mark: both comparisons correct (=< in Prolog).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Describe the main characteristic of each programming paradigm.
(i) low-level (ii) imperative (procedural) (iii) object-oriented (iv) declarative
parts.answer: (i) Instructions closely match the processor's instruction set (assembly/machine code), working directly with registers and memory addresses. (ii) The program is a sequence of statements that change the program's state, organised into procedures and functions. (iii) The program is built from objects (instances of classes) that combine data and methods, using encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism. (iv) The program states facts and rules; the system works out how to reach a goal.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The program below uses the instruction set: LDR #n (load n into the index register IX), LDM #n (load n into ACC), LDD <address> (load contents of address into ACC), LDX <address> (load contents of (address + IX) into ACC), ADD <address> (add contents of address to ACC), STO <address> (store ACC at address), INC IX / DEC ACC (add/subtract 1), CMP #n (compare ACC with n), JPN <address> (jump if the comparison was not equal), END.
100 LDR #0
101 LDM #0
102 STO 210
103 LDX 200
104 ADD 210
105 STO 210
106 INC IX
107 LDD 211
108 DEC ACC
109 STO 211
110 CMP #0
111 JPN 103
112 END
Memory before running: address 200 = 12, 201 = 7, 202 = 25, 203 = 9, 211 = 4.
State the contents of address 210, address 211 and IX when the program ends, and the number of times the instruction at address 103 is executed.
parts.answer: Address 210 = 53; address 211 = 0; IX = 4; instruction 103 executed 4 times.
parts.working: 1 mark each. 210 holds 12 + 7 + 25 + 9 = 53.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the addressing mode used by the instruction at address 103 and explain why it is useful in this program.
parts.answer: Indexed addressing. The address used is 200 + IX, and IX is increased each time round the loop, so the same instruction reads a different array element (200, 201, 202, 203) on each pass.
parts.working: 1 mark: indexed. 1 mark: IX changes so same instruction accesses successive locations in a loop.

practice.stem:
The processor has an accumulator (ACC) and an index register (IX). It uses this part of the instruction set:
LDM #n: load the number n into ACC
LDD <address>: load the contents of the address into ACC
LDI <address>: the address holds a second address; load the contents of the second address into ACC
LDX <address>: form the address <address> + contents of IX; load the contents of that address into ACC
LDR #n: load the number n into IX
STO <address>: store the contents of ACC at the address
ADD <address> / ADD #n: add the contents of the address / the number n to ACC
SUB <address> / SUB #n: subtract the contents of the address / the number n from ACC
INC <register> / DEC <register>: add 1 to / subtract 1 from ACC or IX
CMP <address> / CMP #n: compare ACC with the contents of the address / the number n
CMI <address>: the address holds a second address; compare ACC with the contents of the second address
JPE <address>: jump to the address if the last comparison was True
JPN <address>: jump to the address if the last comparison was False
JMP <address>: jump to the address
IN: read one character from the keyboard and store its ASCII code in ACC
OUT: output the character whose ASCII code is in ACC
END: return control to the operating system
AND / OR / XOR #n, Bn or &n: bitwise operation between ACC and the operand (# denary, B binary, & hexadecimal)
LSL #n / LSR #n: logical shift left / right of ACC by n places; zeros enter the vacated bits

121: 47
122: 63
123: 120
125: 9

State the contents of ACC after each of these instructions is executed on its own.
(i) LDM #120
(ii) LDD 120
(iii) LDI 120
(iv) LDX 120
(v) LDI 123
parts.working: B1 each. (i) immediate: the operand itself. (ii) direct: contents of 120. (iii) indirect: 120 holds 125, contents of 125 = 9. (iv) indexed: 120 + 2 = 122, contents 63. (v) 123 holds 120, contents of 120 = 125.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the addressing mode used by LDX.
parts.answer: Indexed addressing
parts.working: B1: indexed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe immediate addressing and direct addressing. Give an example instruction for each.
parts.answer: Immediate: the operand is the actual value to be used, e.g. LDM #25. Direct: the operand is the address that holds the value to be used, e.g. LDD 25.
parts.working: 1 mark each: immediate – operand is the data/value itself; example e.g. LDM #25; direct – operand is the address of the data; example e.g. LDD 25 / ADD 40.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe relative addressing and give one advantage of using it.
parts.answer: The address used is found by adding the operand (an offset) to a base address, usually the address of the current instruction in the program counter. Advantage: the program can be loaded anywhere in memory and still work (relocatable code).
parts.working: B1: operand is an offset added to the current/base address (e.g. contents of PC). B1: code is relocatable / jumps still work wherever the program is loaded.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Assembly language instructions can be put into groups. For each instruction, state its group: data movement, arithmetic, compare, jump (conditional or unconditional), or input/output.
(i) STO 300
(ii) JPN 75
(iii) IN
(iv) INC IX
(v) CMP #13
(vi) JMP 40
parts.answer: (i) data movement (ii) conditional jump (iii) input/output (iv) arithmetic (v) compare (vi) unconditional jump
parts.working: B1 each. Accept 'jump' for (ii) and (vi) only if conditional/unconditional is stated correctly.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why each assembly language instruction is said to have a one-to-one relationship with machine code.
parts.answer: Each assembly language instruction translates into exactly one machine code instruction.
parts.working: B1: one mnemonic/instruction becomes one machine code instruction (opcode + operand).

practice.stem: A processor uses 16-bit machine code instructions. Each instruction has a 6-bit opcode followed by a 10-bit operand. The operand is an unsigned binary number.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the meaning of the terms opcode and operand.
parts.answer: Opcode: the part of the instruction that says which operation to perform (e.g. load, add). Operand: the part that holds the data, or the address of the data, that the operation uses.
parts.working: B1 opcode = operation/instruction code; B1 operand = data value or address used by the operation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum number of different opcodes.

parts.label: c

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give the value in the operand of the instruction LDM #300 as a 10-bit binary number.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the contents of addresses 400 and 401 when the program ends.
parts.answer: 400 contains 414; 401 contains 2.
parts.working: B1: 400 = 414 (pointer moved past the last value). B1: 401 = 2 (two values equal 15).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how many times the jump at address 32 takes place.

practice.stem:
A two-pass assembler translates this program. The first instruction is to be loaded at address 500. Each instruction and each data item takes one memory address.
START: LDM #0
       STO TOTAL
LOOP:  LDD TOTAL
       ADD STEP
       STO TOTAL
       CMP LIMIT
       JPN LOOP
       JMP DONE
DONE:  END
TOTAL: 0
STEP:  6
LIMIT: 42

parts.label: a
parts.text: Complete the symbol table: give the address for each of the labels START, LOOP, DONE, TOTAL, STEP and LIMIT.
parts.answer: START 500, LOOP 502, DONE 508, TOTAL 509, STEP 510, LIMIT 511
parts.working: 3 marks for all six correct; 2 marks for four or five; 1 mark for two or three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what happens during the first pass and the second pass of the assembler.
parts.answer: First pass: reads the code line by line, removes comments/white space, and adds each label to the symbol table with its address (forward references such as DONE are entered when found). Second pass: replaces each label in an operand with its address from the symbol table, converts each opcode mnemonic into its binary opcode, and generates the object (machine) code.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 2 per pass. Pass 1: comments/spaces removed; labels found and entered in symbol table; addresses allocated by counting instructions; forward references recorded. Pass 2: symbolic addresses replaced with addresses from table; mnemonics translated to opcodes; machine code produced/output.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how many times the instruction labelled LOOP is executed when the program runs.
parts.working: B1: TOTAL goes 6, 12, …, 42, so 42 ÷ 6 = 7 passes.

practice.stem: An 8-bit register holds the unsigned binary number 00110101.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the contents of the register after a logical shift left of two places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the contents of the original register after a logical shift right of three places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the denary value of the register before the shift and after the shift in part (a), and explain the effect of the shift.
parts.answer: Before: 53. After: 212. A logical left shift of 2 places multiplies an unsigned number by 2² = 4.
parts.working: B1: 53. B1: 212. B1: multiplies by 4 (each left shift doubles), provided no 1s are lost from the left.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the result of part (b) is not exactly 53 ÷ 8.
parts.answer: The three 1/0 bits shifted out on the right (101) are lost, so the result is rounded down to 6 instead of 6.625.
parts.working: B1: bits lost from the right / integer result (truncated).

practice.stem: The accumulator (ACC) holds the 8-bit value 10110110.

parts.label: a
parts.text:

(i) AND B00001111
(ii) OR B00000001
(iii) XOR B11111111
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how a mask is used with the AND operation to test whether one particular bit is 1.
parts.answer: Create a mask with a 1 in the position of the bit being tested and 0s elsewhere; AND it with the value. If the result is 0 the bit was 0, otherwise the bit was 1.
parts.working: B1: mask with 1 only in the required position. B1: result zero means bit 0 / non-zero means bit 1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the difference between a logical shift right and a cyclic shift right.
parts.answer: Logical: bits move one place right, the bit leaving the right end is lost and a 0 enters at the left. Cyclic: the bit leaving the right end is moved round into the left-most position, so no bits are lost.
parts.working: B1 logical – 0 enters at left, bit lost. B1 cyclic – bit leaving the right re-enters at the left.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
An 8-bit register holds 11001011. Give its contents after:
(i) a cyclic shift right of one place
(ii) a cyclic shift left of two places
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one use of cyclic shifts.
parts.answer: e.g. in encryption/hashing algorithms, or to examine each bit of a value in turn without losing it.
parts.working: B1 any sensible use.

practice.stem: An 8-bit register holds 11101000, a two's complement integer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the denary value held.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the contents of the register after an arithmetic shift right of two places, and its denary value.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give the contents after a logical shift right of two places, and explain why this is not suitable for dividing this number by 4.
parts.answer: 00111010 (= 58). Zeros enter at the left, so the sign bit becomes 0 and the number changes from negative to positive.
parts.working: B1: 00111010. B1: sign bit not preserved / result 58 is positive.

practice.stem:
The processor has an accumulator (ACC) and an index register (IX). It uses this part of the instruction set:
LDM #n: load the number n into ACC
LDD <address>: load the contents of the address into ACC
LDI <address>: the address holds a second address; load the contents of the second address into ACC
LDX <address>: form the address <address> + contents of IX; load the contents of that address into ACC
LDR #n: load the number n into IX
STO <address>: store the contents of ACC at the address
ADD <address> / ADD #n: add the contents of the address / the number n to ACC
SUB <address> / SUB #n: subtract the contents of the address / the number n from ACC
INC <register> / DEC <register>: add 1 to / subtract 1 from ACC or IX
CMP <address> / CMP #n: compare ACC with the contents of the address / the number n
CMI <address>: the address holds a second address; compare ACC with the contents of the second address
JPE <address>: jump to the address if the last comparison was True
JPN <address>: jump to the address if the last comparison was False
JMP <address>: jump to the address
IN: read one character from the keyboard and store its ASCII code in ACC
OUT: output the character whose ASCII code is in ACC
END: return control to the operating system
AND / OR / XOR #n, Bn or &n: bitwise operation between ACC and the operand (# denary, B binary, & hexadecimal)
LSL #n / LSR #n: logical shift left / right of ACC by n places; zeros enter the vacated bits

A greenhouse near Multan has a controller. The value at address 70 is a status byte. Each bit shows one device: bit 0 (right-most) is the water pump, bit 3 is the roof vent, bit 5 is the heater. A bit is 1 when the device is ON.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write assembly language code that switches the heater ON without changing any other bit, and stores the result back at address 70.
parts.answer:
LDD 70
OR B00100000
STO 70

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write assembly language code that switches the water pump OFF without changing any other bit, and stores the result back at address 70.
parts.answer:
LDD 70
AND B11111110
STO 70

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write assembly language code that jumps to address 90 if the roof vent is ON.
parts.answer:
LDD 70
AND B00001000
CMP #8
JPE 90
parts.working: B1: load and AND with B00001000. B1: compare with 8 (or compare with 0 and JPN). B1: correct conditional jump to 90.

practice.stem:
The processor has an accumulator (ACC) and an index register (IX). It uses this part of the instruction set:
LDM #n: load the number n into ACC
LDD <address>: load the contents of the address into ACC
LDI <address>: the address holds a second address; load the contents of the second address into ACC
LDX <address>: form the address <address> + contents of IX; load the contents of that address into ACC
LDR #n: load the number n into IX
STO <address>: store the contents of ACC at the address
ADD <address> / ADD #n: add the contents of the address / the number n to ACC
SUB <address> / SUB #n: subtract the contents of the address / the number n from ACC
INC <register> / DEC <register>: add 1 to / subtract 1 from ACC or IX
CMP <address> / CMP #n: compare ACC with the contents of the address / the number n
CMI <address>: the address holds a second address; compare ACC with the contents of the second address
JPE <address>: jump to the address if the last comparison was True
JPN <address>: jump to the address if the last comparison was False
JMP <address>: jump to the address
IN: read one character from the keyboard and store its ASCII code in ACC
OUT: output the character whose ASCII code is in ACC
END: return control to the operating system
AND / OR / XOR #n, Bn or &n: bitwise operation between ACC and the operand (# denary, B binary, & hexadecimal)
LSL #n / LSR #n: logical shift left / right of ACC by n places; zeros enter the vacated bits

The register is 8 bits. Address 90 holds 10110010.
10 LDM #0
11 STO 91
12 LDD 90
13 AND #1
14 ADD 91
15 STO 91
16 LDD 90
17 LSR #1
18 STO 90
19 CMP #0
20 JPN 12
21 END

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the contents of addresses 90 and 91 when the program ends.
parts.answer: 90 contains 00000000; 91 contains 4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how many times the instruction at address 13 is executed.
parts.working: B1: 8 – the value needs 8 shifts before it becomes 0 because its left-most bit is 1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe the purpose of the program and explain how AND #1 and LSR #1 work together.
parts.answer: It counts the number of 1 bits in the byte at address 90. AND #1 masks out everything except the right-most bit, giving 1 or 0, which is added to the count. LSR #1 then moves the next bit into the right-most position. The loop stops when the remaining value is 0.
parts.working: B1: counts the 1 bits (stores count in 91). B1: AND #1 isolates the least significant bit. B1: LSR #1 brings the next bit to bit 0 / loop ends when value becomes 0.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State one disadvantage of the program.
parts.answer: The original value at address 90 is destroyed (overwritten with 0).
parts.working: B1: original data lost / should copy it first.

practice.stem:
The processor has an accumulator (ACC) and an index register (IX). It uses this part of the instruction set:
LDM #n: load the number n into ACC
LDD <address>: load the contents of the address into ACC
LDI <address>: the address holds a second address; load the contents of the second address into ACC
LDX <address>: form the address <address> + contents of IX; load the contents of that address into ACC
LDR #n: load the number n into IX
STO <address>: store the contents of ACC at the address
ADD <address> / ADD #n: add the contents of the address / the number n to ACC
SUB <address> / SUB #n: subtract the contents of the address / the number n from ACC
INC <register> / DEC <register>: add 1 to / subtract 1 from ACC or IX
CMP <address> / CMP #n: compare ACC with the contents of the address / the number n
CMI <address>: the address holds a second address; compare ACC with the contents of the second address
JPE <address>: jump to the address if the last comparison was True
JPN <address>: jump to the address if the last comparison was False
JMP <address>: jump to the address
IN: read one character from the keyboard and store its ASCII code in ACC
OUT: output the character whose ASCII code is in ACC
END: return control to the operating system
AND / OR / XOR #n, Bn or &n: bitwise operation between ACC and the operand (# denary, B binary, & hexadecimal)
LSL #n / LSR #n: logical shift left / right of ACC by n places; zeros enter the vacated bits

ACC is an 8-bit register. A positive integer is stored at address 600.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write assembly language code that multiplies the value at 600 by 10 using shifts and addition only, and stores the result at 602. You may use address 601 for working.
parts.answer:
LDD 600
LSL #3
STO 601
LDD 600
LSL #1
ADD 601
STO 602
parts.working: B1: LSL #3 (× 8). B1: stored temporarily (601). B1: LSL #1 on original (× 2). B1: added and stored at 602. Accept other correct orders, e.g. (×4 + ×1) × 2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the largest value at address 600 for which your code gives a correct result, and explain why a larger value fails.
parts.answer: 25. 25 × 10 = 250 fits in 8 bits, but 26 × 10 = 260 is greater than 255, so a 1 is lost from the left and the result is wrong (260 − 256 = 4).
parts.working: B1: 25. B1: result must be ≤ 255 / bits overflow beyond 8 bits.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why using shifts can be quicker than a loop of repeated additions.
parts.answer: A shift is a single instruction, whereas repeated addition needs many instructions (one pass per addition plus compare and jump).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three factors that affect the performance of a computer system's processor.
parts.answer: Any three of: clock speed, number of cores, size of cache memory, width of the data bus, width of the address bus.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student in Faisalabad replaces a dual-core processor with a quad-core processor of the same clock speed. Explain why her programs may not run twice as fast.
parts.answer: Some programs are not written to run on several cores at once, so tasks cannot be split. Also the cores must communicate/share memory and wait for each other, which takes time.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: software not designed for multiple cores / some tasks must be done in sequence; overhead of communication/synchronisation between cores; other bottlenecks (memory, bus).

practice.stem: A school in Lahore is setting up a classroom computer. It will be connected to a projector, a keyboard, a mouse and a printer.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Describe the purpose of each port.
(i) USB
(ii) HDMI
(iii) VGA
parts.answer: (i) Universal Serial Bus: a standard serial port used to connect many types of device (keyboard, mouse, printer, flash drive) and can supply power. (ii) High Definition Multimedia Interface: carries high-definition digital video and audio to a monitor, TV or projector. (iii) Video Graphics Array: carries analogue video (no audio) to an older monitor or projector.
parts.working: B1 each: USB – connect many peripheral types/data + power; HDMI – digital video and audio; VGA – analogue video only.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The projector has only HDMI and VGA inputs. State which port should be used and give a reason.
parts.answer: HDMI, because it carries digital high-definition video and also the audio, with one cable.
parts.working: B1 HDMI. B1 reason: higher quality digital picture / carries sound too.

practice.stem: A processor has a 24-bit address bus and a 32-bit data bus. Each memory location holds one byte.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of memory locations that can be addressed directly. Give your answer as a power of 2 and in denary.
parts.answer: 2²⁴ = 16 777 216 locations

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the maximum amount of memory, in MiB, that can be addressed.
parts.answer: 16 MiB
parts.working: B1: 2²⁴ bytes ÷ 2²⁰ = 16 MiB.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how increasing the width of the data bus can improve performance.
parts.answer: More bits are transferred at the same time, so fewer transfers are needed to move the same amount of data / a whole word can be moved in one transfer.
parts.working: B1 more bits per transfer. B1 fewer fetches needed / faster data transfer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A processor has a clock speed of 3.2 GHz. Calculate the time for one clock cycle in nanoseconds.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how cache memory improves the performance of a processor.
parts.answer: Cache is fast memory on or near the processor. It holds data and instructions that are used often or are likely to be needed next. The processor can read these from cache instead of the slower main memory, so it waits less.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: faster than RAM; stores frequently used / next instructions or data; checked first before RAM; reduces time the processor waits / fewer RAM accesses.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why doubling the clock speed does not always double performance.
parts.answer: The processor may still have to wait for data from memory or devices (other bottlenecks), and heat may force it to slow down.
parts.working: B1 any valid reason.

practice.stem:
A video-editing student in Islamabad must choose between two laptops.
Laptop P: 8 cores, 2.6 GHz, 24 MiB cache, 64-bit data bus.
Laptop Q: 4 cores, 3.4 GHz, 8 MiB cache, 32-bit data bus.
Her editing software can use many cores at once.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many data bus transfers each laptop needs to move a 4 KiB block of data.
parts.answer: P: 512 transfers; Q: 1024 transfers

parts.label: b
parts.text: Recommend one laptop for the student. Justify your choice by referring to all the factors given.
parts.answer: Laptop P. The software can use many cores, so 8 cores can process more parts of a video at once than 4, which outweighs Q's higher clock speed. The larger cache holds more of the video data and instructions, so fewer slow RAM accesses. The 64-bit data bus moves twice as much data per transfer (512 rather than 1024 transfers per 4 KiB).
parts.working: B1: P chosen with at least one reason. B1: cores vs clock speed argument (multi-threaded software). B1: larger cache benefit. B1: wider data bus benefit. Q with clock-speed argument only can score max 1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the main features of the Von Neumann model for a computer system.
parts.answer: Programs (instructions) and data are stored together in the same main memory; instructions are fetched one at a time and executed in sequence by a single processor; the processor is connected to memory by buses and uses special registers.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: stored program concept; instructions and data in the same memory / same format; single processor / control unit; sequential fetch-execute; uses buses; uses registers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the purpose of the system clock.
parts.answer: It produces timing signals at a regular rate so that the components of the processor work in step (synchronised).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each description, name the register.
(i) Holds the address of the next instruction to be fetched.
(ii) Holds the instruction that is currently being decoded and executed.
(iii) Holds data or an instruction just read from memory, or about to be written to memory.
(iv) Holds the address of the memory location about to be read from or written to.
(v) Holds individual bits (flags) that show the result of an operation, such as a carry or overflow.
parts.answer: (i) Program Counter (PC) (ii) Current Instruction Register (CIR) (iii) Memory Data Register (MDR) (iv) Memory Address Register (MAR) (v) Status Register
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the difference between a general-purpose register and a special-purpose register, naming one example of each.
parts.answer: A general-purpose register can hold any data for the program, e.g. the accumulator (ACC). A special-purpose register has one fixed job, e.g. the PC.
parts.working: B1: general purpose – used for any data/temporary values, example ACC. B1: special purpose – dedicated role, example PC/MAR/MDR/CIR/IX/status register.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the role of each of these buses: address bus, data bus, control bus. Include the direction in which each carries signals.
parts.answer: Address bus: carries memory addresses from the processor to memory/devices; one direction (unidirectional). Data bus: carries data and instructions between the processor, memory and I/O; both directions. Control bus: carries control and timing signals (e.g. memory read, memory write, clock, interrupt) in both directions.
parts.working: B1 each, with direction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the role of the arithmetic logic unit (ALU) and the control unit (CU).
parts.answer: ALU: carries out arithmetic (e.g. addition) and logical operations (e.g. AND, comparisons) on data. CU: decodes instructions and sends control signals to coordinate the movement of data and the operation of the other components.
parts.working: B1 ALU. B1 CU.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the address bus is unidirectional.
parts.answer: Only the processor sends addresses (to memory); memory never needs to send an address back.

practice.stem: A processor adds two 8-bit two's complement numbers in the accumulator: 01100100 + 00111100. The status register has a carry flag (C), a negative flag (N) and an overflow flag (V).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the 8-bit result of the addition.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the value of each flag after the addition. Justify each one.
parts.answer: C = 0: there is no carry out of the most significant bit. N = 1: the result's sign bit is 1. V = 1: two positive numbers (100 and 60) have given a negative result, because 160 is too large for 8-bit two's complement (maximum 127).
parts.working: B1 C = 0 with reason. B1 N = 1 with reason. B1 V = 1 with reason (160 > 127 / sign changed).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how a program could use the overflow flag.
parts.answer: After an arithmetic instruction it can test the flag and jump to error-handling code, so an incorrect result is not used.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Complete the fetch stage in register transfer notation. [ ] means 'the contents of'.
MAR ← ______
PC ← ______
MDR ← ______
CIR ← ______
parts.answer:
MAR ← [PC]
PC ← [PC] + 1
MDR ← [[MAR]]
CIR ← [MDR]
parts.working: B1 each line.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what happens to the instruction in the CIR after the fetch stage.
parts.answer: It is decoded by the control unit and then executed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two different sources of an interrupt.
parts.answer: e.g. a printer running out of paper (hardware), a timer signal, a division by zero (software error), a key being pressed.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two different sources.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how a processor detects and handles an interrupt.
parts.answer: At the end of each fetch-execute cycle the processor checks for interrupts. If there is one of a higher priority than the current task, the contents of the registers (including the PC) are saved on a stack. The address of the matching interrupt service routine (ISR) is loaded into the PC and the ISR is executed. When it finishes, the saved register contents are restored from the stack and the original program continues where it stopped.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 5: checked at end of each cycle; priority compared; registers/PC saved (on stack); ISR address loaded into PC / ISR executed; registers restored afterwards; original task resumes; lower-priority interrupts may be disabled while ISR runs.

practice.stem: The program counter (PC) contains 310. Memory address 310 holds the instruction LDD 452 and address 452 holds the value 87.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the contents of the PC, MAR, MDR, CIR and ACC after the instruction has been fetched and executed. Give the final values only.
parts.answer: PC 311, MAR 452, MDR 87, CIR LDD 452, ACC 87
parts.working: B1 each. During the fetch MAR = 310 and MDR = LDD 452; during execution the operand 452 is copied to MAR and 87 is read into MDR, then copied to ACC.

parts.label: b
parts.text: While LDD 452 is being executed, a keyboard interrupt arrives. Explain why the processor does not deal with it immediately.
parts.answer: The processor checks for interrupts only at the end of each fetch-execute cycle, so it completes LDD 452 first; this means the instruction is not left half-finished and the register values can be saved in a consistent state.
parts.working: B1: checked at end of cycle / current instruction finished first. B1: so that the state can be saved and resumed correctly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give three differences between a local area network (LAN) and a wide area network (WAN).
parts.answer: LAN covers a small area (one building/site), WAN covers a large geographical area (cities/countries). LAN hardware and cables are usually owned by the organisation; WAN uses leased lines/infrastructure owned by telecom companies. LAN usually has higher data rates and fewer errors than a WAN.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three contrasted differences: area covered; ownership of infrastructure; transmission rate; error rate/reliability; media used (LAN – cable/Wi-Fi, WAN – telephone lines, fibre, satellite).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A textile company has offices in Faisalabad and Dubai connected together. State the type of network that connects the two offices.
parts.answer: WAN
parts.working: B1: WAN.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a star topology.
parts.answer: Each device is connected by its own cable to a central device (a switch or hub); all data between devices passes through this central device.
parts.working: B1: each device has its own link. B1: to a central switch/hub/server.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two advantages of a star topology compared with a bus topology.
parts.answer: A fault in one cable affects only one device; data goes only to the destination device through the switch, so fewer collisions/better security and performance; easy to add devices without disrupting the network.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one disadvantage of a star topology.
parts.answer: If the central switch fails the whole network stops; more cable is needed.
parts.working: B1 any one.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the topology described in each case.
(i) All devices are attached to one shared cable that has a terminator at each end.
(ii) Every device has a direct link to every other device.
(iii) Two star networks in separate buildings are joined by a single cable between their switches.
parts.answer: (i) bus (ii) (full) mesh (iii) hybrid
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the cable in topology (i) needs a terminator at each end.
parts.answer: To absorb the signals at the ends of the cable so they are not reflected back and interfere with other signals.

practice.stem: A research lab connects its six servers in a full mesh topology.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of links needed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A seventh server is added to the mesh. Calculate how many extra links are needed.
parts.working: B1: 7 × 6 ÷ 2 = 21; 21 − 15 = 6 (one to each existing server).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of using a mesh topology for these servers.
parts.answer: Advantage: there are alternative routes, so if one link fails data can still get through (fault tolerant / no single point of failure). Disadvantage: many cables and network ports are needed, so it is expensive and hard to set up.
parts.working: B1 advantage (redundant routes / fast direct links). B1 disadvantage (cost / amount of cabling / complex).

practice.stem: A hospital in Peshawar has three buildings. Each building has its own star network with a switch. The three switches are connected to each other.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the name of this topology and give one reason it suits the hospital.
parts.answer: Hybrid topology. Each building can be managed and expanded separately, and a fault in one building's star does not stop the others.
parts.working: B1 hybrid. B1 suitable reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how a data packet is sent from a computer in the X-ray department to a printer in the same building.
parts.answer: The computer sends the packet along its cable to the building's switch. The switch reads the destination MAC address in the packet. It looks it up in its table and forwards the packet only to the port connected to the printer.
parts.working: B1 packet sent to switch. B1 switch reads destination (MAC) address. B1 forwarded only to the printer's port/link.

practice.stem: A small design studio in Karachi uses a bus network with eight computers. It plans to double the number of computers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the performance of the bus network will become worse as more computers are added.
parts.answer: All devices share one cable, so only one device can transmit at a time. More devices means more traffic and more collisions, so data has to be re-sent more often.
parts.working: B1 single shared cable / one transmission at a time. B1 more collisions / more waiting.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what happens to the network if the main cable is cut between the fourth and fifth computers.
parts.answer: The whole network fails / the two halves cannot communicate, and signals reflect from the unterminated broken ends, causing errors even within each half.
parts.working: B1 network (or communication across the break) stops. B1 no terminator at the break – reflections/errors.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Recommend a new topology for the studio and justify your choice.
parts.answer: Star topology with a switch: each computer has its own link, the switch sends data only to the destination so there are far fewer collisions, and it is easy to add computers without stopping the network.
parts.working: B1 star. B1 justification linked to the studio (expansion / performance / fault isolation).

practice.stem: A bank has its head office in Islamabad and 11 branches in other cities (12 sites in total). The sites must be connected so that every branch can exchange data with every other site.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many links are needed if the 12 sites are connected in a full mesh.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many links are needed if every branch is connected only to the head office, in a star arrangement.
parts.working: B1: one link per branch = 11.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Discuss which arrangement the bank should use.
parts.answer: Star: only 11 links so much cheaper; but all traffic passes through head office, which is a single point of failure, and branch-to-branch data must travel two links. Mesh: no single point of failure and direct routes, but 66 links is very expensive. A sensible decision is a star (or partial mesh) with a backup link at head office, because cost matters and most traffic goes to head office anyway.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 4: star cheaper/fewer links; star single point of failure; mesh redundancy/fault tolerance; mesh cost/complexity; reasoned conclusion (e.g. partial mesh / star with backup).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Describe the role of each device in a LAN.
(i) switch
(ii) router
(iii) network interface card (NIC)
(iv) wireless access point (WAP)
parts.answer: (i) Connects devices in a LAN and forwards each frame only to the device it is addressed to, using MAC addresses. (ii) Connects different networks (e.g. the LAN to the internet) and directs packets towards their destination using IP addresses. (iii) Hardware that lets a device connect to the network; it has a unique MAC address. (iv) Lets wireless devices connect to a wired network using radio waves (Wi-Fi).
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the purpose of a modem when a home connects to the internet over a telephone line.
parts.answer: It converts digital signals from the computer into analogue signals for the line, and analogue back to digital (modulation/demodulation).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two advantages of fibre-optic cable compared with copper cable.
parts.answer: Higher bandwidth / data rate; signals travel further before needing to be boosted; not affected by electromagnetic interference; harder to tap (more secure); lighter.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two reasons why copper (twisted-pair) cable is still used inside most office LANs.
parts.answer: It is cheaper; easier to install, bend and join; existing equipment and ports use it; its data rate is enough over short distances.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem: A factory in Sialkot has a long production hall. Computers at both ends of the hall are on the same wired network.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a repeater may be needed in the cable along the hall.
parts.answer: Signals become weaker (attenuated) and distorted as they travel along a long cable. A repeater receives the signal and regenerates/boosts it so it can travel further.
parts.working: B1 signal weakens over distance. B1 repeater regenerates/amplifies it.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The factory office has its own separate network segment. Describe the role of a bridge in joining the office segment to the factory segment.
parts.answer: A bridge connects two LAN segments that use the same protocol so they act as one network; it only passes on frames that are addressed to a device on the other segment, reducing unnecessary traffic.
parts.working: B1 joins two LANs/segments (same protocol). B1 filters traffic / forwards only frames for the other side.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give three differences between a switch and a router.
parts.answer: A switch connects devices within one network; a router connects separate networks. A switch uses MAC addresses; a router uses IP addresses. A router can choose a route for packets and can connect a LAN to the internet / give it a public IP address; a switch cannot.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three contrasted differences.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why a router stores a routing table.
parts.answer: So it can decide which network or next router to send each packet to, to reach its destination.

practice.stem: A village school in Gilgit-Baltistan can connect to the internet either by a geostationary satellite or by a new fibre-optic line. The satellite is 35 786 km above the Earth's surface and radio signals travel at 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the minimum time for a signal to travel from the school up to the satellite and down to the ground station. Give your answer in milliseconds, correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 239 ms

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this delay is a problem for video lessons with a live teacher, even when the bandwidth is high.
parts.answer: A request and reply each go up and down (about 0.48 s round trip), so there is a noticeable lag in a two-way conversation; speech overlaps and the lesson feels delayed. Bandwidth affects how much data arrives, not how long it takes to arrive.
parts.working: B1 round trip roughly double / noticeable lag in two-way communication. B1 latency is different from bandwidth.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one advantage of satellite over fibre for this school.
parts.answer: No cable needs to be laid over mountainous ground; can be set up quickly anywhere with a view of the sky.

practice.stem: A college is setting up a new computer room with 30 desktop computers, a laser printer and a file server. The computers will be used for online practical exams.

parts.label: a
