parts.label: c
parts.text: State the purpose of a report window (also called an output or debug window).
parts.answer: To show the values of variables or messages/output while the program runs, so the programmer can follow what is happening.
parts.working: B1: displays values of variables / program output / error messages during execution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two reasons why a programmer would use an IDE rather than a plain text editor and a separate compiler.
parts.answer: Any two of: all tools are in one place so it is quicker to edit, translate and run; coding features such as prettyprint and auto-complete reduce errors; debugging tools (breakpoints, stepping, watch window) make errors easier to find; errors are reported with the line they occur on.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid reasons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two features of an IDE that help with debugging.
parts.answer: Any two of: breakpoints, single stepping, variable watch window, report/output window.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A programmer at a school in Rawalpindi writes a program that adds up the monthly fees of all the students in a class. The program runs, but the total it outputs is always less than the correct total.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the programmer could use the debugging features of an IDE to find the cause of the error.
parts.answer: Set a breakpoint just before the loop that adds up the fees. Run the program until it stops at the breakpoint. Add the total and the loop counter (and fee) to a variable watch window. Single-step through the loop one line at a time, comparing the values in the watch window with the expected values from a hand calculation, to find the line where the total goes wrong.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 5: set breakpoint at a suitable point (e.g. start of loop); run to breakpoint; use variable watch window for the total/counter/fee; single-step through the code; compare actual values with expected (dry-run) values; identify the statement where the value first becomes wrong; possibly use report window to output values.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the program translated without any error messages even though the total is wrong.
parts.answer: It is a logic error: the code follows the syntax rules of the language, so the translator cannot detect that it does the wrong thing.
parts.working: B1: logic error – syntax is valid so the translator cannot detect it.

practice.stem: A student in Islamabad is learning to program and uses an IDE that has dynamic syntax checking and context-sensitive prompts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how dynamic syntax checking helps the student.
parts.answer: The IDE checks each line as it is typed and highlights (underlines) any syntax error immediately, so the student can correct mistakes straight away rather than waiting until the whole program is translated.
parts.working: 1 mark each: checks syntax while code is typed / as each line is entered; errors highlighted immediately so they are corrected early / saves time.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how context-sensitive prompts help the student.
parts.answer: When the student types part of a keyword, variable or function name, the IDE suggests possible completions (and the parameters a function needs); this reduces typing and spelling errors and helps the student remember the correct names.
parts.working: 1 mark each: suggests/auto-completes keywords, identifiers or parameter lists based on what has been typed; fewer typing/spelling errors / faster / helps remember syntax.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Identify the IDE feature described by each statement.
(i) Keywords are shown in one colour, strings in another and comments in a third, and lines are indented automatically.
(ii) A section of code such as a long procedure can be hidden so that only its first line is shown.
(iii) The programmer can see the current value of chosen variables as the program runs.
(iv) A missing ENDIF is underlined in red as soon as the line is typed.
parts.answer: (i) Prettyprint (ii) Expand and collapse code blocks (iii) Variable watch window (iv) Dynamic syntax checking
parts.working: 1 mark each: (i) prettyprint; (ii) collapsing/expanding code blocks; (iii) watch window; (iv) dynamic syntax checking.

practice.stem: A team of six programmers at a software house in Lahore is building a large ride-booking app. They all use the same IDE.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how prettyprint helps the team members.
parts.answer: Colour-coding and consistent indentation make the structure of the code (e.g. where loops and selections start and end) easy to see, so team members can read and understand each other's code quickly and spot errors such as unclosed strings.
parts.working: 1 mark each: makes code easier to read / structure clear; helps others understand and maintain code / spot errors such as missing quotes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how collapsing and expanding code blocks helps when working with a file that contains several thousand lines.
parts.answer: Modules that are finished can be collapsed to a single line so the programmer can see the overall structure and move quickly to the part being worked on; a block can be expanded again when it needs to be edited.
parts.working: 1 mark each: hides detail of completed/unrelated modules; easier to navigate / see overall structure / focus on one section.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The team lead says that an IDE cannot replace testing with test data. Justify this statement.
parts.answer: IDE features find syntax errors and help locate errors, but they cannot tell whether the program gives the correct results; only testing with normal, boundary and erroneous data against expected results shows that the program meets its requirements.
parts.working: 1 mark each: IDE detects syntax errors only / cannot detect logic errors automatically; test data with expected results needed to show correct output / requirements met.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each error below, state whether dynamic syntax checking would detect it, and give a reason.
(i) A loop is written as WHILE Count < 10 but ENDWHILE is missing.
(ii) A loop is written as FOR Index ← 1 TO 9 when it should process 10 items.
parts.answer: (i) Yes – a missing ENDWHILE breaks the grammar rules of the language, so it is a syntax error. (ii) No – the statement follows the syntax rules; processing 9 items instead of 10 is a logic error.
parts.working: Each: B1 yes/no, B1 reason (syntax rule broken / valid syntax but wrong logic).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the type of error in (a)(ii) and describe one IDE feature that could help find it.
parts.answer: Logic error. A variable watch window with single stepping lets the programmer watch Index and see that the loop stops after 9 iterations.
parts.working: B1: logic error. B1: watch window / breakpoint / single stepping described in context.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State the purpose of each of the following translators.
(i) Assembler
(ii) Compiler
(iii) Interpreter
parts.answer: (i) Translates assembly language into machine code. (ii) Translates the whole of a high-level-language program into machine code (object code) before it is run. (iii) Translates and executes a high-level-language program one statement at a time.
parts.working: 1 mark each: (i) assembly → machine code; (ii) whole HLL program translated at once into an executable/object code; (iii) HLL translated and executed line by line, no executable file produced.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each statement, state whether it applies to a compiler only, an interpreter only, or both.
(i) Translates a high-level language program.
(ii) Produces an executable file.
(iii) Stops at the first error it finds and reports it.
(iv) Must be present every time the program is run.
parts.answer: (i) Both (ii) Compiler only (iii) Interpreter only (iv) Interpreter only
parts.working: 1 mark each. Note for (iii): a compiler reports all errors it finds after reading the whole program.

practice.stem: A developer in Karachi is writing a stock-control program for a chain of pharmacies.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two reasons why an interpreter is useful while the program is being developed.
parts.answer: Any two of: errors are reported as soon as the line containing them is reached, so they can be fixed and the program continued; the program can be run before it is complete; there is no need to recompile the whole program after every small change; easy to test parts of the code.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two reasons why the finished program should be compiled before it is distributed.
parts.answer: Any two of: the compiled program runs faster; users do not need the translator installed; the source code is not given out, so it cannot easily be copied or changed; the executable can be run many times without being translated again.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a program written in Java is translated and executed.
parts.answer: The source code is compiled into intermediate code (bytecode). The bytecode is distributed and then interpreted (or just-in-time compiled) by a Java Virtual Machine on the computer that runs it, which converts it into that computer's machine code.
parts.working: 1 mark each: compiled to intermediate code / bytecode; bytecode run on a virtual machine; VM interprets/translates bytecode into machine code for the specific processor.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one benefit of this two-stage approach.
parts.answer: The same bytecode can run on any computer that has a suitable virtual machine (portability), without being recompiled.
parts.working: B1: portability / platform independence; or source code not distributed; or faster than pure interpretation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a program that is interpreted usually runs more slowly than the same program after it has been compiled.
parts.answer: Each statement must be translated every time it is executed, including every time a loop repeats; a compiled program is translated once in advance, so only machine code is executed.
parts.working: 1 mark each: translation happens during execution / each time; statements in loops translated repeatedly; compiled code already machine code.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A compiler lists 14 errors after translating a program. Explain why this can be harder for a beginner to deal with than the error reporting of an interpreter.
parts.answer: All the errors are reported together after the whole program has been read, and some may be caused by earlier errors, so it is hard to know where to start; an interpreter stops at the first error so the beginner fixes one error at a time in context.
parts.working: 1 mark each: errors reported all at once after full translation / one error can cause others; interpreter reports one error at a time at the line where it happens.

practice.stem: A games company in Lahore has written a mobile racing game in a high-level language and is about to sell it online.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Recommend whether the company should distribute the game as compiled code or as source code to be interpreted. Justify your recommendation.
parts.answer: Compiled code. The company's source code stays secret so competitors cannot copy or change it; the game runs faster, which matters for smooth graphics; players do not need an interpreter installed; there is no translation delay each time the game starts.
parts.working: B1: compiled. Then 1 mark each for up to 3 justifications in context: protects intellectual property / source code hidden; faster execution for real-time game; no translator needed on players' phones; no repeated translation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one drawback of distributing compiled code for this company.
parts.answer: A separate compiled version is needed for each type of processor/operating system the game runs on.
parts.working: B1: must be compiled for each platform / executable not portable / bugs need a new version compiled and distributed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what an assembler does when it translates an assembly language program.
parts.answer: It converts each mnemonic (opcode) into its binary machine-code opcode, converts operands such as symbolic addresses and labels into actual (binary) addresses, and produces machine code (object code) — normally one machine instruction per assembly instruction. A two-pass assembler builds a symbol table of labels on the first pass.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 3: mnemonics replaced by binary opcodes; labels/symbolic addresses replaced by numeric addresses (symbol table); one-to-one translation; produces object/machine code; directives processed / comments removed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why an assembly language program written for one processor will not usually run on a computer with a different type of processor.
parts.answer: Assembly language is specific to a processor's instruction set; a different processor family has different instructions, opcodes and registers, so the machine code produced will not be understood.
parts.working: 1 mark each: assembly/machine code is processor-specific (tied to its instruction set); different processors use different opcodes / registers / addressing modes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a computer needs an operating system.
parts.answer: The OS provides an interface between the user/applications and the hardware, so users do not have to control hardware directly; it manages the computer's resources (processor, memory, devices, files) so programs can run.
parts.working: 1 mark each: provides interface between user/application and hardware; manages resources / hides complexity of hardware.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two functions of an operating system, other than providing a user interface.
parts.answer: Any two of: memory management, file management, process management, hardware (device) management, security management.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Identify the operating system function that is described by each statement.
(i) Allocates time on the processor to each running program.
(ii) Requires a username and password and sets access rights for users.
(iii) Keeps a directory structure and records where each file is stored.
(iv) Loads a device driver when a new webcam is connected.
parts.answer: (i) Process management (ii) Security management (iii) File management (iv) Hardware (device) management
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe memory management.
parts.answer: The OS decides which processes are allocated which parts of memory and keeps track of what is free; it loads programs and data into memory and frees memory when a program ends; it stops one process from accessing memory allocated to another (memory protection); it may use virtual memory when RAM is full.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 3: allocation of memory to processes; tracking free/used memory; deallocation when finished; memory protection between processes; virtual memory/paging.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe file management.
parts.answer: The OS provides a file naming system and a directory (folder) structure; it keeps track of where each file is stored on secondary storage; it allows files to be created, opened, saved, copied, moved and deleted; it controls access rights to files.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 3: naming conventions; hierarchical folder/directory structure; locates where files are stored; operations such as create/save/delete/copy; access control / permissions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe process management.
parts.answer: The OS manages the programs (processes) that are running: it schedules which process uses the processor and for how long, so several can appear to run at once (multitasking); it allocates resources to processes, handles interrupts, and resolves conflicts such as two processes wanting the same resource.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 3: scheduling processes on the CPU; multitasking; allocation of resources to processes; handling interrupts / priorities; preventing deadlock / conflicts between processes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the operating system manages hardware such as a printer.
parts.answer: It uses a device driver to communicate with the printer, translating general instructions into commands that device understands; it handles the printer's interrupts and manages a queue (spooling) of print jobs from different programs.
parts.working: 1 mark each: installs/uses device drivers; sends data / handles interrupts / buffers / queues jobs.

practice.stem: A delivery rider in Faisalabad uses a smartphone. While a navigation app shows a map using the phone's GPS receiver, the rider also plays music through headphones.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain three ways in which the phone's operating system manages the device while the user does this.
parts.answer: Process management: the OS schedules the navigation app and the music app so both get processor time and appear to run at the same time. Memory management: it allocates RAM to each app, keeps them separate, and may close/suspend background apps if memory runs low. Hardware management: it uses drivers to receive data from the GPS receiver and to send sound to the headphones/speaker. (Also accept: security management – checking that the navigation app has permission to use the location.)
parts.working: For each of three functions: B1 named function, B1 explanation in the context of the phone/apps. Generic descriptions not in context max 1 per function.

practice.stem: A shared computer in a school staff room in Abbottabad is used by both teachers and students.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the operating system provides security management on this computer.
parts.answer: It requires each teacher and student to log in with their own user account and password (authentication). It gives each account access rights, so students cannot open or change files in the teachers' folders while teachers can. It keeps logs of log-ins and file access, and it can install security updates and run firewall software to block unauthorised access.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 4: user accounts / authentication (password, biometrics); access rights / permissions on files and folders; different privileges for different users (e.g. admin vs student) in context; logging/auditing; firewall / updates / protecting memory of other processes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why giving all users administrator rights would be a risk.
parts.answer: Any user could install software or change system settings, so malware could be installed or settings damaged (accidentally or deliberately); users could also view or change other users' files.
parts.working: 1 mark each: can install software / change settings / delete system files; risk of malware / damage / access to private files.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State the purpose of each of the following utility programs.
(i) Virus checker
(ii) Disk formatter
(iii) File compression utility
parts.answer: (i) Scans files and memory for malware, then quarantines or deletes infected files. (ii) Prepares a disk for use by setting up its file system (tracks/sectors), deleting existing data. (iii) Reduces the size of files so they take less storage space and are quicker to send.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how defragmentation software can improve the performance of a computer with a hard disk drive.
parts.answer: Over time, files are saved in pieces (fragments) scattered over the disk. Defragmentation moves the fragments of each file so they are stored in contiguous blocks, and groups free space together. The read/write head then moves less to read a file, so files are opened faster.
parts.working: 1 mark each: files become fragmented / stored in non-contiguous blocks; defragmenter reorganises data so each file's blocks are together (and free space combined); less head movement → faster access.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why defragmentation is not needed on a solid state drive (SSD).
parts.answer: An SSD has no moving parts, so the time to read data does not depend on where it is stored; extra rewriting would also wear out the flash memory cells.
parts.working: 1 mark each: no moving read/write head – access time the same anywhere; unnecessary writes reduce SSD lifespan.

practice.stem: A small travel agency in Multan keeps all its customer bookings on one office computer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how back-up software helps the business.
parts.answer: It makes copies of the business's files to a different storage device or the cloud. It can be scheduled to run automatically (e.g. every night), copying only files that have changed since the last backup. If the original files are lost, corrupted or encrypted by ransomware, they can be restored from the backup.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 3: copies data to another location/device; scheduled automatically; full or incremental (only changed files); allows restoring after loss/corruption/attack.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one other utility the business should use, and explain why.
parts.answer: A virus checker – to detect and remove malware that could delete or steal customer records.
parts.working: B1 utility, B1 reason in context. Accept disk repair / disk analysis, compression etc. with suitable reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what disk repair software does.
parts.answer: It scans the disk for errors such as bad sectors and corrupted file-system entries; it marks bad sectors so they are not used, repairs inconsistencies and tries to recover data from damaged areas.
parts.working: 1 mark each: checks disk for errors/bad sectors; repairs file-system errors / marks bad sectors unusable / recovers data.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A technician is about to format a USB flash drive. State one consequence of formatting it, and one reason for doing so.
parts.answer: Consequence: all data on the drive is erased (or made inaccessible). Reason: to set up a new file system / prepare a new drive / remove all data before giving it away / fix a corrupted drive.
parts.working: B1 consequence; B1 reason.

practice.stem: An accountant's office computer in Sukkur has a hard disk drive that is almost full. Files take a long time to open and the computer sometimes shows unexpected pop-up adverts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Recommend three different utility programs that could help with these problems. For each one, explain how it helps.
parts.answer: Disk contents analysis: shows which files and folders use the most space, so large unneeded files (e.g. old videos) can be found and deleted. Defragmentation: puts fragmented files on the hard disk back into contiguous blocks, so files open faster. Virus checker: the slowdown and pop-ups could be caused by malware, which it can detect and remove. (Also accept: file compression to save space; disk repair to fix bad sectors causing errors.)
parts.working: For each of three utilities: B1 name, B1 explanation linked to the problem (space, speed, errors). Max 6.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a library routine.
parts.answer: A pre-written, pre-tested, (usually pre-compiled) subroutine that can be called from a program.
parts.working: B1: pre-written / pre-tested code (subroutine) that programmers can use in their own programs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two benefits to a programmer of using library routines.
parts.answer: Any two of: saves development time as the code does not need to be written; already tested so it is reliable; may be written by experts so it is efficient; can be used in many programs.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a dynamic link library (DLL).
parts.answer: A library file of compiled routines that is not included in the executable; it is loaded and linked to the program at run time when the program needs it.
parts.working: 1 mark each: library of compiled routines stored separately; linked/loaded at run time (not at compile time).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two benefits of using DLL files instead of including all the library code in each executable file.
parts.answer: Executables are smaller because the library code is not copied into each one, saving storage. One copy of the DLL in memory can be shared by several running programs, saving RAM. If the DLL is updated (e.g. a bug fix), every program that uses it benefits without being recompiled.
parts.working: Two benefits, 2 marks each (point + explanation): smaller executable files; shared in memory by several programs; updating the DLL updates all programs without recompiling; only loaded when needed.

practice.stem: A programmer is writing an app for a cricket academy in Rawalpindi. The app needs to calculate square roots and standard deviations of players' scores and sort large lists of results.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the programmer should use library routines for these tasks rather than writing their own code.
parts.answer: The library routines have already been thoroughly tested, so they are much less likely to contain errors than new code — important when the app's results must be accurate. They are likely to be efficient because they were written by specialists, and using them saves the time it would take to design, write and test the code, so the app is finished sooner.
parts.working: 2 marks per reason (point + development in context): tested/reliable; efficient/optimised; saves development time/cost; programmer does not need specialist knowledge of the algorithm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one possible disadvantage of using a library routine written by someone else.
parts.answer: The programmer cannot see or change how it works, so it may not do exactly what is needed (or may have a bug the programmer cannot fix).
parts.working: B1: may not fit exact requirements / cannot modify / may contain unknown errors / licence restrictions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain three drawbacks of programs relying on DLL files.
parts.answer: If the DLL file is missing or deleted, programs that need it will not run. If the DLL is updated to a new version that is not compatible, programs written for the old version may stop working or behave wrongly (version conflicts). A malicious DLL with the same name could replace the real one, so malware runs whenever the program calls it. The programmer has no control over changes made to the DLL by others.
parts.working: Three drawbacks, 2 marks each (point + explanation), max 6: missing DLL – program fails; incompatible version / changed routine breaks programs; DLL replaced by malware / security risk; programmer cannot control DLL contents.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why protocols are needed for communication between devices.
parts.answer: A protocol is an agreed set of rules (e.g. for data format, addressing, error checking, timing); devices from different manufacturers and with different software can only communicate if they follow the same rules.
parts.working: 1 mark set of rules for data transmission; 1 mark allows different devices/systems to communicate/understand each other.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the four layers of the TCP/IP protocol suite, from the top layer down.
parts.answer: Application, Transport, Internet (Network), Link (Network access).
parts.working: 2 marks all four in the correct order; 1 mark four correct in the wrong order or three correct in order.

practice.stem: A web-design agency in Lahore uses several protocols.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each protocol, state the TCP/IP layer at which it operates: (i) HTTP (ii) TCP (iii) IP (iv) IMAP.
parts.answer: (i) Application (ii) Transport (iii) Internet (iv) Application.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which protocol would be used for each task: (i) uploading the pages of a website from a developer's laptop to a web server; (ii) sending an email from a mail client to the mail server.
parts.answer: (i) FTP (ii) SMTP.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Amina in Karachi sends an email to her friend Kofi in Toronto.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the role of SMTP when Amina sends the email.
parts.answer: SMTP is a push protocol that transfers the email from Amina's mail client to her mail server, and then from her mail server to the recipient's mail server.
parts.working: 1 mark sends/pushes email from client to sender's server; 1 mark relays it between mail servers to the recipient's server.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Kofi reads his emails on a phone and a laptop and wants both to show the same inbox. State which protocol his devices should use to retrieve email, and explain why.
parts.answer: IMAP. Emails stay on the server and the devices synchronise with it, so reading, deleting or moving a message on one device is shown on the other. With POP3 messages are usually downloaded to one device and deleted from the server.
parts.working: 1 mark IMAP; 1 mark messages kept on the server / synchronised; 1 mark contrast with POP3 downloading and deleting.

practice.stem: A photographer in Nairobi uploads large image files to a print company's server.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the purpose of FTP.
parts.answer: To transfer files between a client and a server over a network.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two features of FTP.
parts.answer: Client can log in with a username and password (or anonymously); supports commands to list, upload, download, rename and delete files on the server; uses separate control and data connections; can transfer in text or binary mode.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one reason why FTP should not be used to upload confidential files without additional security.
parts.answer: Standard FTP sends data, usernames and passwords as plain text, so they could be intercepted and read.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the most suitable protocol for each situation: (i) a browser requesting a web page; (ii) retrieving emails so they are kept on the server for access from several devices; (iii) downloading pieces of a large file from many other users at once; (iv) moving a backup file to a remote server using a dedicated file-transfer client.
parts.answer: (i) HTTP (ii) IMAP (iii) BitTorrent (iv) FTP
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the layer of the TCP/IP suite that is responsible for each task: (i) deciding the route a packet takes between networks; (ii) providing the email or web service that the user interacts with; (iii) converting frames into signals sent over the cable; (iv) numbering segments so they can be reassembled.
parts.answer: (i) Internet (ii) Application (iii) Link (iv) Transport
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare POP3 and IMAP. Give three differences.
parts.answer: POP3 downloads messages to the client and normally deletes them from the server; IMAP leaves them on the server. IMAP synchronises folders/read status across many devices; POP3 does not. POP3 messages can be read offline after download and use little server storage; IMAP needs a connection (or a cached copy) and uses server storage. IMAP can download headers only and fetch the body when opened.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three valid differences (each must state both sides or be clearly comparative).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A field researcher works in remote areas of Gilgit-Baltistan with an internet connection only once a week, using a single laptop. Suggest which protocol is more suitable and justify your choice.
parts.answer: POP3 – all messages are downloaded when connected and can then be read offline for the rest of the week on the single laptop; synchronisation across devices is not needed.
parts.working: 1 mark POP3; 1 mark justification linked to offline reading / one device.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the role of the transport layer when a large file is sent across the internet using TCP.
parts.answer: Splits the data into segments (packets); adds a header with source/destination port numbers so data reaches the correct application; adds sequence numbers so the receiver can reassemble segments in order; receiver sends acknowledgements and missing segments are retransmitted, giving reliable delivery; also controls flow (rate of sending).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: segmentation; port numbers; sequence numbers / reassembly; acknowledgements; retransmission of lost segments; flow control; establishes the connection (handshake).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the role of the internet layer.
parts.answer: Adds the IP header containing source and destination IP addresses, and routes each packet across networks (via routers) towards the destination.
parts.working: 1 mark IP addressing (source and destination IP in header); 1 mark routing packets between networks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the role of the link layer.
parts.answer: Places the data on the physical medium: puts packets into frames with MAC (hardware) addresses for the next device on the local network, and transmits them as signals over the cable or wireless link.
parts.working: 1 mark framing / MAC addresses of next hop on the local network; 1 mark physical transmission of bits over the medium; accept error detection on the link.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two benefits of using a layered protocol suite such as TCP/IP.
parts.answer: Each layer has a separate job, so a layer's protocol can be changed or improved (e.g. replacing wired Ethernet with Wi-Fi at the link layer) without changing the other layers. Different manufacturers can develop hardware/software for one layer independently, and products still work together because the interfaces between layers are standard. Complex communication is broken into simpler parts that are easier to design and debug.
parts.working: 2 marks per benefit (identify + explain), any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A user in Islamabad types the address of a news website into a browser. Describe how the TCP/IP layers on the user's computer prepare the request for transmission.
parts.answer: Application layer: the browser creates an HTTP GET request for the page. Transport layer: TCP opens a connection, splits the request into segments and adds a header with port numbers (e.g. destination port for HTTP) and sequence numbers. Internet layer: each segment is put in an IP packet with source and destination IP addresses. Link layer: each packet is put in a frame with MAC addresses and transmitted over the Wi-Fi/Ethernet link to the router.
parts.working: 1 mark HTTP request at application layer; 1 mark TCP segments with sequence numbers; 1 mark port numbers; 1 mark IP header with addresses; 1 mark link layer framing and transmission. Max 5.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what happens to these headers at the web server.
parts.answer: Each layer removes (strips) its own header and passes the data up to the layer above until the HTTP request reaches the web-server application.

practice.stem: A university in Ghana distributes a large open-source operating-system image using BitTorrent.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define each of these BitTorrent terms: (i) swarm (ii) seed (iii) tracker (iv) leech.
parts.answer: (i) Swarm: all the peers connected and sharing the same torrent/file. (ii) Seed: a peer that has the complete file and uploads pieces to others. (iii) Tracker: a server that keeps a list of the peers in the swarm and tells a new peer which peers to connect to. (iv) Leech: a peer that downloads much more than it uploads (has a poor share ratio), harming the swarm.
parts.working: 1 mark each. For leech also accept: a peer that is still downloading and does not yet have the complete file.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why BitTorrent is described as a peer-to-peer protocol.
parts.answer: Each computer (peer) downloads pieces of the file from other peers and also uploads pieces it has to others; there is no single central server sending the whole file.
parts.working: 1 mark peers both download and upload / act as client and server; 1 mark no central server supplies the file.

practice.stem: An indie game studio in Lagos releases a free game update through BitTorrent.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a new user downloads the file using BitTorrent.
parts.answer: The user obtains the torrent file (metadata including the tracker address and the hashes of each piece) and opens it in a BitTorrent client. The client contacts the tracker, which returns a list of peers in the swarm. The client connects to several peers and requests different pieces simultaneously. Each piece is checked against its hash and re-requested if corrupt. As soon as it has pieces, the client uploads them to other peers. When all pieces are received the file is reassembled, and the user may stay as a seed.
parts.working: 1 mark each to max 5: torrent file with metadata; contacts tracker; receives list of peers; downloads different pieces from several peers in parallel; pieces verified with hash; uploads pieces it has to others; reassembly / becomes a seed.

practice.stem: A college in Jeddah runs an online examination portal.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the transport layer makes sure that data arriving at the server is passed to the correct application.
parts.answer: Each segment's header holds a destination port number that identifies the application/service (e.g. web server or mail server); the receiving computer uses the port number to pass the data to that application.
parts.working: 1 mark port numbers in transport-layer header; 1 mark port identifies the application/process on the host.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how TCP makes sure all the data of an online exam submission arrives correctly, even if some packets are lost or arrive out of order.
parts.answer: Each segment has a sequence number; the receiver uses these to put segments back in the right order. The receiver sends acknowledgements for segments received. If the sender gets no acknowledgement before a timeout, it retransmits the segment. A checksum detects corrupted segments, which are discarded and resent.
parts.working: 1 mark each: sequence numbers; reordering at receiver; acknowledgements; timeout and retransmission; checksum for errors. Max 4.

practice.stem: A tourism website promotes Hunza Valley.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what happens, in terms of HTTP, when a user clicks a link to a page on a web server.
parts.answer: The browser (client) sends an HTTP request (GET) with the address/resource of the page to the web server; the server processes the request and sends back an HTTP response containing a status code (e.g. 200 OK or 404 Not Found) and the HTML of the page; the browser renders the page and makes further requests for images, style sheets, etc.
parts.working: 1 mark HTTP request (GET) from client to server; 1 mark response with status code; 1 mark page content (HTML) returned and rendered / further requests.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the TCP/IP layer at which HTTP operates and the transport-layer protocol it normally uses.
parts.answer: Application layer; TCP.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A packet travels from a laptop in Multan to a server in Frankfurt through 12 routers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two items found in an IP packet header and explain why each is needed.
parts.answer: Source IP address – so a reply/error message can be returned to the sender. Destination IP address – so routers can forward the packet towards the correct host. Time to live (hop limit) – so a packet that cannot be delivered is discarded instead of circulating forever. Header checksum – to detect errors in the header. Protocol field – identifies the transport protocol (e.g. TCP) to pass the data to.
parts.working: 2 marks per item (name + reason), any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the destination IP address stays the same for the whole journey but the link-layer (MAC) address changes at every router.
parts.answer: The IP address identifies the final destination host, so it is not changed; the MAC address is only used on each local link, so each router re-frames the packet with the MAC address of the next device (next hop).
parts.working: 1 mark IP is end-to-end/final destination; 1 mark MAC addresses are local to each link, replaced at each hop.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the process of encapsulation in the TCP/IP suite, and explain why it means a router does not need to process the application data.
parts.answer: Data from the application layer is passed down; each layer treats what it receives as its payload and adds its own header (TCP header, then IP header, then link-layer header and trailer). At the receiver, each layer removes its header and passes the payload up. A router works only up to the internet layer: it removes the link-layer frame, reads the IP header to choose the next hop, and re-frames the packet; it never opens the TCP segment or the application data inside, so it does not need to understand HTTP, SMTP etc.
parts.working: 1 mark data passed down the layers; 1 mark each layer adds a header (and trailer at link layer) to the data from the layer above; 1 mark headers removed in reverse order at the receiver; 1 mark router only uses link and internet layers / reads IP header; 1 mark payload above IP left unchanged/unread.

practice.stem: A 1.5 GiB video of a science lecture series is shared by BitTorrent with a piece size of 512 KiB.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of pieces the file is split into.
parts.answer: 3072 pieces

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a client requests the rarest pieces in the swarm first.
parts.answer: If a rare piece is held by only one or two peers who then leave, nobody can complete the file; downloading and re-sharing rare pieces first spreads them so the swarm keeps every piece available.
parts.working: 1 mark rare pieces could be lost if their holders leave; 1 mark spreading them keeps the whole file available / speeds up overall distribution.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why BitTorrent can deliver this file to 10 000 users faster than a single web server using HTTP.
parts.answer: With HTTP every user downloads from one server whose upload bandwidth is shared by all users; with BitTorrent every peer also uploads, so total upload capacity grows as more users join.
parts.working: 1 mark single server bandwidth is a bottleneck; 1 mark peers contribute upload bandwidth / load spread across many computers.

practice.stem: A 6000-byte message is sent using TCP/IP. Each segment can carry at most 1460 bytes of message data, and each segment has 40 bytes of TCP and IP headers in total. Ignore link-layer headers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of segments needed to send the message.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total number of bytes transmitted, including headers.
parts.answer: 6200 bytes

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of transmitted bytes that are message data. Give your answer correct to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the last segment is less efficient than the others.
parts.answer: It carries only 160 bytes of data but still needs the full 40-byte header.

practice.stem: Bilal, whose email provider is based in Islamabad, sends an email to Fatima, whose email address is with a company based in London.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the email travels from Bilal's computer to Fatima's phone. Refer to the protocols used and to the role of DNS.
parts.answer: Bilal's mail client uses SMTP to send the email to his mail server (the Islamabad provider). The sending server uses DNS to look up the mail (MX) record for Fatima's domain and find the IP address of her mail server. It then uses SMTP to transfer the email to Fatima's mail server, where it is stored in her mailbox. Fatima's phone uses IMAP (or POP3) to retrieve the email from her mail server. Underneath, TCP and IP carry the data, split into packets routed across the internet.
parts.working: 1 mark each to max 6: SMTP client to sender's server; DNS lookup of recipient's domain (mail server record); server-to-server transfer with SMTP; stored on recipient's server/mailbox; retrieval by IMAP/POP3; reference to TCP/IP packets across the internet.

practice.stem: A gaming company in Riyadh must deliver a 4 GiB update to 200 000 players on the same day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The company is deciding whether to distribute the 4 GiB update with HTTP from its own servers or with BitTorrent. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of BitTorrent for this company.
parts.answer: Advantages: the load is shared between peers, so the company needs far less server bandwidth and cost; download speed can increase as more users join; no single point of failure. Disadvantages: needs enough seeds – early in the release, or for unpopular files, downloads may be slow; users' upload bandwidth and data allowances are used, which customers may dislike; some networks block BitTorrent traffic; the company has less control/monitoring of who downloads; peers' IP addresses are visible to the swarm (privacy).
parts.working: Max 4 for one side only. 1 mark per valid point, max 6, at least one advantage and one disadvantage, related to the scenario.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe circuit switching.
parts.answer: A dedicated communication path (circuit) is set up between the two ends before any data is sent; it is reserved for the whole communication and released at the end.
parts.working: 1 mark dedicated path set up before transmission; 1 mark reserved for the whole session and all data follows the same route.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe packet switching.
parts.answer: The data is split into packets, each with a header containing the destination address and sequence number. Packets are sent independently and may take different routes, decided by routers. They are reassembled in order at the destination.
parts.working: 1 mark split into packets with headers; 1 mark each packet routed independently / may take different routes; 1 mark reassembled using sequence numbers.

practice.stem: A telephone company in Peshawar compares switching methods.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two advantages of circuit switching for a live telephone call.
parts.answer: Data arrives in order along a dedicated route; constant bandwidth and very little delay/jitter, so speech is not broken up; no reassembly needed.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two disadvantages of circuit switching.
parts.answer: The circuit's bandwidth is wasted when no data is being sent (e.g. silences); the circuit must be set up first, which takes time; if a link fails the connection is lost; no other user can use the reserved channel.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem: A farm in Punjab is choosing how its soil sensors will report to a central computer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the three stages of a communication that uses circuit switching.
parts.answer: 1 Circuit establishment: a dedicated path through the switches/exchanges is set up between sender and receiver. 2 Data transfer: all data is sent along this path, in order, using the reserved bandwidth. 3 Circuit disconnection: when the communication ends the path is released so its links can be used by others.
parts.working: 1 mark each stage described.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one reason why the set-up stage makes circuit switching unsuitable for sending many short messages, such as sensor readings every few seconds.
parts.answer: Setting up (and releasing) a circuit takes time and resources each time, which is large compared with the tiny amount of data sent.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the role of a router in a packet-switched network.
parts.answer: A router receives a packet, reads the destination IP address in its header, looks it up in its routing table and forwards the packet to the next router (next hop) on the best available route; it can choose another route if a link is busy or has failed.
parts.working: 1 mark reads destination address; 1 mark uses routing table; 1 mark forwards to next hop / chooses route depending on traffic or failures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why packets from the same message may arrive out of order, and how the receiver deals with this.
parts.answer: Routers choose routes for each packet independently, so packets can take different paths with different lengths and congestion; the receiver uses the sequence numbers to reassemble them in the correct order, and asks for any missing packet to be resent.
parts.working: 1 mark different routes; 1 mark different delays/congestion; 1 mark reorder using sequence numbers (request missing packets).

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each use, state whether circuit switching or packet switching is more suitable and justify your choice: (i) downloading a 200 MB software update; (ii) a traditional landline call between Karachi and Quetta.
parts.answer: (i) Packet switching – no need for a dedicated line; the network bandwidth is shared efficiently; lost or delayed packets can be resent and data reassembled; delay does not matter for a download. (ii) Circuit switching – a dedicated channel gives constant bandwidth and no delay or jitter, which real-time speech needs.
parts.working: 1 mark each choice; 1 mark each justification.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three items of data that are found in the header of each packet in a packet-switched network.
parts.answer: Any three: source IP address; destination IP address; sequence number / packet number; total number of packets; packet length; time to live (hop count); protocol; checksum.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why packet switching uses network capacity more efficiently than circuit switching.
parts.answer: Links are shared – packets from many users are interleaved on the same links and no bandwidth is reserved while a user is silent or idle, so capacity is used whenever there is data to send.
parts.working: 1 mark links shared by many communications; 1 mark no capacity reserved/wasted during gaps.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A video-conference between doctors in Karachi and Kuala Lumpur uses the internet. Explain why packet switching on the internet can cause problems for real-time video, and describe one way the problem is reduced.
parts.answer: Packets take different routes and meet different congestion, so they arrive with variable delay (jitter), out of order, or are lost; real-time video cannot wait for retransmission, so the picture freezes or breaks up. Reduced by buffering packets at the receiver before playing, by giving video packets priority (quality of service), or by lowering resolution/compression when bandwidth drops.
parts.working: 1 mark variable delay/jitter; 1 mark lost or out-of-order packets; 1 mark effect on real-time video; 1 mark a valid method of reducing it.

practice.stem: A hospital in Peshawar sends a 2 000 000-byte scan to a specialist using a packet-switched network. Each packet carries at most 1480 bytes of data and a 20-byte header.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the minimum number of packets needed to send the file.
parts.answer: 1352 packets

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total number of bytes sent, including headers.
parts.answer: 2 027 040 bytes

parts.label: c
parts.text: One router on the route fails during the transfer. Explain why the transfer can still complete with packet switching but a circuit-switched transfer would fail.
parts.answer: Routers send the remaining packets by another route and missing packets are retransmitted; in circuit switching the single dedicated path is broken and the circuit must be set up again.
parts.working: 1 mark rerouting of packets around the failure; 1 mark circuit uses one fixed path which is lost.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of the time-to-live (TTL) field when the packet arrives at the destination, if it started at 64 and passed through 9 routers, each of which reduces the TTL by 1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the purpose of the TTL field in a packet-switched network.
parts.answer: It limits the number of hops a packet can make; when it reaches 0 the router discards the packet, so packets caught in a routing loop or that cannot be delivered do not circulate forever and waste bandwidth.
parts.working: 1 mark decremented at each router and discarded at 0; 1 mark stops packets circulating indefinitely / congestion.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Another packet starts with TTL 8 and the route to its destination has 11 routers. State what happens to it.
parts.answer: It is discarded by the 8th router (TTL reaches 0) and never arrives; the sender may be notified with an error message.

practice.stem: A circuit-switched call reserves a 64 kbps channel for its whole length of 10 minutes. The callers are speaking for only 40 % of the time.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount of data capacity, in megabytes, that is reserved for the call. 1 MB = 1 000 000 bytes.
parts.answer: 4.8 MB

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the amount of reserved capacity, in megabytes, that is wasted.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how a packet-switched voice-over-IP call would avoid this waste, and describe one problem packet switching can cause for voice calls.
parts.answer: During silences VoIP sends few or no packets, so the shared links carry other users' packets instead. Problem: packets can be delayed by different amounts (jitter) or lost, causing gaps, echoes or out-of-sync speech; buffering adds delay.
parts.working: 1 mark no packets/bandwidth used in silence; 1 mark capacity shared with others; 1 mark problem: latency/jitter/lost packets with effect on speech.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A school in Peshawar has a network of 120 computers. Describe the difference between a virus and a worm.
parts.answer: A virus attaches itself to (is hidden inside) another program or file and needs that file to be run/opened to spread; a worm is a standalone program that replicates itself and spreads across the network on its own, without a host file or user action.
parts.working: 1 mark: virus needs a host file / user action to run and spread. 1 mark: worm is standalone and self-replicates across the network by itself.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what spyware does and give one way it could harm the school.
parts.answer: Spyware secretly monitors/records activity on a computer (e.g. key presses with a key-logger) and sends the data to a third party. Harm: teachers' passwords or students' personal data could be stolen.
parts.working: 1 mark: secretly records/monitors user activity and sends it to a third party. 1 mark: a relevant harm in context, e.g. stolen login details giving access to the results system.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one software measure that protects the network against both viruses and spyware.
parts.answer: Anti-malware software (anti-virus / anti-spyware) that is kept up to date.
parts.working: B1 anti-virus or anti-spyware/anti-malware software (accept up-to-date scanning software).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Customers of an online bank receive an email that looks as if it is from the bank. It asks them to click a link and 'confirm' their card details. Identify this threat and describe how it works.
parts.answer: Phishing. A legitimate-looking email is sent to many people; the link leads to a fake website; details the user types in are captured by the criminal.
parts.working: B1 phishing. Then 1 mark each for any two of: email/message pretends to be from a trusted organisation; contains a link to a fake website; user is tricked into entering personal/financial details; details are sent to the criminal.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Another customer types the bank's correct web address but is taken to a fake site. Identify this threat and explain how it differs from the threat in (a).
parts.answer: Pharming. Malicious code on the user's computer or a compromised (poisoned) DNS server redirects the correct URL to a fake website. Unlike phishing, the user does not have to click a link in a message – typing the genuine address is enough.
parts.working: B1 pharming. 1 mark: malicious code installed on the computer / DNS cache or server altered. 1 mark: redirection happens even when the correct URL is typed / no email link needed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one action a customer can take to avoid being caught by the threat in (a).
parts.answer: Do not click links in unexpected emails; type the bank's address directly / check the sender and the URL carefully.
parts.working: B1 any sensible action.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A small accountancy firm in Dubai connects its LAN to the internet. Describe how a firewall helps to protect the LAN.
parts.answer: The firewall sits between the LAN and the internet and examines every packet entering or leaving. It compares packets with a set of rules/criteria (e.g. allowed IP addresses, ports, protocols). Packets that do not meet the rules are blocked; it can also log traffic and stop unauthorised access from outside.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: positioned between LAN and internet (or on a computer); monitors incoming and outgoing traffic/packets; checks against rules/criteria set by the administrator; blocks/rejects packets that fail; can block certain IP addresses/ports/websites; keeps a log of attempted access.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two other security measures the firm could use to protect client data on its server, other than a firewall.
parts.answer: Any two of: strong passwords / user accounts; access rights; encryption of stored data; anti-malware software; biometrics; two-step verification.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two distinct measures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the terms plaintext, ciphertext and encryption key.
parts.answer: Plaintext: the original, readable data before encryption. Ciphertext: the scrambled data produced by encryption, unreadable without the key. Key: a value used by the encryption algorithm to encrypt/decrypt the data.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct definition.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the difference between symmetric and asymmetric encryption.
parts.answer: Symmetric encryption uses the same (secret) key to encrypt and decrypt. Asymmetric encryption uses a pair of mathematically related keys: a public key and a private key – data encrypted with one key can only be decrypted with the other.
parts.working: 1 mark: symmetric – one shared secret key. 1 mark: asymmetric – public/private key pair.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how quantum cryptography is used to share an encryption key.
parts.answer: The key is sent as a stream of photons (light particles) whose polarisation represents the bits, using a quantum key distribution protocol. The receiver measures the photons with randomly chosen filters and the two sides compare which filters they used to build a shared key. Any attempt to observe the photons changes their state, so eavesdropping can be detected.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: uses the properties of photons/quantum mechanics; bits represented by polarisation; quantum key distribution (QKD); measuring a photon changes its state; eavesdropper is detected; key is then used for encryption.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one benefit and one drawback of quantum cryptography.
parts.answer: Benefit: eavesdropping on the key exchange can always be detected, so the key is (in theory) completely secure / longer keys can be shared. Drawback: needs expensive specialist hardware/dedicated fibre links, limited distance, and the technology is still developing.
parts.working: 1 mark for a benefit; 1 mark for a drawback.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A college in Multan stores student marks in a database. Explain what is meant by access rights.
parts.answer: Permissions given to each user (or group of users) that control which data/files they can see and what they can do with them, e.g. no access, read-only, or read/write.
parts.working: 1 mark: permissions set per user/group. 1 mark: levels such as read-only / read-write / no access.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest suitable access rights for students, teachers and the examinations officer, and give a reason for each.
parts.answer: Students: read-only access to their own marks – they need to see results but must not change them. Teachers: read and write access to marks for their own classes – they enter and correct marks. Examinations officer: full access (read/write/delete) to all records – manages all results.
parts.working: 1 mark for each user type with suitable rights and a reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hospital in Karachi gives doctors access to patient records. At present each doctor logs in with a user ID and password. Explain why adding two-step (two-factor) verification would make the system more secure.
parts.answer: A second, different factor is required (e.g. a one-time code sent to the doctor's phone, or a fingerprint). A criminal who has stolen or guessed the password still cannot log in without that second factor.
parts.working: 1 mark: a second, independent form of authentication is needed (something you have/are). 1 mark: a stolen/guessed password alone is no longer enough.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The hospital considers fingerprint scanners instead of passwords. Give one advantage and one disadvantage of using biometrics in this situation.
parts.answer: Advantage: fingerprints are unique and cannot be forgotten, shared or guessed. Disadvantage: e.g. scanners may fail with dirty or gloved hands (doctors wear gloves) / cost of equipment / biometric data cannot be changed if stolen.
parts.working: 1 mark for a valid advantage; 1 mark for a valid disadvantage (credit context such as surgical gloves).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how access rights should be used so that reception staff cannot view patients' medical history.
parts.answer: Each user account is placed in a group with set permissions. Reception staff are given access only to contact/appointment data (read/write) and no access (or read-only to limited fields) for medical history, which only doctors can read/edit.
parts.working: 1 mark: different users/groups given different permissions. 1 mark: reception have no access to medical-history data while doctors do.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A photographer in Lahore stores all her client images on one external hard disk. Identify two ways her data could be lost other than by malware or hacking.
parts.answer: Any two of: hardware failure of the disk; accidental deletion/overwriting; physical damage (fire, flood, dropping it); theft/loss of the disk; power cut while writing corrupts data.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two distinct causes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two measures she could take to reduce the risk of losing her data, and explain how each helps.
parts.answer: Regular backups to a second device or cloud storage, kept in a different place – a copy can be restored if the original is lost or damaged. Disk mirroring (RAID 1) – data is written to two disks at the same time so if one fails the other still has the data. (Also accept: UPS to allow safe shutdown in a power cut; keeping disk in a fireproof safe; making files read-only.)
parts.working: For each of two measures: 1 mark naming/describing it, 1 mark explaining how it prevents loss.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how anti-virus software detects and deals with a virus.
parts.answer: It scans files (on access or on a schedule) and compares their code with a database of known virus signatures; heuristic checking looks for virus-like behaviour in unknown files; a suspicious file is quarantined (isolated) or deleted, and the user is alerted; the signature database must be updated regularly.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: scans files/memory; compares with known signatures; heuristic/behaviour analysis; quarantines infected files; deletes/repairs files; alerts the user; needs regular updates of the database.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a computer with up-to-date anti-virus software can still be infected.
parts.answer: A brand-new virus may not yet have a signature in the database (zero-day), and heuristics may not spot it, so it is not detected until an update is released.
parts.working: 1 mark: new/unknown virus not in the signature database. 1 mark: so it is not recognised until the database is updated / heuristics miss it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ayesha wants to send a confidential file to Bilal using asymmetric encryption so that only Bilal can read it. State which key Ayesha uses to encrypt the file and which key Bilal uses to decrypt it.
parts.answer: Ayesha encrypts with Bilal's public key; Bilal decrypts with his own private key.
parts.working: B1 Bilal's public key. B1 Bilal's private key.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a person who intercepts the file cannot read it, even though Bilal's public key is freely available.
parts.answer: The file can only be decrypted with the matching private key, which only Bilal holds and never shares; the public key cannot be used to decrypt it (and the private key cannot practically be worked out from the public key).
parts.working: 1 mark: only the private key can decrypt. 1 mark: only Bilal has the private key / it is never transmitted.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Bilal replies with a message that Ayesha must be sure came from him. Describe how keys are used so that Ayesha can be sure of this.
parts.answer: Bilal encrypts (a digest of) the message with his own private key; Ayesha decrypts it with Bilal's public key – if it decrypts correctly it must have come from Bilal, because only he has the private key.
parts.working: 1 mark: Bilal uses his private key. 1 mark: Ayesha uses Bilal's public key, proving the sender.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A software company in Bengaluru signs every update it releases with a digital signature. Describe how the digital signature is produced.
parts.answer: A hashing algorithm is applied to the update file to produce a message digest. The digest is encrypted with the company's private key. The encrypted digest (the digital signature) is attached to/sent with the file.
parts.working: 1 mark each: hash/digest of the file; digest encrypted with the sender's private key; signature sent with the file.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how a user's computer checks the signature before installing the update.
parts.answer: It decrypts the signature using the company's public key to recover the original digest. It applies the same hashing algorithm to the received file to make a new digest. If the two digests match, the file is genuine and unaltered; if not, it is rejected.
parts.working: 1 mark each: decrypt signature with company's public key; re-hash the received file with the same algorithm; compare digests – match means authentic and unchanged.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the purpose of the TLS protocol.
parts.answer: To provide a secure (encrypted) connection between a client and a server across the internet, giving confidentiality, integrity of the data and authentication of the server.
parts.working: 1 mark: encrypts data in transit/secure connection. 1 mark: authenticates server / ensures data not altered.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two situations where TLS is used.
parts.answer: Any two of: HTTPS web browsing (e.g. online banking/shopping); secure email transfer (SMTP/IMAP over TLS); VoIP/video calls; online payment systems; VPN connections.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe what is meant by a session key in TLS.
parts.answer: A symmetric key that is agreed/created during the handshake and used only for the current session to encrypt the data exchanged; it is discarded at the end.
parts.working: 1 mark: symmetric key created in the handshake. 1 mark: used only for that session.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
An online shoe shop based in Islamabad reports these problems:
1. Staff passwords were captured by a program that recorded every key pressed.
2. An attachment opened by one employee copied itself into many other files on the server.
3. Someone outside the company gained access to the customer database by guessing a weak administrator password.
For each problem, identify the threat and recommend one specific measure that would have prevented it. Justify each recommendation.
parts.answer:
1. Spyware (key-logger) – anti-spyware software / use of on-screen or drop-down entry of password characters / two-step verification so a captured password alone is useless.
2. Virus – anti-virus software scanning email attachments; staff training not to open unknown attachments.
3. Hacking (unauthorised access) – strong password policy (length, mixed characters, changed regularly) plus lock-out after several failed attempts / firewall / two-step verification.
parts.working: For each of the three problems: 1 mark for the correct threat; 1 mark for a suitable measure with a justification linked to the problem (a measure without a reason scores 0 for that mark).

parts.label: a
parts.text: An online university portal uses a digital certificate. Describe how the university obtains its digital certificate.
parts.answer: The university generates a public/private key pair and sends a request containing its public key and identity details to a Certificate Authority (CA). The CA checks the university's identity. The CA issues the certificate containing the public key and details, signed with the CA's own private key.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: applies to a Certificate Authority; supplies public key and identification details; CA verifies identity; CA creates certificate and signs it with the CA's private key; certificate issued with expiry date.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three items of information that a digital certificate contains.
parts.answer: Any three of: the owner's (subject's) name/domain; the owner's public key; the name of the issuing CA; the CA's digital signature; serial number; validity (start and expiry) dates; algorithm used.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how a student's browser uses the certificate to decide whether to trust the portal.
parts.answer: The browser checks the CA's signature on the certificate using the CA's public key (which it already trusts); it also checks the certificate has not expired/been revoked and that the domain name matches the site. If all checks pass, it trusts the public key in the certificate.
parts.working: 1 mark: verifies CA signature with CA's public key. 1 mark: checks validity dates/domain/revocation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the main steps of a TLS handshake between a browser and a web server.
parts.answer: The client sends a 'hello' listing the TLS versions and cipher suites it supports. The server replies, choosing the version/cipher suite, and sends its digital certificate. The client checks the certificate with the CA's public key. The client and server then agree a session key – e.g. the client creates a secret and encrypts it with the server's public key, and only the server can decrypt it with its private key. Both sides derive the same symmetric session key and confirm the handshake is finished; data is then encrypted with that key.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five of: client hello with supported versions/ciphers; server hello choosing cipher; server sends certificate/public key; client verifies certificate (via CA); key exchange using server's public key (or key-agreement method); server uses private key; both generate same session key; 'finished' messages / encrypted data transfer begins.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why TLS uses asymmetric encryption only during the handshake and symmetric encryption for the data that follows.
parts.answer: Asymmetric encryption solves the problem of sharing a key securely but is slow/processor-intensive; symmetric encryption is much faster, so it is used for the bulk of the data once the session key has been shared safely.
parts.working: 1 mark: asymmetric allows secure key exchange (no shared secret needed in advance). 1 mark: symmetric is faster/less processing for large amounts of data.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student says: 'A digital signature is made by encrypting the whole document with the sender's private key.' Explain why a hash (message digest) is signed instead of the whole document.
parts.answer: The digest is short and of fixed length, so encrypting it with the private key is much quicker than encrypting a large document; it still identifies the document uniquely because any change to the document gives a different digest.
parts.working: 1 mark: digest is small/fixed length – faster to encrypt and send. 1 mark: digest still detects any change to the document.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A contract file signed by a lawyer in Faisalabad has one figure changed in transit. Explain how the receiver detects this.
parts.answer: The receiver hashes the received (altered) file and gets a new digest; this does not match the digest recovered by decrypting the signature with the lawyer's public key, so the file is shown to have been altered.
parts.working: 1 mark: new hash computed from received file differs. 1 mark: compared with digest from decrypted signature – mismatch shows tampering.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a digital signature on its own does not prove that the public key used really belongs to the lawyer, and state what solves this problem.
parts.answer: Anyone could create a key pair and claim the public key is the lawyer's; a digital certificate issued and signed by a trusted Certificate Authority links the public key to the lawyer's identity.
parts.working: 1 mark: public key could belong to an impostor. 1 mark: digital certificate from a CA.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A research group of 12 scientists in different countries each wants to exchange private messages with every other member. Calculate how many different secret keys are needed if symmetric encryption is used with a separate key for each pair of members.
parts.answer: 66 keys
parts.working: M1 number of pairs = n(n − 1) ÷ 2. A1 12 × 11 ÷ 2 = 66.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many keys in total are needed if asymmetric encryption is used instead.
parts.answer: 24 keys (one public and one private key for each of the 12 members)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Apart from the number of keys, explain one other problem with symmetric encryption that asymmetric encryption solves.
parts.answer: The key distribution problem: the shared secret key must first be sent to the other person, and if it is intercepted in transit the messages can be read. With asymmetric encryption the public key can be sent openly and the private key never leaves its owner.
parts.working: 1 mark: secret key has to be shared/transmitted and could be intercepted. 1 mark: asymmetric public key can be shared openly; private key never sent.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between validation and verification.
parts.answer: Validation is an automatic check by the computer that data is reasonable/sensible and follows set rules (it cannot tell if the data is actually correct). Verification checks that data has been copied or entered accurately, i.e. it matches the original.
parts.working: 1 mark: validation – checks data is sensible/meets rules. 1 mark: verification – checks data matches the source/is copied correctly.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two methods of verification that could be used when a clerk types customers' names into a utility company's system.
parts.answer: Double entry: the name is typed twice (possibly by two people) and the computer compares the two versions; if they differ the clerk is asked to re-enter. Visual check (proof-reading): the clerk compares the data on screen with the original paper form before confirming.
parts.working: For each method: 1 mark for the name, 1 mark for a description.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
An online form for a cricket academy in Rawalpindi collects the data below. For each item, identify the most suitable validation check.
(i) The player's age, which must be between 8 and 18.
(ii) The player's email address, which must contain one '@'.
(iii) The player's surname, which must not be left blank.
(iv) The batting style, which must be one of 'Left', 'Right'.
parts.answer: (i) Range check. (ii) Format check. (iii) Presence check. (iv) Lookup (existence/list) check.
parts.working: 1 mark each. Accept 'character check' for (ii); accept 'list check' for (iv).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why validation cannot ensure that a player's date of birth is correct.
parts.answer: Validation only checks the date is reasonable/possible (e.g. a valid date in a sensible range); a wrong but valid date, such as 12/03/2012 typed instead of 21/03/2012, would still be accepted.
parts.working: 1 mark: validation only checks data is sensible/follows rules. 1 mark: a plausible but wrong value passes (example).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how an echo check verifies data sent from a computer to a remote device.
parts.answer: The receiving device sends a copy of the data it received back to the sender. The sender compares the returned data with the original. If they are different, an error occurred and the data is sent again.
parts.working: 1 mark each: data sent back to sender; compared with original; resent if different.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one drawback of an echo check.
parts.answer: It doubles the amount of data transmitted / if they differ you cannot tell whether the error was on the outward or the return journey.
parts.working: B1 either point.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A warehouse in Sialkot gives each product a five-digit code followed by a modulo-11 check digit. The weights 6, 5, 4, 3, 2 are applied to the five digits from left to right. The check digit is 11 minus the remainder when the weighted sum is divided by 11 (a result of 11 becomes 0 and a result of 10 becomes X). Calculate the check digit for the code 70386. Show your working.
parts.answer: Check digit = 9 (full code 703869)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a check digit detects an error when the code is typed in.
parts.answer: The computer recalculates the check digit from the first five digits entered and compares it with the check digit typed; if they differ, an error (e.g. a wrong or transposed digit) has occurred and the code is rejected.
parts.working: 1 mark: check digit recalculated from the entered digits. 1 mark: compared with entered check digit – mismatch means error.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A system uses even parity, with the parity bit as the most significant bit of each byte. Write the 8-bit byte that is sent for each of these 7-bit data values.
(i) 1011001
(ii) 0110100
(iii) 1111111
parts.working: 1 mark each. (i) four 1s → parity bit 0. (ii) three 1s → parity bit 1. (iii) seven 1s → parity bit 1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The byte 10110110 is received using even parity. State whether an error has been detected and explain your answer.
