Expand L (13): M (12, 5, 17); N (13, 0, 13).
Expand N (13) – goal.
Order H, J, L, N. Path H → J → L → N, cost 13.
parts.working: 1 mark J and K from H; 1 mark K improved to g 5 via J; 1 mark L f 13 chosen before K f 14; 1 mark M and N values; 1 mark order and path/cost 13.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Dijkstra's algorithm would make H, J, K, M and L permanent before N. Explain, with reference to the heuristic values, why A* reached N after expanding fewer nodes.
parts.answer: K and M have large h values (9 and 5) because they lead away from N, giving them f values of 14 and 17, higher than N's 13; A* never expands them, while Dijkstra expands every node closer to H than N.
parts.working: 1 mark K/M high f because of h; 1 mark Dijkstra uses only g (distance from start).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning.
parts.answer: AI is the general ability of a computer system to perform tasks that normally need human intelligence; machine learning is a type of AI in which the system learns from data and improves its performance without being explicitly programmed with rules.
parts.working: 1 mark AI definition; 1 mark ML learns from data / improves with experience without explicit programming.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what is meant by deep learning.
parts.answer: A form of machine learning that uses artificial neural networks with many hidden layers to learn complex patterns from large amounts of data (e.g. images, speech).
parts.working: 1 mark neural networks with many (hidden) layers; 1 mark learns features/patterns from large amounts of (unstructured) data.

practice.stem: An agricultural research institute in Faisalabad uses machine learning to help wheat farmers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe supervised learning, using an example from this scenario.
parts.answer: The model is trained on labelled data where the correct output is known, e.g. thousands of leaf photos each labelled 'healthy' or 'rust disease'; it learns to predict the label for new photos.
parts.working: 1 mark labelled training data / known outputs; 1 mark example (labelled leaf photos).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe unsupervised learning, using an example from this scenario.
parts.answer: The model is given unlabelled data and finds patterns or groups (clusters) by itself, e.g. grouping farms into clusters with similar soil readings and yields.
parts.working: 1 mark unlabelled data, finds its own patterns/clusters; 1 mark example.

practice.stem: A bank in Nairobi is building a machine-learning system to detect fraudulent card payments.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between labelled and unlabelled data.
parts.answer: Labelled data includes the correct output/answer for each item (e.g. an email marked 'spam'); unlabelled data has only the inputs, with no known output.
parts.working: 1 mark labelled has known output/tag; 1 mark unlabelled has none.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the available data is split into a training set and a test set.
parts.answer: The model learns from the training set; the separate test set, which the model has never seen, is used to check how accurately it works on new data (that it has not just memorised the training data).
parts.working: 1 mark training set used to learn/adjust model; 1 mark test set of unseen data measures real accuracy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each task, state whether supervised, unsupervised or reinforcement learning is most suitable: (i) an email filter trained on messages marked 'spam' or 'not spam'; (ii) a program that learns to play a racing game by being given points for finishing laps quickly; (iii) grouping news articles into topics without any topic labels; (iv) predicting house prices in Islamabad from past sales.
parts.answer: (i) supervised (ii) reinforcement (iii) unsupervised (iv) supervised (regression)
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how reinforcement learning could be used to train a robot vacuum cleaner to clean a room efficiently. Use the terms agent, environment, action, reward and policy.
parts.answer: The robot is the agent and the room is the environment. In each state the agent chooses an action (move forward, turn, etc.). It receives a reward for cleaning new floor and a penalty (negative reward) for bumping into furniture or re-cleaning. By trial and error it updates its policy – the rule for choosing actions in each state – to maximise the total reward over time.
parts.working: 1 mark each correct use of: agent; environment; action; reward/penalty; policy updated to maximise cumulative reward.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the structure of an artificial neural network.
parts.answer: Made of artificial neurons (nodes) arranged in layers: an input layer, one or more hidden layers and an output layer. Each connection between neurons has a weight. Each neuron adds its weighted inputs (plus a bias) and applies an activation function to produce its output, which passes to the next layer.
parts.working: 1 mark each to max 4: input layer; hidden layer(s); output layer; weighted connections; neuron sums weighted inputs + bias; activation function.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how artificial neural networks have helped machine learning.
parts.answer: They can learn complex, non-linear patterns directly from large amounts of raw data, such as images or speech, without a programmer defining the rules or features; this has made tasks like face and speech recognition far more accurate.
parts.working: 1 mark learn complex/non-linear relationships or features automatically; 1 mark example/improved accuracy in recognition tasks.

practice.stem: A single artificial neuron in a fire-alarm system has three inputs x₁, x₂, x₃ (each 0 or 1) with weights 0.6, −0.4 and 0.3, and a bias of −0.5. It outputs 1 if the weighted sum (including the bias) is ≥ 0, and 0 otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the weighted sum and the output of the neuron for the inputs x₁ = 1, x₂ = 0, x₃ = 1.
parts.answer: Sum = 0.4, output 1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the weighted sum and the output for x₁ = 0, x₂ = 1, x₃ = 1.
parts.answer: Sum = −0.6, output 0

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what happens to the weights during training when the output is wrong.
parts.answer: The weights (and bias) are adjusted to reduce the error.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how back propagation of errors is used to train an artificial neural network.
parts.answer: Training data is passed forward through the network to give an output. The output is compared with the expected (labelled) output to find the error. The error is passed backwards through the network, layer by layer, to work out how much each weight contributed to it. Each weight is adjusted (e.g. by gradient descent) to reduce the error, and the process is repeated over many examples/epochs until the error is acceptably small.
parts.working: 1 mark each to max 4: forward pass; compare with expected output to calculate error; error sent backwards from output layer through hidden layers; weights adjusted in proportion to their contribution; repeated many times until error minimised.

practice.stem: An online clothing store in Lahore has data about 200 000 customers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how unsupervised learning could be used by the store to group its customers, and give one way the store could use the results.
parts.answer: Customer data (purchases, spending, frequency, location) is given to a clustering algorithm without labels; it finds groups of customers with similar behaviour, e.g. 'students buying on discount days'. The store can then send targeted offers or adverts to each group.
parts.working: 1 mark unlabelled customer data; 1 mark algorithm finds clusters of similar customers itself; 1 mark use: targeted marketing/stock planning.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why supervised learning could not be used for this task at first.
parts.answer: There are no labels – the groups are not known in advance, so there are no correct answers to train with.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between machine learning and deep learning in the way features are identified.
parts.answer: In traditional machine learning a human usually chooses the features to use (e.g. size, colour); in deep learning the many layers of the neural network learn the relevant features automatically from raw data.
parts.working: 1 mark ML: features selected/engineered by people; 1 mark DL: network learns features itself from raw data.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two reasons why deep learning needs more computing resources than simpler machine-learning methods.
parts.answer: It has millions of weights to adjust; it needs very large training datasets; training needs many repeated passes (epochs) and powerful GPUs.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem:
A small neural network has inputs A and B (0 or 1). Each neuron outputs 1 if its weighted sum (including bias) is ≥ 0, otherwise 0.
Hidden neuron h₁: weights 1 (from A), 1 (from B), bias −0.5
Hidden neuron h₂: weights 1 (from A), 1 (from B), bias −1.5
Output neuron: weights 1 (from h₁), −2 (from h₂), bias −0.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Complete a table showing h₁, h₂ and the output for all four combinations of inputs A and B.
parts.working: 1 mark h₁ column; 1 mark h₂ column; 2 marks output column (1 mark for three correct).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the logic function that the network carries out, and explain why a network with a hidden layer is needed for it.
parts.answer: XOR. The outputs cannot be separated by a single straight line (not linearly separable), so a single neuron cannot do it; the hidden layer combines OR and AND results.
parts.working: 1 mark XOR; 1 mark not linearly separable / needs combination of hidden neurons.

practice.stem: An agricultural extension service in Punjab wants to help farmers who cannot easily reach an expert.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how deep learning could be used to build a system that identifies crop diseases from photographs taken by farmers' phones. Refer to the data needed, training, testing and use of the system.
parts.answer: Collect a large set of leaf photos labelled by experts with the disease (or healthy). Split into training and test sets. Train a deep neural network with many hidden layers: the images are input as pixel values; early layers learn simple features (edges, colours), deeper layers learn complex features (lesion shapes); back propagation adjusts weights to reduce errors. Test on unseen photos to measure accuracy, and retrain/tune if poor. Deploy in an app: a farmer's photo is fed through the network and the most probable disease is output, with advice. New labelled photos can be used to keep improving it.
parts.working: 1 mark each to max 6: large labelled dataset; training/test split; deep network with many layers learning features automatically; back propagation/weight adjustment; testing on unseen data for accuracy; using the trained model to classify new photos; continued learning / retraining.

practice.stem:
A tutoring centre in Dubai trained a linear regression model to predict test score (y) from hours of study (x): y = 6x + 38. The data used to test it is:
Hours | Actual score
2 | 49
4 | 63
5 | 66
7 | 82

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by regression in machine learning.
parts.answer: A supervised learning method that models the relationship between input variables and a continuous numerical output, so it can predict a value (e.g. a score) for new inputs.
parts.working: 1 mark predicts a continuous/numeric value; 1 mark learned from the relationship in (labelled) training data.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the model to predict the score of a student who studies for 6 hours.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mean squared error of the model on the four data points.
parts.working: M1: predictions 50, 62, 68, 80; M1: errors −1, 1, −2, 2 and squares 1, 1, 4, 4; A1: 10 ÷ 4 = 2.5.

practice.stem: A perceptron has two inputs with weights w₁ = 0.2 and w₂ = −0.5, and a bias of 0.1 (treated as a weight on a constant input of 1). It outputs 1 if the weighted sum ≥ 0, otherwise 0. The training rule is: new weight = old weight + η × (target − output) × input, with learning rate η = 0.1. A training example has inputs (1, 1) and target output 1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the output of the perceptron before training for the input (1, 1).
parts.answer: Output 0

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the training rule to calculate the new values of w₁, w₂ and the bias.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Show that the perceptron now gives the target output for this input.
parts.answer: 0.3 − 0.4 + 0.2 = 0.1 ≥ 0, so output 1 = target.

practice.stem:
A warehouse robot in Port Qasim is trained by reinforcement learning. Each move costs a reward of −1, reaching the loading bay gives +10, and hitting a shelf gives −10 and ends the episode.
Episode 1: 3 moves then reaches the loading bay (rewards −1, −1, −1, +10)
Episode 2: 5 moves then reaches the loading bay (rewards −1, −1, −1, −1, −1, +10)
Episode 3: 2 moves then hits a shelf (rewards −1, −1, −10)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total reward for each episode and state which episode the agent should learn to repeat.
parts.answer: Episode 1: 7; Episode 2: 5; Episode 3: −12. Episode 1 (highest total reward).
parts.working: 1 mark episodes 1 and 2; 1 mark episode 3; 1 mark episode 1 chosen.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the difference between exploration and exploitation in reinforcement learning, and why the agent needs both.
parts.answer: Exploitation: choosing the action currently believed to give the highest reward (e.g. repeating episode 1's route). Exploration: trying new or less-tried actions to discover whether they give more reward. Without exploration the agent may never find a better route; without exploitation it never benefits from what it has learned, so a balance is needed.
parts.working: 1 mark exploitation; 1 mark exploration; 1 mark reason for balance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why copyright legislation is needed for software.
parts.answer: Software is easy to copy; copyright law gives the creator legal ownership so others cannot copy, distribute or sell it without permission, which protects the creator's income / rewards the effort and encourages new development.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 2: protects creator's work from copying; protects income/rewards investment; encourages innovation; gives legal recourse.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two methods a software company can use to reduce illegal copying of its software.
parts.answer: Any two: product key / online activation; a licence agreement that the user must accept; distributing only compiled (object) code, not source code; encryption of the program; a hardware dongle; digital rights management that limits installations.
parts.working: 1 mark each, with a brief description.

practice.stem: A small developer in Lahore releases a photo-editing app. Anyone can download it and use it free for 30 days, after which it stops saving files until the user buys a licence key.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the features of shareware, using the photo-editing app as an example.
parts.answer:
1 mark each, max 3:
• it can be downloaded and used free for a trial period (here 30 days) / with limited features
• the user must pay to continue using it / unlock the full version
• the source code is not provided, so users cannot modify it
• the author keeps the copyright
• users may be allowed to pass on copies of the trial version

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one reason why the developer chose to release the app as shareware rather than only selling it.
parts.answer: Users can try it before buying, so more people may try it and then pay / it is free advertising.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each statement, identify which of these licence types it applies to: commercial, shareware, free software, open source. A statement may apply to more than one type.
(i) The source code is supplied with the program.
(ii) The user may give modified copies to other people.
(iii) The program can be used free of charge only for a limited trial period.
(iv) The user pays for a licence before using the program, and may not copy it.
parts.answer:
(i) free software, open source
(ii) free software, open source
(iii) shareware
(iv) commercial
parts.working: 1 mark each; all correct types and no wrong ones.

practice.stem: Ayesha copies a commercial game from her friend's USB flash drive and installs it on her own laptop without buying it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why installing the copied game is illegal.
parts.answer: The game is commercial software protected by copyright; the licence allows only the purchaser to use/install it, so copying it without paying breaches the licence agreement / copyright law.
parts.working: 1 mark copyright/commercial licence; 1 mark copying without permission/payment.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two effects of this kind of copying on the game's developers.
parts.answer: e.g. loss of income from lost sales; less money to develop new games / pay staff; may raise prices for legitimate buyers; may stop releasing games in that country.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what the word 'free' means in 'free software'.
parts.answer: Freedom (liberty) for the user, not necessarily free of charge.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two freedoms that users of free software have.
parts.answer: Any two: run the program for any purpose; study and change the source code; redistribute copies; distribute copies of modified versions.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two similarities between free software (as defined by the Free Software Foundation) and open source software.
parts.answer: Any two: source code is available; users may modify the code; users may redistribute copies (modified or not); neither has to be free of charge.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two differences between free software and open source software.
parts.answer:
Any two:
• free software is based on an ethical idea — users' freedom — while open source focuses on the practical benefits of shared development
• free software (with a copyleft licence such as the GPL) requires modified versions to be released under the same free terms; some open source licences allow modified versions to be made closed / proprietary
• free software guarantees four specific freedoms; open source licences follow the Open Source Definition criteria
parts.working: 1 mark each; must contrast both.

practice.stem: A start-up in Lahore has written an accounting program for small shops and must decide how to licence it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two advantages to the company of selling the program under a commercial licence.
parts.answer: e.g. income from each licence sold; source code kept secret so competitors cannot copy it; control over who uses it / how many installations.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two advantages to the company of releasing the program as open source software instead.
parts.answer: e.g. other programmers can find and fix bugs / add features; wider adoption builds reputation; company can earn from support, training and customisation; lower development cost.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one disadvantage to the company of releasing the program as open source.
parts.answer: e.g. competitors can see and reuse the code / harder to earn money from licence sales / less control over direction of development.

practice.stem: A university in Islamabad needs a learning management system for 12 000 students.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain three reasons why the university might choose open source software for its learning management system.
parts.answer:
1 mark each, max 3:
• no licence fee, which matters with thousands of student users
• source code available, so the university's IT staff can customise it (e.g. add Urdu-language pages / link to its admissions system)
• large community of developers fixes bugs and adds features
• not locked in to one supplier; can continue if the supplier stops trading
parts.working: Must relate to the scenario for full marks.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one drawback of this choice for the university.
parts.answer: e.g. no guaranteed official support; staff need skills to install/maintain it; costs of customisation; quality of documentation varies.

practice.stem: A school in Multan wants to install a commercial programming environment on all 40 computers in its lab.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the most suitable type of commercial licence for the school and explain why.
parts.answer: A site licence (or multi-user licence for 40 users): one licence covers all computers at the school, usually cheaper and easier to manage than 40 single-user licences.
parts.working: 1 mark site / multi-user licence; 1 mark reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what a software licence agreement sets out.
parts.answer: The legal terms of use: e.g. how many computers / users may run it, whether copies may be made or passed on, how long the licence lasts, restrictions on modification/reverse engineering, liability.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 2.

practice.stem: A tax-calculation program sold in Pakistan is supplied with a 25-character product key.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a product key with online activation helps to protect the software.
parts.answer: Each copy needs a unique key that is checked against the company's server when installed; a key already used on the permitted number of devices is rejected, so copies cannot be activated by others.
parts.working: 1 mark unique key; 1 mark checked/limited activations.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one problem this method can cause for a legitimate customer.
parts.answer: e.g. cannot activate without an internet connection / reinstalling after a new hard disk may be refused / key lost.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one other method of protecting software from illegal use.
parts.answer: e.g. licence agreement, encryption, dongle, distributing object code only, DRM.

practice.stem: Bilal finds a free software stock-control program released under the GNU General Public Licence (GPL). He adds a module for Pakistani sales tax and wants to sell the modified program to shops without giving them the source code.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain whether Bilal is allowed to sell his modified version as a closed product.
parts.answer:
1 mark each:
• he is allowed to charge money for the software (free means freedom, not price)
• but the GPL is a copyleft licence, so his modified version must be released under the same licence
• therefore he must make the source code of his changes available and allow buyers to copy/modify it — he may not keep it closed

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how Bilal could still earn money from his work.
parts.answer: e.g. charge for installation, support, training, custom features or hosting.

practice.stem: Sana, a musician in Karachi, posts her original tracks on her website. A game developer downloads three tracks and includes them in a game sold online, without contacting her.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the copyright issue and what the game developer should have done.
parts.answer:
1 mark each:
• Sana owns the copyright in her original music as soon as she creates it
• using the tracks in the game without permission is an infringement, even though they were found online
• the developer should have asked Sana for permission / obtained a licence (possibly paying a fee and crediting her) before using them

parts.label: b
parts.text: A buyer of the game says, 'I paid for my copy, so I own the game and can upload it for others.' Explain why this is wrong.
parts.answer: Buying a copy only gives a licence to use it under the stated terms; the copyright remains with the developer (and Sana for the music), so the buyer has no right to distribute copies.
parts.working: 1 mark licence to use, not ownership; 1 mark copyright stays with creator, no right to distribute.

practice.stem: A private hospital in Rawalpindi with 60 staff needs a patient-records system. It can buy a commercial product with a yearly licence and support contract, or use a free software (GPL) product that its own IT team would install and maintain.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether the hospital should choose the commercial product or the free software product. Give a justified recommendation.
parts.answer: Either choice can score full marks if justified. Model conclusion: the free software product, provided the hospital pays for an external support contract, because it avoids yearly fees for 60 users and lets the IT team adapt and security-check the code; a hospital with no skilled IT staff should choose the commercial product for its guaranteed support.
parts.working:
Indicative content:
Commercial: licence fees for 60 users; guaranteed vendor support and updates; vendor responsible for meeting standards; source code hidden so hospital cannot fix or adapt it; locked in to vendor.
Free software: no licence fee (may still pay for support); source code available so IT staff can adapt it to local forms / check security themselves; community updates; quality and support may vary; hospital needs skilled staff; must still protect patient data whichever is chosen.
Mark bands: 5–6 balanced discussion of both options linked to the hospital, with a justified recommendation; 3–4 points on both options with some reference to the scenario, recommendation may be weak; 1–2 a few simple points, little or no justification.

practice.stem: Omar, a developer in Peshawar, writes a library for converting dates between the Gregorian and Hijri calendars. He is choosing between a permissive open source licence and a copyleft free software licence.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the choice of licence affects a company that wants to include the library in a closed-source (proprietary) product.
parts.answer:
1 mark each:
• under a permissive open source licence (e.g. MIT) the company may use and modify the library inside its proprietary product, usually only keeping the copyright notice
• it does not have to release its own source code
• under a copyleft free software licence (GPL), a product that includes and distributes the library must also be released under the GPL with its source code, so the company could not keep it closed

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one reason why Omar might prefer the copyleft licence.
parts.answer: It ensures improvements made by others remain available to everyone / prevents companies taking his work without giving back.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by artificial intelligence (AI).
parts.answer: The ability of a computer system to perform tasks normally needing human intelligence (e.g. recognising images, understanding speech, making decisions), often by learning from data / experience.
parts.working: 1 mark human-like tasks/intelligence; 1 mark learning/decision-making.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two examples of AI used by people in everyday life.
parts.answer: Any two: voice assistants; route-planning apps predicting traffic; recommendations on video/shopping sites; spam filters; face unlock on phones; machine translation.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A bank in Pakistan introduces an AI chatbot on its website and app to answer customers' questions in English and Urdu.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two benefits to the bank of using an AI chatbot.
parts.answer: e.g. available 24 hours; handles many customers at once; fewer call-centre staff needed, saving money; consistent answers.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two drawbacks for customers.
parts.answer: e.g. may not understand complex questions or regional languages/accents; frustrating with no human to talk to; may give wrong information; concerns about how conversation data is stored.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two ways AI can be used in healthcare.
parts.answer: e.g. analysing X-ray or scan images to spot disease; predicting which patients are at risk; chatbots answering basic health questions; scheduling appointments; drug discovery.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a doctor should still check an AI system's diagnosis.
parts.answer: AI can make mistakes (e.g. if trained on data that does not match local patients); a doctor is accountable and can consider the patient's full history / symptoms the AI did not see.
parts.working: 1 mark AI may be wrong/biased; 1 mark human judgement/accountability.

practice.stem: An agricultural research centre in Faisalabad releases a free smartphone app. A farmer photographs a cotton leaf and the app's AI identifies plant diseases and recommends a treatment.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two positive economic impacts of the app.
parts.answer: e.g. disease spotted early so less crop is lost and farmers earn more; less money wasted on spraying the wrong pesticide; higher yields help exports / food prices.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe one positive environmental impact of the app.
parts.answer: Pesticide is used only where and when needed, so less chemical runs off into soil and water.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe two possible problems with relying on the app.
parts.answer: e.g. misdiagnosis if the AI was trained mostly on images from other countries/crops; farmers without smartphones or internet are left out (digital divide); farmers may lose traditional expertise; data about farms may be misused.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A transport company plans to introduce self-driving electric taxis in Dubai.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe one social, one economic and one environmental impact of introducing self-driving taxis in the city.
parts.answer:
2 marks for each impact (1 identify, 1 develop):
Social: e.g. fewer accidents caused by driver error / tiredness, improving safety; mobility for elderly or disabled people; but questions over who is responsible in a crash.
Economic: e.g. taxi drivers lose jobs; new jobs in maintenance and software; lower fares as no driver wages.
Environmental: e.g. smoother driving and route optimisation reduce fuel use and emissions; but more journeys may increase congestion / energy use of data processing.
parts.working: Max 2 per category.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one negative environmental impact of developing and using large AI systems.
parts.answer: Training and running large AI models requires huge numbers of processors in data centres, which use a lot of electricity (often from fossil fuels) and water for cooling, increasing carbon emissions.
parts.working: 1 mark energy/water use; 1 mark consequence.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one way AI can have a positive environmental impact.
parts.answer: e.g. AI predicts electricity demand and solar/wind supply, so a grid can balance supply and waste less energy / AI optimises delivery routes, cutting fuel use.
parts.working: 1 mark application; 1 mark how it helps environment.

practice.stem: The government wants to use AI to predict floods along the river Indus during the monsoon season.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe three benefits of using AI to predict floods.
parts.answer:
1 mark each, max 3:
• analyses huge amounts of rainfall, river and satellite data faster than humans
• earlier, more accurate warnings so people can evacuate, saving lives
• authorities can plan where to send relief / protect crops and livestock
• models improve as they learn from each season's data

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one limitation of the AI predictions.
parts.answer: e.g. may be wrong for extreme events not in the training data; relies on sensors working; warnings must still reach people without phones.

practice.stem: An online retailer in Karachi replaces many of its warehouse staff with AI-controlled robots that pick and pack orders.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the economic impact of the AI warehouse robots on workers and the company.
parts.answer:
1 mark each, max 4:
• fewer jobs for manual pickers / packers, causing unemployment
• new skilled jobs created in maintaining robots and managing software
• workers need retraining
• company saves on wages and works 24 hours, increasing output
• high initial cost of robots and software
• fewer errors / faster deliveries increase sales
parts.working: At least one point about workers and one about the company for full marks.

practice.stem: An international airport in Lahore plans to use AI facial recognition so that passengers can board flights without showing a boarding pass.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the social impacts of using AI facial recognition at the airport.
parts.answer:
1 mark each, max 4:
• faster boarding / shorter queues for passengers
• improved security: wanted people identified automatically
• privacy: biometric data of every passenger is collected and stored, could be leaked or misused
• bias: systems trained on unbalanced data may misidentify people of some ethnic groups more often
• false matches may lead to innocent people being stopped
• people may feel constantly watched
parts.working: At least one positive and one negative needed for full marks.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two safeguards the airport should put in place.
parts.answer: e.g. delete images after the flight / store encrypted; human officer must confirm any match; test the system for bias across groups; tell passengers and offer an opt-out (manual check).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A multinational company in Dubai uses an AI system to screen job applications. The system was trained on CVs of people the company hired over the last ten years.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the AI system could become biased.
parts.answer: It learns from past hiring decisions; if previous recruiters favoured certain groups (e.g. men, graduates of certain universities), the AI learns to copy that pattern.
parts.working: 1 mark learns from historic data; 1 mark data reflects past bias.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one consequence of this bias for the company.
parts.answer: e.g. good candidates are rejected unfairly; less diverse workforce; legal action / damage to reputation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe two measures the company could take to reduce the risk.
parts.answer: e.g. remove names, gender and other irrelevant data before screening; audit outcomes regularly for different groups; train on balanced data; keep a human reviewer for final decisions; explain decisions to applicants.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A college in Lahore is deciding whether to allow students to use generative AI chatbots for homework and coursework.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the impact of generative AI tools on students and teachers at the college. Include benefits and drawbacks.
parts.answer: A balanced answer: generative AI gives instant explanations and practice, but students may submit AI-written work, receive wrong answers and fail to build their own skills; a sensible conclusion is to allow it for learning with clear rules (declare use, assessed work done under supervision).
parts.working:
Indicative points (1 mark each, max 5; at least one benefit and one drawback):
Benefits: instant explanations and feedback at any time; personalised practice questions; help for students with weaker English; saves teachers time preparing material.
Drawbacks: students may submit AI-written work as their own (academic dishonesty), so assessment becomes less reliable; AI can produce confident but wrong answers; students may not develop their own skills; unequal access to paid tools; privacy of data typed into the tool.
Reward a sensible conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why professional bodies such as the BCS or the IEEE publish codes of conduct for computing professionals.
parts.answer: To set standards of ethical behaviour that members must follow, protecting the public and clients and maintaining trust in / the reputation of the profession.
parts.working: 1 mark sets standards/guidance; 1 mark protects public / reputation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two principles that a computing professional following such a code is expected to keep.
parts.answer: Any two: act in the public interest (health, safety, environment); only work within own competence; be honest and avoid conflicts of interest; respect confidentiality / privacy; keep skills up to date; support colleagues; produce work of high quality.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two ethical responsibilities a software developer has towards the users of their software.
parts.answer: e.g. protect users' personal data / privacy; make software safe and reliable; be honest about what the software does; make it accessible.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why keeping technical skills up to date is part of acting ethically.
parts.answer: Out-of-date skills can lead to insecure or poor-quality software, harming clients and users; professionals should only work within their competence.

practice.stem: Hamza, a programmer at a software house in Lahore, discovers a serious security flaw in an online banking app two days before release. His manager tells him to ignore it so that the deadline is met.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain which ethical principles are involved and what Hamza should do.
parts.answer: Public interest and product quality are at stake; Hamza should report the flaw to his manager in writing and recommend fixing it or delaying the release, telling the client of the risk.
parts.working:
1 mark each, max 4:
• public interest: releasing software with a known security flaw puts users' data at risk
• product: professionals should ensure products meet the highest standards / are properly tested
• honesty to client: the client should be told about the flaw and the risk
• Hamza should report the problem to his manager in writing and recommend delaying the release or fixing it
• if ignored, he may escalate it rather than stay silent

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The ACM/IEEE Software Engineering Code of Ethics groups its rules under eight principles: Public, Client and Employer, Product, Judgement, Management, Profession, Colleagues, Self. Identify the principle that best matches each action.
(i) A developer refuses to sign off a design she believes is unsafe.
(ii) A team leader makes sure new staff are trained before they work on critical code.
(iii) A programmer takes an evening course to learn a new security technique.
(iv) A tester helps a junior colleague understand a difficult bug instead of blaming him.
parts.answer: (i) Judgement  (ii) Management  (iii) Self  (iv) Colleagues
parts.working: 1 mark each. Accept Public or Product for (i) if justified by safety.

practice.stem: Zainab works for a company that makes a free torch app. Her manager asks her to add code that secretly records users' locations so the data can be sold to advertisers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the ethical issues raised by this request and what Zainab should do.
parts.answer: The request breaches users' privacy and honesty (and probably data-protection law); Zainab should raise her concerns with her manager, propose asking users for clear consent, and refuse / report it if the company insists.
parts.working:
Indicative points (1 mark each, max 5):
• collecting location data without consent breaches users' privacy and may break data-protection law
• it is dishonest to users — the public interest principle is put below the employer's wishes
• users of a free torch app would not expect location tracking
• selling data could put users at risk (stalking, profiling)
• Zainab's duty to her employer does not override her duty to the public
• she should raise the concern with her manager, explain the legal/ethical risks and suggest asking users for clear consent
• if the company insists, she may refuse / report it, as allowed by professional codes
Reward a reasoned conclusion.
